headline: Bronte Capital uses AMP's 40-year decline as a cautionary tale of management failure through short-term incentive misalignment destroying a once-dominant Australian financial institution
reasoning: AMP was one of five pillars of the Australian financial system in the mid-1980s, with a captive tied-planner network that dominated the Australian savings market. Open-architecture competitors (e.g. MLC) began winning share because they offered a wider product menu; this continued for four decades. AMP management knew that opening up its network was the right strategic response but refused to do so because it would have halved profits in the short term. No CEO was willing to take that pain, so the decision was deferred until AMP became irrelevant. Bronte Capital draws the explicit contrast between AMP's passive decline and Google's proactive pivot into AI, using AMP as the archetypal case of bad short-term incentives producing atrocious long-term outcomes.
quote: AMP management knew that this was coming — and that the right thing to do was to open up the AMP network. But the moment they did so, 30-50% of the money would leave to other providers. No AMP CEO wanted to make the decision that would halve profits so they all deferred the decision. For 40 years. Until they were irrelevant. Bad short-term incentives led to atrocious long-term outcomes. Google faces a similar threat — but its management is superior to AMP's.

headline: Bronte Capital warns AI-driven labour displacement could drive OECD unemployment to 10–20% in the short term if AI achieves the revenue required to justify its CapEx
reasoning: To justify US$1.8 trillion in annual AI token revenue, businesses must save roughly double that amount in labour costs, implying displacement of nearly 10% of the entire OECD wage bill of ~US$40 trillion within four to five years. Bronte notes Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei previously warned AI could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs, potentially driving unemployment to 10–20%, a number Bronte believes was not arbitrary. Workers are unlikely to be displaced unless AI saves at least 50% of their cost, given the friction of hiring, onboarding new processes, and change management. In the long run, technology historically drives total factor productivity gains as displaced labour finds new uses, but the short-term adjustment could be severe.
quote: Alas $1.8 trillion per annum of token spend has to displace a lot of labour to be justified. The total wage bill of the United States in 2025 was between $12 trillion and $13 trillion, based on the Bureau of Labor Statistics' employment and wages data set (with the range of uncertainty resulting from seasonal adjustments). With the help of AI, we worked out the wage bill for the OECD as a whole is likely under $40 trillion. You are not going to sack a worker or change your process in the short term unless the AI saves you 50%... That means we will need labour savings of maybe double the $1.8 trillion in token spend in the next four or five years — nearly 10% of the entire OECD's wage bill.

headline: Bronte Capital continuing to trim Alphabet as core search business faces existential disruption risk despite admiration for management quality.
reasoning: Bronte Capital holds Google but is actively trimming the position. They view Google's core search business as facing potentially total disruption from AI, and the company's response — spending $180-190 billion in 2026 alone, exceeding its cumulative profits over the entire 2010s — is a massive bet with highly uncertain returns. They note Google has even had to raise cash despite being one of the most cash-generative businesses in history. The team admits genuine uncertainty about the stock's value, seeing binary outcomes: either Google becomes the provider of the world's finest superintelligence, or its core business is destroyed and it has wasted all the money it made during its good years. They are 'squeamish' about the outcome and continue to reduce exposure.
quote: We love Google as a company and think its management team may be amongst the best assembled in the history of capitalism. But the stock is abnormally risky. The core business is being disrupted, and that disruption may be total. The company's reaction is to spend its entire accumulated profits on disrupting itself with no certainty about the outcome, or even whether there is any profit at the end. We keep trimming the stock. And we know in the end we will be squeamish about the outcome. At the one end Google is the provider of the world's finest superintelligence, and is the central company in displacing a good slice of the world's labor (while privatising the profits). At the other end, the company will have its core business destroyed and will have wasted all of the money it made during the good years. We own it. We genuinely have no idea what it is worth.

headline: Bronte Capital warns AI CapEx boom of up to US$3 trillion may not generate adequate returns, drawing parallels with the fibre-optic bust

At the end of this, once we, as a society, find new uses for all that displaced labour, there should be a massive rise of total factor productivity. headline: Bronte Capital continuing to trim Alphabet as core search business faces existential disruption risk while AI capex dwarfs cumulative historical profits.

headline: Concedes position was badly mismanaged at peak valuation, citing failure to sell at 10x revenue despite recognising expensive multiple
reasoning: Bronte owned Spirax as a high-quality business in their sweet spot — a company selling mission-critical small parts of large, valuable processes with high switching costs. The Watson Marlow peristaltic pump division, which sells highly specified tubing into biotech drug manufacturing, consistently earns margins above 30%. However, Covid-era supply-chain disruptions caused massive over-ordering of consumable tubing (at ~50% incremental margins), which inflated reported growth and margins materially beyond the sustainable run-rate and briefly pushed the stock to 10x revenues. Bronte knew the valuation was stretched but failed to recognise how much of the apparent quality improvement was temporary, and because the position was performing well they turned a blind eye. They sold some near the top but not enough, and bought back too early on the way down, costing the fund several percentage points. They remain confident Spirax is a great underlying business but acknowledge the valuation discipline failure was significant.
quote: Our mistake was underrating the importance of this tubing kit, and what that implies. The tubes are mission-critical, so the global supply-chain scare during Covid — which was particularly acute in biotech as demand rose — caused people to over-order. The over-ordering was large and probably carried 50% incremental margins. This caused Spirax to look faster-growing, and with better-improving margins, than the underlying business would normally possess. The stock traded briefly at 10x revenue — a figure inflated by the temporary lift from macro conditions. We knew it was trading at an expensive multiple, but we failed to see that this was boosted by supply-chain/Covid factors. Because the position was doing so well, we turned a blind eye to the valuation. We should have sold. Obviously we were smashed. We did sell some near the top, but nowhere near enough. And we bought some too early on the way down. We remain confident this is a great business, but we were dopey about global trends and valuation.

headline: Bronte Capital candidly acknowledges errors in both the long book and the short book, noting the long book has been a recent problem while the short book has performed well since mid-October 2025

headline: Bronte Capital argues that negative interest rates pre-Covid were the key driver of quality-stock outperformance, and their reversal explains subsequent underperformance of quality portfolios
reasoning: Between 2010 and 2020, long-dated interest rates went negative in large parts of the world, especially Europe, causing high-quality companies to appear extraordinarily valuable because low discount rates dramatically inflate the present value of far-future earnings. Bronte uses the contrast between Coca-Cola (valued for 2065 earnings) and a coal mine (valued for near-term cash flows) to illustrate the sensitivity. Post-Covid, discount rates reappeared and quality stocks underperformed sharply. Bronte characterises negative interest rates as a pre-Covid anomaly and notes this dynamic explains a substantial portion of both Fund A's outperformance and subsequent underperformance, as well as their own long-book results.
quote: Between 2010 and 2020, long-dated interest rates went negative in large parts of the world — notably Europe (which is important for our discussion). High-quality companies in these markets thus became very valuable because discount rates have an outsized impact on the perceived present value (e.g. stock price) of their expected future earnings. To explain with examples: You buy Coca-Cola for its earnings in 2065 — and at a low (even negative) discount rate, you value those far-future earnings very highly. By contrast, when you invest in a coal mine, you are buying it for earnings next year and the year after — because you can all but assume there are no earnings in 2035 — so the discount rate matters far less. In the post-Covid economy, discount rates reappeared. (In retrospect, negative interest rates appear to be a pre-Covid anomaly.)

headline: Bronte Capital highlights West Perth mining promoters as archetypal short candidates where rising gold prices create persistent short squeeze risk
reasoning: Bronte uses the example of a gold mine controlled by a repeat promoter based in West Perth — a geography it associates with many mining frauds — to illustrate the three ways a short thesis can fail: the gold is real, the hype escalates further, or the gold price rises and lifts all gold stocks regardless of asset quality. The firm notes that the third failure mode — macro gold price appreciation — has recently been the dominant source of losses on the short book. The firm manages this risk through extreme diversification across hundreds of positions.
quote: A gold mine is controlled by a repeat promoter of failed companies who is based in West Perth, the hometown of many mining frauds. The company claims to have 2 million ounces of gold somewhere in remote Western Australia. We short the company on the assumption that given the people involved, the claims about the mine probably are vastly overstated. There are three main ways we can be wrong: A. The gold really is there, and they find more. B. The gold isn't there, but they hype it even more by suggesting they have 10 million ounces. The market believes them and the stock goes up. C. The 2 million (fictitious) ounces never get developed, but the gold price goes up and the stock goes along with all other gold stocks. All three of these ways have cost us at various times. Lately, the third is (by far) the dominant problem.

headline: Bronte Capital issues formal thesis update on Spirax, admitting both macro (UK listing discount) and stock-specific (valuation discipline) errors
reasoning: Bronte frames their Spirax experience as two distinct error types: a Type A macro mistake (buying UK-listed quality stocks into a period of negative European discount rates that later reversed) and a Type B stock-specific mistake (failing to sell when valuation reached 10x revenues). On the macro side, they acknowledge that UK capital markets have suffered relative to US markets, and that European quality stocks broadly underperformed as discount rates normalised from deeply negative levels. On the stock-specific side, they admit that 10x revenue is almost never justifiable, citing Scott McNeally's well-known critique of Sun Microsystems, and that the conditions that can justify such a multiple — very high incremental margins, fast sustainable growth — were emphatically absent from Spirax. They view the error as costing several percentage points of the fund and commit to applying this lesson going forward.
quote: It was stupid not to sell all of our Spirax at 10x revenue. Few businesses can justify a 10x sales valuation... This makes 10x sales hard to justify, but we can, at least, answer Scott McNeally's question: Investors were thinking the company had very high incremental margins, was growing fast, and would continue to grow — things that were true of Microsoft but not of Sun Microsystems. It was emphatically not-true of Spirax. Our failure to see this cost several percentage points of the fund.

headline: Bronte Capital trimming Alphabet position after it has more than doubled from its May low; now views it as a better-than-average business at a better-than-market price rather than a bargain
reasoning: Bronte originally bought Google when it appeared to be a better-than-average business at a market multiple with what looked like a grab-bag of vanity projects. Those 'vanity projects' — Waymo (self-driving), TPU chips, and AI/Gemini — have turned out to be highly prescient and valuable. Waymo appears to work and is scaling, Google has what Bronte believes is the best AI model, and TPUs are being sold to Meta and Nvidia. The stock has more than doubled since its May low. However, it is now trading at a better-than-market price, so Bronte no longer loves it and is likely to trim further. The AI threat to core search is being addressed via Gemini, which integrates advertiser links into its itinerary outputs.
quote: Google, however, was addressing the threat well... What has really changed at Google is that these 'vanity projects' have turned out to be highly prescient and valuable bets on the future. Self-driving cars (Waymo; W in the alphabet) looks like it works and is about to take over the world. This should make a large but indeterminate amount of money. The self-teaching chess engine was a precursor to today's AI models — and Google already appears to have the best AI model. The TPU chips, which we originally thought might be useful for Waymo, are now apparently extremely useful for artificial intelligence. Alphabet is selling TPUs to Meta (Facebook) and Nvidia. Google is still a better-than-average business — but it is trading at a better-than-market price. We still like the stock, but we don't love it. If anything, we are likely to trim a little more out.

headline: Bronte Capital acknowledges painful underperformance on short book through mid-October but affirms conviction that speculative longs will eventually fall 90%+ from peak
reasoning: Bronte confesses that over 50 of its 500+ shorts had the kind of parabolic chart seen in names like Oklo, Centrus, and IonQ — stocks up 100-300% YTD that peaked around October 14. The fund received redemptions and clients questioned the strategy. Since mid-October the short book has performed well on almost every day except Thanksgiving week. Bronte reaffirms that stocks currently down 40% from peak but still up 100%+ YTD will eventually trade well below their January 1 price — the path to 90% down from peak runs through the current -40% level. The firm cautions it would be premature to declare victory as the stocks' holders still have bragging rights.
quote: Alas — and this is a confession — the 500-odd stocks we were short included over 50 stocks with this sort of chart... In mid-October we were not feeling very good, and some of our clients thought we were idiots. We had redemptions. But since mid-October, the short book has felt at least relatively good every day except three sessions during Thanksgiving week... We think that the vast majority of the 'peaked mid-October but still up over 100 percent' stocks will eventually trade well below their 1 January price. We think the people who own these stocks (and who are currently exhibiting 'extreme fear') have a reason to be fearful. These stocks, now down 40 percent, will soon be down 90 percent. At the risk of jinxing it, we want to remind people that a stock that is down 90 percent is one that was down 40 percent, and then halved, and then lost a further two-thirds.

headline: Bronte Capital notes the paradox of CNN extreme fear index at market near all-time highs, attributing it to retail investor psychology around speculative stock losses
reasoning: Despite the US market sitting less than 2% off all-time highs at month-end, CNN's greed-and-fear index is showing extreme fear. Bronte argues this is explained by the sharp reversal in speculative retail-favoured stocks since mid-October: many retail investors are individually down 40%+ on their high-profile picks even as market indices remain elevated. The aggregates have not meaningfully declined, but individual retail investors who owned speculative names are feeling battered. Bronte views this as psychologically driven rather than reflective of macro deterioration.
quote: This is one of the more peculiar markets we have known. The press and the language of this market is about fear. CNN's well publicised greed-and-fear index is showing extreme fear... And yet, at month's end, the market is less than 2% off all-time highs. Extreme fear is something you would expect near market bottoms, when falling prices have deflated retail investors' optimism — not market tops. With the market less than 2% off a high that we could only have dreamt about for the past decade, you would expect to see elation, not fear.

headline: Bronte Capital short IonQ and quantum computing stocks broadly, categorising them as 'science experiments' unlikely to produce a working quantum computer in 15 years
reasoning: Bronte describes IonQ and the quantum computing sector as 'science experiments' with aggregate market caps that at peak approached $100 billion, yet with no credible path to a workable quantum computer in the next fifteen years. IonQ peaked on October 14 and is down 40% since. The firm notes these stocks are heavily promoted to and owned by retail speculators, and places them in the category of 'overhyped stocks' that will eventually trade well below their January 1 price.
quote: The quantum-computing stocks have similar charts. IonQ is the biggest pure-play quantum computing stock. It is only up 8% year-to-date — but it is down 40% since its peak on, yes, October 14... We put the quantum stocks, for instance, in the camp of 'science experiments'. They have not shown anything suggesting a credible possibility of producing a workable quantum computer in the next fifteen years, yet they have a very high aggregate market cap (at peak almost $100 billion) and made many promises that few people are qualified to assess.

headline: Bronte Capital broadly short quantum computing sector, viewing the entire category as hype with no viable commercial product within 15 years
reasoning: Bronte maintains a broad short position across the quantum computing sector, which it characterises as 'science experiments' making promises few people are qualified to assess. At peak, the aggregate market cap of quantum stocks approached $100 billion, which Bronte views as wholly unjustified. We put the quantum stocks, for instance, in the camp of 'science experiments'. They have not shown anything suggesting a credible possibility of producing a workable quantum computer in the next fifteen years, yet they have a very high aggregate market cap (at peak almost $100 billion) and made many promises that few people are qualified to assess.

headline: Bronte Capital views MP Materials as grossly overvalued at ~$15bn market cap despite having a real mine, down 40% from October 14 peak

quote: MP Materials is a producer of rare earths ore. The company has a mine, so there is some revenue — though nothing close to supporting the market cap of almost $15 billion. The stock is up over 300% year-to-date — but it, too, peaked on October 14. MP is down 40% from its peak.

headline: Bronte Capital short Centrus Energy, a highly-leveraged nuclear fuel company at high multiples down 40% from peak but still up 200% YTD
reasoning: Centrus Energy is described as highly leveraged and trading at high multiples, with a market cap of $4.7 billion after falling about 40% from its mid-October peak. quote: Centrus Energy Corp, a highly-leveraged U.S. nuclear fuel company trading at high multiples, has a market cap of $4.7 billion — after falling about 40% from its peak in mid-October. The stock remains up over 200% year-to-date.

headline: Bronte Capital identifies mid-October 2025 as a turning point where speculative retail-driven stocks peaked and began a sharp reversal
reasoning: Bronte Capital observes that dozens of high-flying speculative stocks — including small nuclear, quantum computing, rare earths, and AI names — all peaked around October 14, 2025, after rising 100-300% year-to-date. Since that peak, many have fallen 40-60%. The firm argues this explains the paradox of CNN's 'extreme fear' index sitting alongside markets near all-time highs: many retail investors are individually down heavily even as indices hold up. Bronte believes the majority of these 'peaked mid-October but still up 100%+' stocks will eventually trade well below their January 1 price — potentially down 90% from peak. The firm acknowledges it was short over 50 such stocks and suffered through the painful run-up before mid-October.
quote: The chart pattern is common. We could play this game with dozens of stocks that are up 100-200% year-to-date but have lost 40-60% since a peak on October 14. Many more peaked on days other than October 14 — but the turnaround on or about that day was sharp. None of these stocks actually matter in terms of market cap or the indices. NVIDIA has a $4 trillion market cap. Google and Apple have market caps of over $3 trillion. But these smaller stocks matter psychologically — especially for retail investors.

headline: Bronte Capital views SoundHound AI as an unconvincing AI story, down 50%+ from its October 14 peak and negative year-to-date

headline: Bronte Capital views Givaudan as probably overpriced relative to DSM-Firmenich's superior perfume and beauty business
reasoning: Bronte uses Givaudan's EV/sales multiple of 4.6x as a valuation benchmark for the Firmenich perfume and beauty segment, but explicitly states they believe Givaudan is probably overpriced. They argue that Firmenich's perfume business is better than Givaudan's on a per-sales-dollar basis due to a measurable technical lead in perfumery, suggesting the market is rewarding the wrong company with the premium multiple.
quote: We think Givaudan is probably overpriced — but we think that Firmenich's perfume and beauty business is sales dollar-for-sales dollar better than Givaudan. We think they have a technical lead and we can measure that. We think over time that will translate into better margins.

headline: Bronte Capital views IFF as a poorly managed business that has failed to recover despite an excellent underlying industry position.
reasoning: IFF was once the dominant player in the flavours and fragrances industry, benefiting from proprietary fragrances (tetramethyl acetyloctahydronaphthalenes) that helped win client briefs. However, a double-whammy of patent cliffs and slowing industry sales growth exposed deep mismanagement. The company has gone through eight CEOs in 27 years, mostly external hires with constantly changing strategic direction. Despite the underlying business quality, the stock is only up approximately 25% since 1998. The view is that without the excellent underlying business, this level of mismanagement would have bankrupted the company.
quote: IFF has gone through eight CEOs over 27 years trying to fix this business. Most CEOs were external hires, and there were many strategic changes in direction as CEOs came and went. Generally it was terribly managed, and had the underlying business not been excellent this level of mismanagement would have bankrupted the company. We will come back later in this note to one of IFF's strategic changes of direction.

headline: Bronte Capital is cautious on the animal nutrition and bulk vitamin businesses within DSM-Firmenich due to Chinese competition and poor feedlot economics
reasoning: DSM's legacy animal nutrition business — which provides amino acid and vitamin optimisation supplements to large-scale farming operations — sits in the less attractive part of the specialty chemicals spectrum, sold by the drum or truckload rather than as high-value 'magic pixie dust.' The vitamin segment has been commoditised by low-cost Chinese producers and has produced losses. Feedlot profitability is currently weak, depressing demand for optimisation supplements, though margins are said to be marginally improving at time of writing. Bronte values these businesses at well over 1x sales and reasonably 1.5x sales in normalised conditions, but they are clearly not the reason for owning DSM-Firmenich.
quote: The agricultural business aspired to optimise feedstock for animals... This was probably sold by the drum or the truckload to large chicken farms. It was somewhere on the 'specialty spectrum,' but not at the very good end of it. This is no recombinant hyaluronic acid... It wasn't an awful business, but then again, it hasn't been great lately, either. This business is going to be better when the price of meat is high relative to the price of grain and feed-lot farming is profitable. That is not now, although at pixel time the economics are getting marginally better. There was a vitamin business there too... Either way this business has been commoditised. The Chinese make this product cheaply and well — and competing against them has not been much fun.

headline: Bronte Capital draws a negative structural analogy between IFF's DuPont-heritage texture businesses and dsm-firmenich's taste, texture and health segment
reasoning: Bronte notes that dsm-firmenich's taste, texture and health segment is burdened by texture businesses similar to the DuPont-origin businesses at IFF, which it uses as a reference point for lower-quality revenue that dilutes the aggregate segment valuation. The comparison is used to explain why the high-value flavours revenue within the segment is obscured by lower-quality components.
quote: It is unfortunately aggregated with some texture business (similar to the DuPont businesses at IFF) and it is aggregated as taste, texture and health.

headline: Bronte Capital views Firmenich as technical leader in fragrances and expects supernormal returns following heavy R&D investment
reasoning: Firmenich, traditionally the number-three player in the F&F oligopoly, recognised a decade ago that it was falling behind Givaudan on technical matters and invested heavily to close the gap, acquiring companies like Senomyx and hiring top scientists. Bronte believes this spending mostly worked, and that Firmenich now has a larger library of scent ingredients than both Givaudan and IFF, making it the technical leader in fragrances specifically. The firm expects this technical leadership to generate supernormal returns going forward. The investment constrained dividends and hurt some family shareholders, but the long-term positioning is viewed favourably. Firmenich is considered the leader in fine fragrances and laundry — the two biggest fragrance segments.
quote: Going out on a limb though, and with our patchouli-price reservation in mind, we think that Firmenich's spending mostly worked. The company has demonstrated many products like the recombinant patchouli, and has a larger library of scent ingredients than Givaudan and IFF... This, however, is a key assertion about where the company is: We think it is now the technical leader in fragrances (not flavours) and that this should generate supernormal returns in future.

headline: Bronte Capital notes Novonesis is the global leader in specialty recombinant enzymes, having acquired DSM's enzyme business
reasoning: Bronte flags Novonesis (the merged entity of Novozymes and Chr. Hansen, formerly Novazymes in the letter) as the global leader in specialty recombinant enzymes, with DSM having sold its enzyme business — described as the highest-value part of DSM's legacy nutrition segment — to Novonesis. The comment is contextual and descriptive rather than an explicit buy call, but it indicates Bronte views recombinant enzyme capability as highly valuable and positions Novonesis as a quality operator in that niche.
quote: The highest-value bit of this — which was enzymes (sometimes made recombinantly) to optimise feedstock — was sold to their partner Novazymes (now Novonesis). Novazymes is the global leader in making specialty recombinant enzymes.

headline: Bronte Capital identifies ETFs and zero-dated options (0DTEs) as the two main accelerants fueling the current retail market mania
reasoning: Bronte Capital argues that every retail market mania needs an enabler, citing tulip contracts, 1920s margin lending, and E*TRADE in the 1990s as historical examples. Today's two main accelerants are ETFs (which have evolved into leveraged, inverse, and single-stock instruments) and 0DTE options (which were introduced during COVID and now comprise over 60% of S&P 500 options volume in 2025). Social media amplifies these tools by creating constant sentiment feedback loops and distortions.
quote: Every retail market mania needs an enabler. These have ranged from 17th-century tulip contracts to margin lending in the 1920s and online brokerages like E*TRADE in the 1990s. The current market bubble has two main accelerants: the ETF and the zero-dated option (0DTE). ETFs, once a simple index-following tool, have evolved into leveraged, inverse, and single-stock instruments, amplifying exposure to volatile themes like crypto and AI. They simplify complex options for novice investors. 0DTEs, introduced during COVID, are purely for intraday trading, causing extreme volatility as marketmakers hedge aggressively. In 2025, 0DTE options comprised over 60% of total S&P 500 options volume.

headline: Bronte Capital notes it was profitably short all three synthetic biology companies (Ginkgo, Intrexon, Amyris) where Firmenich's chief scientist previously worked
reasoning: Bronte Capital was profitably short Ginkgo, Intrexon, and Amyris — all companies where Firmenich's chief scientist Dr. Sarah Reisinger previously worked. The firm characterises all three as 'science experiments with real scientists and less-than-wonderful management.' Their only viable revenue model was outsourced recombinant manufacturing for the fragrances industry, not standalone businesses. This context is offered as background on Firmenich's scientific hiring rather than an active current position.
quote: For reference, we were profitably short all three companies where Dr. Reisinger had worked. In all cases they were science experiments with real scientists and less-than-wonderful management. The only worthwhile revenue model these companies ever developed was outsourced (often recombinant) manufacturing of products for the fragrances industry.

headline: Bronte Capital sees an unusually strong opportunity set on both the long and short sides despite recent losses, expecting the current environment to be rewarding longer-term
reasoning: Bronte Capital observes that normally when short-side opportunity is great, long-side opportunity is poor. However, the current market presents attractive opportunities simultaneously on both sides of the book — a rare configuration. While this has been difficult in the short term due to the junk rally squeezing positions, the fund believes this dual opportunity set should be 'wonderful' over a longer horizon. The fund expects speculation to eventually run its course as retail investors suffer losses.
quote: Normally we think if the opportunity set on the short side is great, then the opportunity on the long side is poor. In other words, when the market is high people will experiment in junk stocks. That does not appear to be the case at the moment. The opportunity set is very good both on the long side and the short side. That should be wonderful for us (longer-term), but short term it has been difficult.

headline: Bronte Capital flags OpenAI's $300B Oracle services commitment relative to only $13B revenue as symptomatic of current market excess, though views it as less egregious than Korean stock-trading room speculation
reasoning: Bronte Capital uses the OpenAI-Oracle deal as one example of the 'new normal', noting that OpenAI committed to buy $300 billion in services from Oracle despite having only $13 billion in revenue. They acknowledge this is at least plausible given OpenAI has a real product and real revenue. They contrast this with Korean stock-trading rooms where stocks with no obvious short interest can rise 4-5x because they become an 'esport', catching Bronte's 500+ shorts.
quote: The most told one is that OpenAI agreed to buy $300 billion in services from Oracle despite OpenAI having only $13 billion in revenue. That story, though, is plausible; OpenAI at least has a real product and real revenue. Far sillier is what is going on in Korean stock-trading rooms. Stock and crypto trading is an esport, watched and imitated by adoring fans. This is amusing until you are short a nonsense stock with no obvious short interest that suddenly rises 4-5x because it is the new traded thing.

headline: Bronte Capital is long Regeneron, citing its potential to reverse severe allergies affecting hundreds of millions worldwide
reasoning: Bronte Capital expresses optimism about Regeneron's capability to reverse severe allergies, which affect hundreds of millions of people globally. This is cited as part of their long quality book thesis, representing a high-quality company with a genuine medical innovation story. quote: Regeneron will be capable of reversing severe allergies, which affect hundreds of millions of people worldwide.

headline: Bronte Capital sees current market as a late-stage mania with AI and SAAS buzzword stocks likely to fall 90% within a few years
reasoning: Bronte Capital describes the current environment as the sharp end of a wild bull market, comparing it to December 2000. They identify stocks that should be down 90% within a few years as easy to find on the short side ('like shooting fish in a barrel'), but note that these shorts continue to trade against them in the near term. They believe the mania will end but are uncertain of timing and are managing through the pain.
quote: At the moment, finding stocks that will be down 90 percent within a few years — that is, what should be very good shorts — is like shooting fish in a barrel. We used precisely that simile in the December 2000 letter — and we appended the tart rejoinder 'except that the fish shoot back'. They will stop shooting someday shortly. They are shooting back now — and with just as much intensity as then.

headline: Bronte Capital puzzled by Givaudan's CEO transition and questions valuation at 4.6x EV/revenue
reasoning: Givaudan is described as a high-quality flavours and fragrances company with EBIT margins in the high teens for most of the past 25 years, never exceeding 20%. The company has diversified into adjacencies such as recombinant hyaluronic acid production. However, the firm expresses uncertainty around the incoming CEO, who is being appointed from Danone — an outsider appointment typically made when a business is struggling, which doesn't appear to be the case here. At 4.6x EV/revenue, the valuation is only justified if Givaudan continues to grow sharply. The departing CEO Giles Andrier was prescient in rejecting the IFF-style strategy of merging with commodity ingredient businesses.
quote: We are a little puzzled by Givaudan lately though. Giles Andrier is retiring and the company is appointing an outsider — in this case someone from Danone (the yogurt maker). Usually you appoint an outsider to shake things up when things are not going well — and there is little evidence that Givaudan is travelling badly. The stock is not cheap. EBIT margins have been high teens for most of the last twenty five years. Margins have never been above twenty percent. The stock is priced at 4.6 EV to revenue. This makes sense only if you think Givaudan will continue to grow sharply.

headline: Views as deeply undervalued at 1.6x EV/sales with most of its business historically generating >16% margins
reasoning: Bronte Capital argues dsm-firmenich is trading at just 1.6x EV/sales despite most of its business historically generating margins above 16%, and believes the stock will reach 11x earnings or better quickly. The perfume and beauty business (Firmenich) is assessed as superior to Givaudan on a per-sales-dollar basis, with a measurable 15-year technical lead that should translate into better margins over time. The flavours, taste, texture and health segment contributes over 2.5 billion euro in high-value revenue once the troubled vitamin business is excluded. Management is seen as highly rational — high-grading the portfolio by selling animal products businesses and buying back stock — and the balance sheet is virtually debt-free. The main headwinds are Firmenich family shareholder dissatisfaction and a 'show-me' problem on earnings growth caused by the vitamin segment drag, which Bronte acknowledges has kept the stock falling even as they've held. A large disclosed short position (attributed to Ilex Capital in London) is noted but Bronte says they have been unable to learn the bear case.
quote: We think Givaudan is probably overpriced — but we think that Firmenich's perfume and beauty business is sales dollar-for-sales dollar better than Givaudan. We think they have a 15 technical lead and we can measure that. We think over time that will translate into better margins. On top of this is a flavours business... The full segment has 3.2 billion euro in revenue — and if you take off the vitamin business (which may be worth very little), there is still well over 2.5 billon euro in high-value revenue here... The whole enterprise has an EV-to-sales at 1.6 times and most of the business has traditionally had margins above 16%. No matter how we add it up, this is inexpensive. It will wind up being 11 times earnings or better very quickly. Moreover, the management seem highly rational. They are high-grading their business, selling some animal products businesses and mostly buying back their own stock... We love the stock. We do not see how you can lose from here.

headline: Bronte Capital views quality European stocks as objectively inexpensive and a key long opportunity, with some at 2011 valuations
reasoning: Bronte Capital describes the long book opportunity set as much better than it was in early 2021 and specifically highlights quality European stocks as objectively cheap, with some trading at 2011 valuations. They express a desire to get even longer European quality stocks but are constrained by their focus on managing the short book. They contrast this with the early 2021 period when 'old fashioned non-mania stocks' were only cheap relative to bonds.
quote: This time we think some of our long book — especially the quality European stocks — is objectively inexpensive. Some of it is at 2011 valuations. We have an example attached at the end of this letter. The stock at the end of this letter is not the only really attractive European long. We would love to get even longer quality European stocks.

headline: Bronte Capital is long Alphabet, believing it will master self-driving and successfully defend its core search business from AI disruption
reasoning: Bronte Capital holds Alphabet as a long quality position, expressing optimism that the company will master autonomous driving and also address the threat that new AI-powered search poses to its core advertising business. This reflects the fund's view that Alphabet is a high-quality, durable business capable of navigating technological disruption. It is cited as a blue-chip holding they would not want to sell to speculate in junk.
quote: Alphabet (Google) will master self-drive. It will also ameliorate the threat to its core business from new artificial intelligence search.

headline: Bronte Capital describes a market environment that is actively hostile to their long-short strategy, requiring significant risk cutting while both long and short books are viewed as simultaneously attractive.
reasoning: The fund notes a rare situation where both the long and short books are seen as attractive at the same time, which should bode well for future returns. However, the current market requires active risk cutting due to the hostile environment. Bronte is also working on a mathematical hedge involving active trading of approximately a thousand stocks, designed to improve correlation between the long and short books, though implementation risk and slippage between back-test and live trading remain concerns.
quote: This is one of the few times where we find the longs and the shorts in our book simultaneously attractive. This should bode well for the future. One day we hope the lack of correlation in our book is for better and not for worse. That said, we have to get through to the future — and that involves for the moment quite a lot of risk cutting. This market is actively hostile to us. Longer term, we would like a better mathematical hedge to ensure that our long book is better correlated to our short book.

headline: Bronte Capital notes structural shift in F&F industry toward recombinant ingredients, favouring companies with superior synthetic biology capabilities
reasoning: The flavours and fragrances industry is undergoing a structural shift toward recombinant (synthetic biology) production of ingredients, which are often cheaper, environmentally less destructive, and can be made without allergens. Companies that have invested in this technology — such as Givaudan and Firmenich — are better positioned than those that have not. The sector is also benefiting from a post-Covid recovery in fine fragrances, driven by social media influencers who have successfully sold fragrances online to consumers who have never smelled them. This reverses a prior multi-year trend of flavours growing faster than fragrances, partly because fragrances were hard to sell online.
quote: Recombinant ingredients are often much cheaper (and environmentally less destructive) than natural ingredients — but they can also be made without the allergenic properties of some of the natural ingredients. The recombinant product is cheaper and better... During Covid the fragrance industry started selling fine fragrances online to people who never smelled them. We are not marketing people and can't really explain how it is done but somehow influencers in social media achieved this.

headline: Bronte Capital views CoreWeave as a poster child of the current AI mania, with the stock's extreme borrow costs and leveraged ETF engineering highlighting the speculative excess
reasoning: CoreWeave began as a crypto miner, pivoted to AI data centres, and became heavily reliant on Microsoft as a customer while using leverage to buy more Nvidia chips. Its IPO was dramatically scaled back (raising $1.5B vs a $2.5B target at $40/share vs $55 marketed), yet the stock subsequently ran to $187. The 150-200% annualised borrow cost on the stock enabled Wall Street professionals to extract approximately $100 million by creating 2x leveraged ETFs funded via stock-lending swaps. Bronte Capital uses this as an illustration of the 'new normal' in retail mania and financial engineering, not as a position they hold.
quote: After the IPO it became a retail favourite. One retail investor with a large social media following observed that it was good to buy a stock that had unlimited demand for its product. The stock peaked at $187 a share — amazing given the IPO was dramatically scaled back only a few months ago... Because of this the borrow cost in the stock market went as high as 200% and was above 150% for a couple of months... ETF providers started offering 2x levered Coreweave ETFs designed to deliver 2x the Coreweave return to unit holders. These ETFs raised over $200 million... On our estimate they pocketed about $100 million. It was an astonishingly profitable deal for the stock-lenders.

headline: Bronte Capital notes that the opportunity set is unusually strong on both the long and short side simultaneously, but short-term losses are mounting due to low correlation between longs and shorts
reasoning: Bronte Capital observes that normally a great short opportunity set implies a poor long opportunity set (high market conditions push capital into junk). Currently both sides are attractive, which should be good long-term but has been difficult short-term because longs and shorts in the portfolio have very low correlation, meaning the hedges are not working and losses are accumulating on both sides until the mania ends.
quote: The opportunity set is very good both on the long side and the short side. That should be wonderful for us (longer-term), but short term it has been difficult. Longs and shorts in our portfolio have particularly low correlation (which when you are losing money is known as 'the hedges are not working').

headline: Bronte Capital views IFF as value trap after DuPont acquisition destroyed value and forced sale of crown-jewel assets
reasoning: IFF's $26.5bn acquisition of DuPont's Nutrition & Biosciences business is described as its biggest strategic blunder, against a current market cap of only $16bn and EV of $22bn. The cultures of the two businesses — one with 30% gross margins and commodity-like sales, the other with 50% gross margins and artistic sales — were incompatible, as Givaudan's CEO had predicted at the time. IFF became a forced seller of assets including the highly innovative Lucas Meyer cosmetics business. While EBIT margins were previously around 20%, they have fallen to high-single-digit, and at 1.9x EV/sales the stock is not obviously a good buy given that the crown jewels have been sold.
quote: The pricing of IFF stock IFF's stock has (deservedly) had a rough time of it. The stock now looks inexpensive. EV to sales is now 1.9 times. EBIT margins used to be about 20% (higher even than Givaudan) and the company did worthwhile research. headline: Bronte Capital views the flavours and fragrances industry as a structurally attractive sector exhibiting the 'trifecta' of high-quality business characteristics.
reasoning: The F&F sector provides a small but important part of big consumer products, has high switching costs due to brand-fragrance linkage, and is a consumable — all hallmarks of a high-quality business. Fragrance may represent only 3% of the cost of a product like Dove soap, yet the brand is entirely dependent on it, giving fragrance houses strong pricing power. Growth slowed in developed markets after 2000 but remains high-single-digit in developing markets. The sector has also become increasingly technical with recombinant ingredient production improving quality and reducing cost.
quote: The flavours and fragrances (F&F) business meets the pattern of many good businesses. It provides what we think of as 'the trifecta'. It provides a small but important part of big things. It has high switching costs and it is a consumable. Take, for example, the smell of Dove soap. You know it, and if I gave you a bottle of that fragrance you would recognise it instantly, even if you could not describe it. The brand is quintessentially linked to that smell — to the point that the smell is its defining characteristic. Fragrance is probably only three percent of the production cost of Dove soap. But if it were not there the brand would fall apart.

headline: Bronte Capital views Givaudan as the standout compounder in the flavours and fragrances industry, benefiting from technical excellence and long-tenured CEO-led strategy.

Givaudan has also successfully diversified into adjacencies such as hyaluronic acid, and has provided innovation tools to serve the growing proliferation of new brands driven by social media. The F&F business itself exhibits the 'trifecta': a small but important part of big products, high switching costs, and a consumable nature.

Givaudan was run for over twenty years by a single CEO (Giles Andrier) who is everything you would want a CEO to be. These days there are a plethora of new brands and product variations driven by social media and the endless need to renew and innovate on old brands — and Givaudan has provided the tools necessary to produce this product.

headline: Bronte Capital warns of an unprecedented second 'junk rally' in five years, with institutional and retail investors driving extreme short squeezes that are damaging long-quality/short-junk strategies
reasoning: Bronte Capital notes that historically, intense 'sell quality to buy junk' events occurred at most once a generation — citing the 1969 go-go market and the 2000 tech bubble. However, the fund has now experienced two such total manias in five years, with the current episode notable for institutional participation alongside retail investors. Unlike the previous retail-led mania driven by Robinhood users, this iteration targets high-short-interest stocks but also seemingly random names. The fund acknowledges the strategy felt broken in this environment but expresses doubt the world has become permanently crazy. They note losses on both sides of the book, requiring sharp position cuts for risk management.
quote: At Bronte we are long quality stocks and short junk. The worst possible scenario for us is a market so crazy that people sell the more reliable blue chips — the ones that are nearly guaranteed to have passable returns in the future — to play the worst junk. When that happens, we lose on both sides of the book and have to cut positions sharply for risk management purposes. We used to think really intense 'sell the good stuff to buy junk' events — at least on any scale — were rare... Alas we have now had two of these total junk rallies in five years. We don't really have an explanation, other than that for a variety of reasons the world has got crazier.

headline: Bronte Capital cites Brambles as their best recent example of a company that stopped doing 'stupid things', noting the stock has been the best-performing large-cap in Australia since their write-up
reasoning: Bronte references Brambles as a precedent for the Holcim thesis: when a company stops unprofitable activities, it can be a well-timed entry point. Brambles went on to be the best-performing large-cap Australian stock from the time of Bronte's note, with coverage in the Australian Financial Review. However, Bronte views Brambles more favourably than Amrize/Holcim structurally, noting Brambles is by far the largest player in a global duopoly with multiple levers to grow profits over decades, while Amrize and Holcim are more competitive businesses still dominated by cement.
quote: The last company we wrote up where the company stopped doing stupid things was Brambles. That note was very well timed – and the stock has been the best performed large cap stock in Australia – and the run is roughly timed from when we wrote the note. If we compare this to say Brambles (the other recent write-up where the thesis was at least in part the company had stopped doing stuff that was stupid) we do not love it. Brambles is by far the large player in a global duopoly and there are several ways that it can be tweaked over decades to make more money. Amrize and Holcim are more competitive businesses, and they are still dominated by cement rather than gravel – and hence there is a limit to how far they can grow profits.

headline: Bronte Capital notes European environmental standards are raising cement margins by hurting competitors more than Holcim, though net-zero uncertainty remains a risk
reasoning: Holcim's European business has become more profitable as environmental regulation disproportionately burdens competitors, and Bronte expects this trend to continue. However, the firm adds an explicit caveat that the long-term business model is uncertain in a world truly serious about net-zero carbon emissions, flagging this as a key structural risk for the cement sector broadly.
quote: Europe has become more profitable based on environmental standards hurting their competitors more than them. Margins are rising. That will likely continue (with the caveat that we do not know what cement businesses look like in a world truly serious about net-zero carbon emissions).

headline: Bronte Capital views Marietta Materials as the gold standard in US aggregates but notes the stock is richly valued at 5.9x trailing revenue, above even Alphabet
reasoning: Marietta Materials is used as a comparator to illustrate the power of incentive-aligned US management in the aggregates sector. Senior management have accumulated net worth over USD100 million through stock options, and the company has vastly outperformed Holcim over decades. However, Bronte does not present Marietta as a current buy; instead it highlights the valuation anomaly where the market values gravel at a higher revenue multiple (5.9x) than Google (5.8x), suggesting the stock may be fully priced.
quote: Marietta Materials trades at 5.9 times trailing revenue. It is fat margin revenue, and yes it has been managed well. But 5.9 times is higher than Alphabet (Google) which trades at 5.8 times trailing revenue. The market thinks that gravel is either fatter margin or higher growth than Google – an astonishing thought. By contrast the Swiss trade at about 2 times revenue. Amrize never has to be as profitable as Marietta to be a good stock.

headline: Holcim's newly spun-out US business viewed as the primary attraction given tariff tailwinds, incentive-aligned management, and margin expansion potential
reasoning: Amrize was spun out of Holcim in June 2025 and holds a large US cement plant plus quarries, some with 50% margins. Bronte believes American management will optimise the business for stock price appreciation, and without European environmental reporting burdens, costs will fall. Tariffs on Vietnamese ocean-borne cement will raise domestic cement prices and expand US margins further. The valuation is also compelling: Amrize trades at approximately 2x revenue (as part of Holcim Swiss) versus Marietta Materials at 5.9x, leaving significant room for both profit improvement and multiple re-rating. Bronte notes Amrize never needs to match Marietta's profitability to be a good stock.
quote: The real attraction of Holcim is that they spun out the American business (during June 2025). The American business has a large cement plant in the US and a bunch of quarries of various profitability. We think that American management with these assets (including some quarries with 50 percent margins) will – driven by incentives – optimise this business for stock price appreciation. Moreover, they will not have to deal with burdensome European environmental reporting standards. Their costs will go down. There is more though. The competitor is Vietnamese ocean-borne cement. Tariffs will drive up that price – and hence drive up American domestic margins. Future profitability will be considerably higher.

headline: Bronte Capital believes Trump tariffs will ultimately destroy value but the market is not pricing this risk, having misread the sloppy initial announcement as a negotiating starting point
reasoning: The fund acknowledges they largely missed the signal from Trump's disorganised tariff announcement — that the tariffs were not well considered and therefore not meant to be fully implemented. The consensus has now coalesced around the view that Trump will not implement anything sharply market-negative. Bronte regards this consensus as too sanguine, arguing that policy made on the fly and shaped by Trump's peculiar politics is likely to have negative consequences. They believe the tariffs that will actually be implemented will mostly destroy value, potentially a lot of value, but the market is not pricing this.
quote: The meaning of President Trump's sloppy tariff announcement should have been clear to us – but we largely missed it. If the tariffs were not well considered that meant that they were not meant to be implemented. They were a starting point for discussion – not the final draft. What will eventually be implemented is some combination of what can be negotiated and what will not upset the market and Trump's constituency too much. The consensus has become that Trump will not implement anything that is sharply market negative. TACO is the slogan: Trump Always Chickens Out. That consensus we think is too sanguine. Policy on the fly and suiting Trump's peculiar politics is likely to have some negative consequences – though very few are visible so far. And we think the tariffs that will actually be implemented will mostly destroy value. Maybe a lot of value – but the market is not pricing that.

headline: Bronte Capital highlights Martin Marietta Materials as a 15-bagger exemplar of the superior gravel/aggregates business model, contrasting it favourably with Holcim
reasoning: Martin Marietta Materials has been a 15-bagger over 25 years while paying dividends throughout, demonstrating the power of focusing on high-quality, logistics-protected gravel quarries. Bronte attributes this outperformance to disciplined focus on profitable protected assets rather than pursuing scale in lower-quality businesses. The company is presented as a model for identifying businesses with durable local monopoly characteristics. Bronte uses this as a framework for identifying similar opportunities in European building materials companies.
quote: Now consider two companies – Marietta Materials – a US company which is largely a roll-up of gravel quarries and Holcim – a Swiss based roll up of cement factories. It is a 15 bagger – and it has had a dividend the whole time. This stock has had more than adequate returns to shareholders. Marietta focused on what was profitable – protected gravel mines.

headline: Bronte Capital views aggregates/gravel quarries with strong logistics as highly attractive local monopoly businesses, far superior to cement
reasoning: The gravel business is structurally superior to cement because at roughly $10 per tonne, logistics advantages are everything and create overlapping local monopolies. A quarry with an $8/tonne logistics advantage effectively captures that entire margin. Permitting barriers make it near-impossible to open new quarries in dense urban markets like San Francisco, Paris or Sydney. Cement at ~$100/tonne is more expensive but competes globally with seaborne cement from Vietnam, China and Algeria, eliminating any local advantage. Emerging market cement is even worse, with no environmental standards and poor last-mile logistics.
quote: If you own a gravel quarry with good logistics on the outskirts of San Francisco or Paris or Sydney it is a license to print money. It is hard to the point of impossible to get a new quarry approved and if you have a $8 per tonne logistics advantage over your competitors that $8 a tonne becomes your margin. What you have is a lot of overlapping local monopolies. Cement by contrast is more expensive and the logistics are global. There are only a handful of cement plants in North America – and they produce less than the US consumes. Cement comes from as far afield as Vietnam, China and Algeria.

headline: Bronte Capital is actively investing in European and Swiss companies, finding them cheaper than US peers despite comparable global business mixes
reasoning: John Hempton and David recently returned from weeks visiting companies in Germany and Switzerland. Many of these businesses have a similar geographic revenue mix to their US competitors (e.g. 40% Americas, 30% Europe, 30% rest of world) yet trade at a consistent discount and have persistently underperformed. Bronte believes the underperformance is puzzling and partly attributable to management incentives rather than business quality, creating an opportunity for patient investors willing to do shoe-leather research.
quote: It is deeply unfashionable to like Europe. We know why it is unfashionable. It has underperformed for a long time. But with shoe leather (often literally a lot of travel) we find the odd thing. Two of us (John and David) have just come back from a few weeks visiting companies in Germany and Switzerland. Many of these are global businesses – and their business and jurisdictional mix is roughly the same as their American competitors. But they have often underperformed their American competitors and they are almost always cheaper than their American competitors.

headline: Bronte Capital draws parallels between current market mania and historical speculative bubbles, describing current conditions as potentially the biggest mania they have observed
reasoning: The fund references their extensive library of over 100 books on financial manias, noting that with hindsight all historical manias look obvious but seem sui generis to participants at the time. They cite the 1969 Australian nickel stock mania as an example of the kind of behaviour that looks silly in retrospect. The fund describes the current mania as appearing bigger than past episodes, with a colleague tartly noting this may be because they were not participants in prior manias. This framing supports their structural short book in low-quality and speculative stocks.
quote: Manias in financial markets have been a thing for a very long time. Our bookshelf contains over 100 books where the subject is some financial mania or another. John's favourite (back in print) is a classic description of the 1969 nickel stock mania in Australia (The Money Miners by Trevor Sykes) but there are many more. With hindsight, all these manias look obvious. Grown men hanging out of the Sydney stock exchange so they can (with binoculars) look at the chalkboards to see the minute-by-minute price that their favourite speculative (possibly fraudulent) nickel exploring stock promote is trading at just seems silly. But it happened. All these books describe behaviours that are so silly you would (falsely) think that the boom you just went through was sui generis. With the perspective of distance these manias all appear quaint in retrospect. The current mania seems to be bigger.

headline: Bronte Capital views the US equity market rebound as dangerously complacent, with speculative and low-quality stocks reaching frothy levels reminiscent of early 2021

quote: That said, the sharp rebound in the market has convinced people that the solution is to take more risk. Garbage stocks have risen aggressively. This is an environment like early 2021 when the consensus rapidly became that you should buy frauds because they will squeeze higher. People seriously talked about fraud as an asset class. We do not think it is that bad yet. But it is extremely frothy by historic standards – and as we tend to be short the worst stocks in the market this level of ebullience is not comfortable for us. We are managing through it – but that is all.

headline: Sees current US retail trading mania as larger and more dangerous than dot-com, driven by social media coordination and 40 million new brokerage accounts
reasoning: John Hempton and Simon draw on their experience of the dot-com bubble and argue the current mania is bigger and more dangerous. The number of new brokerage accounts (around 40 million, 25 million at Robinhood alone) dwarfs the couple of million opened during dot-com. Social media enables coordinated crowd belief on a scale never previously seen, amplifying manias far beyond what uncoordinated crowds produce. Bronte's bookshelf of 100+ books on financial manias informs their view that this time is not different and the mania will end, though they cannot pinpoint the top.
quote: John and Simon however were around for dot-com – and this is crazier than that. The couple of million who opened accounts in the dot-com period is small-beer compared to the 40 million or so who have opened accounts recently. (25 million of these are at Robinhood.) The mania should be and is bigger. But this mania also comes with social media. If you want to talk about the stock of a collapsing movie exhibition centre all day you can do so in some social media group with a hundred thousand of your best friends. This allows a coordination in mania on a scale never known in history. We figure this mania is going to end. This time is not different.

headline: Bronte Capital initiates small position in Holcim on business improvement and Amrize spin-off optionality
reasoning: Bronte Capital purchased a small stake in Holcim after years of viewing it as a poorly managed business, citing two catalysts: the Swiss company has abandoned unprofitable emerging market cement operations and is focusing on higher-return markets in Europe, Latin America, and Mexico, where margins are rising; and the spin-off of the US division as Amrize creates a separately listed vehicle with strong quarry assets and incentive-aligned American management. The firm explicitly notes this is not and will not be a large position, and describes the stocks as 'for sale' when better ideas emerge. Management at Holcim historically optimised for size rather than profitability, in contrast to US peers, but recent strategic changes suggest the company has stopped doing 'stupid things', a pattern Bronte has previously found to be a good entry signal (referencing Brambles).
quote: Despite all this we went and purchased a small stake in Holcim. It is not a big position, and it never will be. So why now? Well two reasons a). the Swiss company has improved and b). the American division of the Swiss company (now a separately listed company called Amrize) looks fabulous to us. When a company with an okay business stops doing stuff that is unprofitable it is often a good time to buy the stock. The stocks are 'for sale' when we find a better idea. But they should be good for a while.

headline: Bronte Capital uses Holcim as a cautionary example of value destruction through pursuing cement scale in emerging markets rather than focusing on high-quality aggregates assets
reasoning: Holcim's stock has been roughly flat over 25 years with several severe drawdowns, in stark contrast to Martin Marietta's 15-bagger return. Bronte attributes this to Holcim's strategic decision to chase growth in emerging market cement, which is a poor business due to global competition from seaborne cement and lack of logistics advantages. Holcim also sold gravel operations to fund this cement expansion, destroying value by exiting the better business. Bronte sees the root cause as management incentives that rewarded scale over profitability, a common European corporate governance issue.
quote: Holcim decided that what it wanted to be was the world's biggest cement company. Being the world's biggest cement company meant they went where the growth was – emerging markets- and they discovered that cement in say the Philippines is not a good business at all. It is competitive with cheap Pacific seaborne cement, and nobody has a substantial logistics advantage. In their quest to be 'big' Holcim did low-profit things for decades. And they funded this at least in part by selling gravel operations. The management of Holcim decided to focus on less profitable things than the management of (the much smaller) Marietta Materials – and over a couple of decades the resulting difference was obvious.

headline: Bronte Capital acknowledges persistent negative short-book alpha through 2024 and into early 2025, citing both market conditions and internal monitoring failures as the portfolio scaled to 700+ short positions
reasoning: The manager admits to sharply negative alpha on the short book across every month of 2024, worsening at year end. There were two problems: a) Firstly, it was just a moment in time – a period like early 2021 when crappy stocks rose simply because they were rising and the most egregious promotes made new highs simply because they were going up and buyers had a fear of missing out, b) The second problem was more serious. We made errors (particularly with monitoring old shorts) as the portfolio went from 300 shorts to about 700 shorts. We expected the first problem would go away at some point simply because manias end. The second problem involved extremely intensive work from us. Christmas and the New Year in Australia is like the July - August summer vacation season in Europe and North America but, at Bronte, it entailed numerous position reviews and the upgrading of our monitoring systems. Whilst the problem is not entirely fixed it is under control. Serious issues have been neutered, often just by cutting positions, but more often by putting in improved computer alerting systems. headline: Bronte Capital believes the post-COVID bioprocessing bust is a temporary inventory cycle and that long-term growth in the sector will resume.

quote: There has been a notable post-covid bioprocessing bust. This is a growth industry. Volumes that looked like they could never go down went up faster than normal around covid and then started declining. Stocks like Sartorius lost well over half their value. Spirax's 2022 annual report disclosed that 25 percent of their revenue was from bioprocessing, mainly from Watson Marlow but also from Spirax Sarco (for steam sterilization and other processes). By the 2023 annual report that number had dropped to 18 percent. Bioprocessing revenues thus dropped by a hundred million pounds.

It is not a desert island stock now – but for what we think is a superlative quality business that should grow for the next 15 plus years it is just fine. Yes – if it fell a further 25% we would buy a fair bit more. But we do not think this will happen.

headline: Bronte Capital reflects on 2024 speculative momentum environment as analogous to but distinct from the 2021 everything bubble, with short-selling strategies failing
reasoning: Bronte draws a parallel between the 2021 'everything bubble' — where over 50 of their shorts more than doubled in January alone — and 2024's market environment, where momentum-driven moves in questionable or fraudulent companies caused significant losses on their diversified short book. They note that trading strategies that worked in 2021 (fighting the bubble and adding on the way down) have not worked in 2024, requiring adaptation. The firm describes a large group of retail players actively hunting short sellers, complicating the ability to publicise specific short ideas. They have now largely exited the most problematic momentum shorts and intend to re-enter when market sentiment changes.
quote: Our private hell that ended Valentines Day 2021 was the 'everything bubble'. We got thumped by almost everything. In January alone we had over 50 shorts that more than doubled in the month... This time trading strategies that worked in the past have led us astray this cycle. Moreover, many of the current big movers have been complete and demonstrable frauds. Some started as frauds but raised so much money in the rally that they are frauds no longer.

headline: Bronte Capital warns that as the current market normalises, many investments will be exposed as unfounded — referencing the Buffett 'swimming naked' analogy

As this market normalizes many investments will be found to have been based on nothing. Many investors will be exposed as swimming naked. For most people that is yet to come.

headline: Bronte Capital flags Apple as trading at ~10x sales, arguing such a valuation requires 20%+ sustained revenue growth to justify.
reasoning: Bronte Capital notes that even Apple — which they regard as by far the best consumer electronics manufacturer — is currently trading at 9.9x sales. They argue that unless a company can sustain revenue growth of 20% or more, investors should exit stocks trading at or above 10x sales. The Scott McNeally argument is invoked: at 10x revenues, a 10-year payback requires zero costs, zero taxes and zero R&D, which is economically absurd. This is presented as a general valuation warning rather than a specific short call, but the implication is that Apple is at risk of disappointment.
quote: Even Apple – by far the best manufacturer of electronics – a position you would once have assigned to Sun Systems – is trading at 9.9 times sales. Those prices can be justified with a lot of growth. But unless you are prepared to justify sustained revenue growth of 20 percent or more you probably should get out of the stock.

headline: Bronte Capital believes bioprocessing growth has resumed but uncertainty remains on pace — low single digits vs historical low double-digit rates
reasoning: Bronte conducted primary research at a major bioprocessing trade show in Boston in October, asking every salesperson to compare recent monthly sales to one and two years prior. The consistent answer was up versus one year ago but down versus two years ago, giving Bronte confidence that the post-COVID destocking cycle has ended and growth has resumed. However, there is genuine uncertainty about whether the recovery is low single-digit growth or a return to the historical low double-digit rates the industry has sustained for decades. The firm notes that the XBI equal-weighted biopharma index is flat on the year, which does not support a 10% biopharma growth narrative in the market's eyes, creating a wide gap between company guidance and consensus. Bronte sides with management that long-term structural drivers — single-use bioreactor adoption, mRNA and personalised medicine pipeline growth, and increased drug approvals — remain intact for the next 10-20 years.
quote: In October our biotech/pharma analyst Thomas alongside John went to a bioprocessing sales show in Boston. We asked every salesperson the same question: how were your numbers last month versus one year ago and two years ago. In every instance we got the same answer – up on a year ago, down on two years ago. We are about as sure as we can be that growth has resumed – though it is hard to tell whether this is low single digit growth or the low double-digit growth the industry has had for decades.

headline: Bronte Capital's 'trifecta' framework targets companies that sell critical consumable inputs to large processes with high switching costs as core long positions
reasoning: More than half of Bronte Capital's long positions share three characteristics: they sell a small but critical part of a big process (allowing value-based pricing), they have high switching costs making competitor substitution difficult, and they sell consumables rather than capital items. Bronte calls this combination 'the trifecta'. They discover candidates by searching for companies with unusually high ('magical') margins, then investigate whether those margins stem from cyclicality, fraud, or genuinely superior business models. The framework has been central to their investment in Spirax Engineering and similar compounders.
quote: More than half the stocks we like as longs have the following three characteristics: i. They do a small part of a big thing. They are in some sense the critical ingredient in a big process, and they can charge by the value they bring to the big process. ii. There is some difficulty in switching the part/product for a competitor product (a high switching cost), and iii. They sell a consumable product rather than a capital item. We call the combination 'the trifecta'. Business with a full trifecta range from okay to outright delicious.

headline: Bronte Capital shorted Summit Therapeutics on scientific scepticism around Ivonescimab's bispecific PD-1/VEGF mechanism, forced to largely cover after ~10x stock move
reasoning: Bronte initially scored Summit as 'light-amber' rather than a strong short, partly because of CEO Duggan's prior success with Pharmacyclics (Ibrutinib). However, the firm's core thesis was scientific: combining a PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor and a VEGF inhibitor into a single bispecific molecule (Ivonescimab) should offer no meaningful advantage over using both approved drugs separately, as prior combination studies showed no additive benefit. When Summit released phase 3 data from a China-only trial claiming a ~2x improvement over Keytruda in non-small cell lung cancer on a progression-free survival endpoint, the stock rose ~10-fold. Bronte identified multiple caveats: the trial was China-only and inadmissible for US approval, used a weaker control arm than current US standard of care, measured only progression-free survival (not overall survival), and may have suffered from selection bias. The firm was mostly forced to cover, taking a loss of under 1% of fund due to the small starting position. They remain sceptical and will reassess on US phase 3 results.
quote: Summit released phase 3 results claiming that Ivonescimab performed twice as well as Keytruda alone in the context of patients with locally advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer. This is a very big indication. To say the stock was strong is understating it. It climbed about 10-fold from where we first looked at it. There are however significant caveats. • The trial was conducted in China alone and is non-admissible for getting the drug approved in the USA. • The trial used a weaker control arm than the current standard of care in the US. • The company claimed a benefit on 'progression-free survival', which is merely a surrogate endpoint for (and far less important than) 'overall survival' (lifespan). Improvements on progression-free survival often do not translate to overall survival. A drug that improves progression-free survival but not overall survival is useless. Ivonescimab's effect (or lack thereof) on overall survival has not been determined. • Since US patients are inherently different than Chinese patients and Chinese clinical trial standards are different to the US, any 'benefit' seen in China may not translate to the US. (Several Chinese trial results have not been reproduced outside China.) • There are a few reasons to believe the trial may have suffered from selection bias. For example, the control arm performed worse than the control arm in other trials – raising the possibility that the trial was biased by over-weighting very sick patients into the control arm. We largely had to cover the stock because it got big the wrong way. Our loss was well under a percent of the fund but only because our starting position was tiny.
