headline: Bronte Capital views distressed bank mergers as a recurring source of investment opportunity, citing JP Morgan/WaMu as success and Lloyds/HBOS as cautionary tale.
reasoning: Bronte Capital considers distressed bank mergers — particularly those facilitated by regulators — as analytically interesting and potentially profitable situations. Their framework distinguishes between acquirers that are strengthened (e.g. JP Morgan buying Washington Mutual from the FDIC during the GFC) and those that are nearly destroyed by importing bad assets and culture (e.g. Lloyds buying Halifax Bank of Scotland). This framework was applied to evaluating whether to buy acquirers of Silicon Valley Bank, Signature Bank, and Credit Suisse.
quote: Buying a distressed bank from the regulator (or at the behest of and with the assistance of the regulator) is either a great bargain (the normal case) or a disaster (when you import all the bad assets and culture). We have seen both cases. In the global financial crisis JP Morgan was strengthened by buying Washington Mutual from the FDIC. By contrast Lloyds Bank (by far the best UK retail bank at the time) nearly destroyed itself buying Halifax Bank of Scotland. We are very interested in distressed mergers of banks because – with some analysis – they offer opportunities for profits.

headline: Bronte Capital trimmed its largest position in Alphabet on concerns about AI capex returns, though it remains the fund's top holding.

There is no guarantee Google earns a great return on that investment, and if it doesn't, the stock is overpriced. Bronte has trimmed slightly but notes that many businesses it considers superior carry similar stock-specific risks.
quote: We have been long Google for years. It is our largest position. Google capex used to run at about 5-8 billion USD per quarter. It is now running at 13 plus billion per quarter. The driver of all that additional capital expenditure is the requirement to buy Nvidia chips to keep up in the artificial intelligence race. There is no guarantee Google gets a great return on that investment and if they don't then Google stock is overpriced. We have trimmed a little Google (now traded as Alphabet) but many of the businesses we think are superior also contain similar stock specific risks and there is no guarantee you are being compensated for those risks either.

We never even looked at First Citizens Bank (the acquirer) but we figured buying a good bank at a distressed price was likely to work out very well. This was a great decision. headline: Bronte Capital's John Hempton flags multiple macro risks suggesting markets may be near a top, while Simon takes a more bullish risk-management view.
reasoning: John identifies several macro risks that could go wrong: the rise of protectionism, deeply disruptive technology change (EVs, AI), rising militarism particularly around Taiwan, and demographic issues. He suggests bells are ringing at or near a market top. Simon, responsible for risk management, is less certain and notes earnings are fine, inflation is abating, and buy-the-dip investors stand ready — arguing that a bullish market perspective is actually a conservative stance for Bronte given its portfolio construction as committed short-sellers.
quote: There are a lot of things that can go wrong, and we do not know how any of them will play out. The rise of protectionism – we are all protectionists now. Deeply disruptive technology change – e.g. electric cars, artificial intelligence. The rise of militarism (and above all troubles in Taiwan). Demographic issues catching up with the world generally. At the risk (almost guaranteed) of looking stupid John (but not Simon) thinks bells are ringing now. It may be wishful thinking for John when he suggests we are near a top. We would like it to be – we are committed short-sellers. And the observation that nobody rings a bell applies to us too. But the market does feel 'toppy'. Simon, by contrast, isn't as certain. Everything is going swimmingly well. Earnings are fine. Inflation is abating. The buy-the-dip crowd are ready to swoop on the slightest market fall, and market bounces have often proven detrimental to our returns.

headline: Bronte Capital uses French Connection UK as a cautionary tale for top-down stock selection — strong ROE and growth metrics masked fatal fashion risk
reasoning: French Connection UK displayed impressive ROE approaching 30% and double-digit revenue growth throughout the late 1990s and early 2000s, making it appear a high-quality business on pure accounting metrics. However, the FCUK brand's shock value faded, the brand became unfashionable, and the stock ultimately lost over 90% of its value before going private after more than a decade of losses. Bronte notes this as a classic trap in top-down analysis: good historical numbers are visible and priced in, while the top-down approach systematically misses the break in whatever made the business wonderful — in this case a fashion change. They never held a position in the stock.
quote: From the top-down this really looks like a wonderful business. The return on equity is pushing 30 percent. The growth rate in revenue is double-digit in most years and the growth in earnings is over 20 percent. If you chose stocks by accounting metrics of what was a wonderful business, you would buy it at any reasonable multiple – and it traded at a seemingly reasonable multiple. When the growth slowed it traded at what might appear an astonishingly low price. Alas it was a disaster. The stock lost over 90 percent of its value, and it eventually went private after having lost money for over a decade straight.

quote: Flavors and fragrances is a great business. Technical flavoring products are critical to making pre-packaged food taste good... The flavors are maybe 2-3 percent of the cost of goods sold. If the price of flavoring goes up by 20 percent, it barely affects the yogurt company, but it makes the economics of the flavoring company extremely good. Flavors are a small but critical part of a big thing (processed food) and hence have pricing power. We have a high single digit percentage of your portfolio invested in flavors and fragrance companies.

headline: Bronte Capital maintains large Alphabet position despite inexplicable valuation, flagging irregular trims as better ideas emerge
reasoning: Bronte Capital has held Google since 2011 and despite being comprehensively wrong in their original terminal value framework — which capped combined Google/Facebook value at ~$970bn versus today's ~$3.4 trillion — they continue to hold because they cannot find sufficiently better ideas. quote: We hold the position subject to finding sufficiently good ideas to replace it. The uncomfortable implication is that the main reason we have held Google is that we could not find anything we liked more. We did not hold it because we were smart and realized the revenue would go to seemingly well over a quarter of a percent of global GDP. We were utterly wrong about how good Google's prospects were. Our estimates – with the benefit of hindsight – are simply comically low. But, if we look at Google against current multiples and growth, it is just not that expensive. But it is also just not that explicable. And we do not see good reason for holding 12 percent of the portfolio at a valuation and business performance we see as inexplicable. Expect us to trim it irregularly – maybe sharply if we find a position we like more.

headline: Bronte Capital argues online advertising structurally raises total ad spend above historical GDP ratios as measurability and new online-native businesses create incremental demand
reasoning: Bronte articulates a structural thesis that online advertising does not merely shift spend from traditional media but actually grows the total advertising market as a share of GDP. Two mechanisms are identified: first, online advertising is measurable and as advertisers verify it works, they buy more; second, new online-native businesses (e.g. local fishing guides buying Google keywords instead of putting up shop signs) represent net-new advertising demand that did not exist in the offline world. This is cited as the key reason their 2015 assumption of 1% of global GDP as an upper bound for advertising spend proved too low.
quote: Online advertising can be measured – and as people worked out advertising actually works they buy more of it, and online creates new people that must advertise. Once for example there was a fishing shop at Hyams Beach, a tourist town south of Sydney. It has closed now – at least in part because people buy fishing tackle online. The online replacement must advertise. But more importantly the local fishing guides used to advertise by sticking a sign up in the local fishing shop. Now they buy words like 'deep sea fishing Jervis Bay' on Google. Total advertising spend thus rises.

headline: Questions whether superstore-and-A-mall model is compatible with Hibbett's underserved-community strategy following the acquisition
reasoning: JD Sports operates a superstore and A-mall destination strategy, sharing online channels with brand partners and prioritising the JD Sports brand. Hibbett operates an underserved-community-first omnichannel model with almost no store overlap with JD Sports. While JD Sports management described this as complementary, Bronte views this as a potential merger of very different cultures. Bronte also highlights that Nike — which is central to Hibbett's proposition — has not clearly signalled its comfort with the combined entity, and this uncertainty remains unresolved.
quote: JD Sports by contrast is a super-store and A-mall strategy – again with an omnichannel twist. The JD Sports mega-stores are destinations – and they share the online channel with their brand partners. JD runs other brands (such as Finish Line) – but it is explicitly a strategy that prioritizes the JD Sports brand and destination locations. In the conference call JD Sports management noted that there was almost no store overlap. They thought this was complementary. And maybe complementary might be the polite way to describe what might wind up being a merger of companies with very different cultures. We are interested in how this plays out.

headline: Bronte Capital admits their 2015 terminal value framework for Google/Facebook was 'comprehensively wrong' — underestimating GDP growth, ad spend penetration, margins, and multiples
reasoning: In their 2015 client letter, Bronte had estimated a maximum terminal value of ~$970bn for Google and Facebook combined, based on: global GDP of $77tn, advertising spend of 1% of GDP, Google/Facebook capturing 30% share, 40% pre-tax margin, 30% tax, and a 15x terminal multiple. Every single assumption proved too conservative: global GDP is now ~$110tn; online advertising has lifted total ad spend above 1% of GDP as measurability drives more spending and new online-native businesses create incremental demand; Google and Facebook already exceed 30% of global advertising; Meta margins hit 40% and Google is in the low 30s; effective tax rates are below 30%; and terminal multiples exceed 15x. The combined market cap of Alphabet and Meta is now ~$3.4 trillion, roughly 3.5x their estimated maximum terminal value.
quote: It is worth stating how we were wrong. 1. Global GDP is closer to $110 trillion than $77 trillion. We should have included some growth in global GDP. 2. Advertising spend keeps going up and will wind up over 1 percent of global GDP – primarily driven by online and, of course, Google... 3. Facebook and Google are already over 30 percent of global advertising. Google's advertising revenue alone is now about a quarter of a percent of global GDP and growing much faster than global GDP. 4. We underestimated the long-term margin. Meta margins are just on 40 percent now, Google is in the low 30s... 5. The tax rates paid are going to wind up less than 30 percent, and 6. The end multiple will wind up being more than 15 times earnings – especially as these are somewhat inflation resistant businesses. In other words, we were close to comprehensively wrong.

headline: Bronte Capital was short Signature Bank for over a year prior to its collapse, identifying deposit instability and governance red flags

quote: We have been short Signature Bank for over a year. While we first noticed its substantial cryptocurrency exposure in 2021, the position's origin was an article in American Banker from March 2022... We did not know whether the new problem assets were one bank with approximately 120 billion in assets or two banks summing to 120 billion in assets. Whatever: if it was one bank there was only one bank it could be—which was Signature Bank. No other bank was within 10 billion dollars of the required 120 billion. Regardless, we began digging. The more we looked the less we liked Signature Bank. We shorted it... At $300 a share Signature Bank was one of the biggest shorts at Bronte. We covered about half the position at $120 on the way down. We did not have any idea that the complete collapse of the bank was nigh. By the time the bank collapsed our position was very small.

headline: Bronte Capital views the end of Swiss banking secrecy as a structural negative for Swiss banks, having permanently impaired their profitability model and leaving UBS and Credit Suisse with excessive costs and large US government fines.
reasoning: The fund argues that Swiss banks historically derived outsized profitability from banking secrecy, which attracted wealthy clients who had no alternative for hiding assets. The end of secrecy eliminated this captive client base, left banks with bloated cost structures, and resulted in large US government fines. Both UBS and Credit Suisse responded by taking more risk to compensate for lower profitability, but UBS reversed course after 2008 while Credit Suisse continued down a risky path. This structural analysis underpinned both the Credit Suisse short and the subsequent UBS long.
quote: Swiss banks were sharply weakened by the end of banking secrecy. Historically, Switzerland was a clean place to hide your dirty money and Swiss Banking was almost synonymous with tax avoidance. Swiss banking secrecy is now extinct, and many American clients either paid their back taxes or were prosecuted. Secrecy made Swiss banks profitable despite excessive cost structures. They had many rich customers who really couldn't move their money elsewhere. The end of banking secrecy left Swiss banks with unhappy clients who could now move their money elsewhere, excessive cost structures and big fines from the US Government.

If they don't our UBS stock position probably won't work that well. But the merger integration plans are not yet nailed down, so we consider this position provisional.

headline: Bronte Capital admits Herbalife long thesis has not worked, citing post-Covid sales attrition and dangerous leverage build-up from buybacks
reasoning: Bronte Capital was publicly long Herbalife in size, believing the company was misunderstood by Wall Street and that the multi-level marketing model provided genuine community support for weight loss rather than being a scam. Volume points exploded during Covid as online communities formed, but when Covid ended many new customers left and old customers did not fully return. Management, also believing in the sales trajectory, bought back stock aggressively, leaving the company over-levered. In hindsight, Bronte acknowledges they should have scaled back the position given the leverage. The CEO was fired and a prior CEO brought back; senior distributors are optimistic about a rebound but Bronte notes these are congenitally optimistic salespeople. They are keeping the position but not adding substantially, classifying it as 'very cheap but problematic'.
quote: We have been publicly long Herbalife in size on our view that the company was widely misunderstood by Wall Street. This has not worked. Herbalife sells weight loss shakes through a multi-level marketing scheme... Alas, volume points exploded during Covid. People organized online communities for weight loss. But the existing sales structures atrophied. When Covid went away many of the online-style customers ceased being customers and the old customers did not fully return. This surprised us. We believed the sales would continue to do well. We drank the Kool-Aid... Importantly though they bought back stock on the presumption that the sales will continue to do well. This has left the company precariously over-levered. In hindsight, given the leverage, we should have scaled back the position earlier... We are not selling the position – but we are also not substantially adding to it. We think it is in the very-cheap but problematic bucket now.

headline: Bronte Capital expects garbage/junk stocks to continue declining toward zero despite periodic short-covering rallies, and does not anticipate a repeat of the 2021 junk-market excess
reasoning: Bronte argues that many lower-quality stocks still have substantial market caps yet are heading toward zero or cash backing. They note that many retail investors have already lost substantial money in speculative stocks and crypto, and it typically takes more than ten years to attract a new generation of speculative buyers.
quote: We don't see a near term future like that. There are plenty of garbage stocks that are still going to zero (or at least to cash backing) and still have substantial market caps. And high-quality companies – although not cheap – are back to maybe 2017 valuations. We think long quality - short junk will continue to work – outperforming falling markets and perhaps, in our case, even outperforming modestly rising markets because we are slightly levered to quality. We expect bounces in the garbage stocks – but they are suckers' rallies. They will last long enough to finish off the latest generation of crazy speculators and that is all.

That is an abrogation of responsibility to fix it themselves – but alas that responsibility was abrogated some time ago. The Christmas gift to us is that we will probably be taken out at a profit albeit there is also a possibility that worse is still to come. It should have been a good year for us and (mostly) it was. We say the 'book' is working. But, if we are being self-critical, it is not working quite as well as we would like. headline: Bronte Capital outlines the structural decline of Swiss asset management after the collapse of banking secrecy, leading to bloated cost structures and falling profitability.
reasoning: Swiss banks historically relied on secrecy rather than performance or low fees as their competitive moat. After the 2001 terrorist attacks, banking secrecy became politically untenable and was eventually abandoned, leaving Swiss asset managers with middling performance and high cost structures. In response, both banks and independent asset managers tried to offset earnings declines by taking on more risk, with disastrous consequences — Credit Suisse became 'accident prone' and GAM suffered a catastrophic blow-up through Greensill-linked illiquid securities. This structural context explains why GAM's stock fell 99% from peak and why the situation remained dire without aggressive cost-cutting.
quote: Switzerland was a place to leave your money hidden from your home-jurisdiction tax authorities. The money was stuck and secrecy rather than low fees or performance was the basis for Swiss asset management. Swiss Bank asset management wasn't very good (it didn't need to be) and it had high fees and a bloated cost structure. After the 2001 terrorist attacks banking secrecy became problematic... Eventually Swiss financial institutions gave up secrecy and even surrendered the identities of large numbers of tax evaders. After that Swiss Banks had middling performance, bloated cost structures and angry clients.

headline: Bronte Capital self-assessment finds robust alpha on short book but only modest outperformance on longs, despite significant stock-selection effort

quote: On shorts our analysis shows that over the long term, and more so recently, we have generated 'alpha' on the short book. We have had well over a thousand shorts in the history of the fund and currently have about 500 shorts – and those stocks have simply performed atrociously (which means shorting them has generally, but not always, been good). Alas it is only on the short side where we can be so confident. And, on the long side, the self-assessment is less rosy. We are not bad long investors – but we cannot argue from our data that we are spectacularly good long investors. We put a lot of effort into finding 'quality' and especially 'quality at a reasonable price' but that effort has, for longs, led to only modest outperformance.

headline: Bronte Capital finds it easier to identify shorts than longs in the current market, with few genuinely cheap high-quality stocks available, and continues to run net short with rising beta as weak shorts have been covered

quote: We are a hedge fund – and we add to both sides – trying to use the profits from our shorts to add to longs at lower prices. But net-net our shorts have done so much better than our longs we have had to add far more to shorts than longs. Indeed, almost every time we add we have been adding more shorts than longs. And despite that our beta has been rising for the past six months – simply because many of the shorts have disappeared – going down 90 percent or more. Despite adding substantial shorts all year our measured beta has dropped only a tiny bit over 2022 – and has crept up by about 20 percentage points since the middle of the year. We are, at writing, still adding more shorts than longs. We still find it easier to find good shorts than good longs. And the number of truly cheap stocks we know is low.

headline: Bronte Capital holds no position in QBE but uses its 2009 currency hedging debacle as a case study in how hedges can destroy shareholder value through liquidity crises
reasoning: Bronte Capital highlights QBE's 2009 annual report, which described how the company had over 75% of shareholders' funds offshore (mostly USD and Sterling) and used forward FX contracts to hedge this exposure. When the Australian dollar collapsed in 2008-2009, QBE faced massive margin calls on its hedges. The company was eventually forced to unwind the hedges near the bottom, only for the AUD to then appreciate, causing a $2.2 billion negative movement in the foreign currency translation reserve. Despite a massive subsequent bull market, QBE's stock remains below half its 2009 price level.
quote: Better disclosed was a debacle at QBE, a major Australian insurance company (in which we have no position). This horror story was laid out rather blandly in the Chairman's letter in the 2009 annual report. We quote: In early 2009, we revised our longstanding practice of fully hedging our investment in foreign operations. With over 75% of shareholders' funds offshore from Australia, the use of forward foreign exchange contracts results in regular settlement funding and, in times of volatility, introduces liquidity risk and fluctuation of Group capital levels... Despite a massive bull market QBE's stock price is a little under half the price it was in 2009. The hedges did not 'hedge' risk, they simply transferred a balance sheet risk into a nastier cash-flow/liquidity risk.

headline: Bronte Capital uses the UK pension LDI crisis to illustrate the broader danger of 'hedging' as risk transformation into worse liquidity risks, a pattern now playing out in bond markets
reasoning: Bronte Capital argues there is no such thing as true hedging — only risk transformation, often to nastier risks. Using examples from Iceland, Australian superannuation funds, and QBE, they show how seemingly sensible hedges created catastrophic margin calls at exactly the wrong time. They extend this framework to UK pension funds that used liability-driven investment strategies — buying long-duration swaps to hedge falling interest rates — which then generated massive margin calls when rates rose sharply in 2022. The lesson is that derivatives-based hedges stabilise risk in one scenario while creating catastrophic exposure in another.
quote: Lots of things go wrong in financial markets when a bear market sets in. Things that looked stable become problematic. Ideas that looked sound in the flush of a bull market are often shown to be deeply problematic. Late in the quarter, one of those seemingly good but (probably) bad ideas was exposed. For those not familiar with fads in pension fund management, the fad – liability driven investment – takes a little explaining. Please bear with us because we think this reveals some more general truths about the world.

quote: Alas it has not been enough to offset some of our weaker stocks, let alone our overweight exposure to the UK (and Europe) which have suffered from both stock and currency weakness.

headline: Bronte Capital sees markets in late-cycle bear market territory, echoing Grantham's Superbubble thesis, with many large-cap assets having no realistic path to returning their valuation to shareholders
reasoning: Bronte Capital finds the Superbubble thesis articulated by Jeremy Grantham rings true, noting that many assets with market caps in the billions have no realistic prospect of returning their valuation to shareholders by 2060. They observe classic late-cycle behaviors in an extreme form and note that in a bear market, assets that appear cheap can still fall 30% further while earnings also deteriorate. They acknowledge seeing this dynamic in a couple of their own portfolio holdings, though they believe most of their longs are 'far from cheap'.
quote: Everything Grantham says about the Superbubble rings true to us. We find plenty of assets with market caps of many billions that have no real hope of returning their valuation to shareholders between now and 2060. Also, the behaviors we witness are just more extreme versions of that described in the many books on our shelves about late market cycle behavior. During the bull market, we saw assets that basic logic indicated were ludicrously expensive. And then their prices doubled. Earnings did often grow faster than one would reasonably think. The bubble itself for instance pushed up the demand for capital equipment and the margins from selling it. A bear market is different. At some point an asset seems unreasonably cheap, so you buy it– and it immediately drops 30 percent. Then of course the downturn drives a recession, making investment spending less attractive, and earnings drop as well.

headline: Bronte Capital holds a small, illiquid UK-listed stock with pension fund exposure but is monitoring for negative surprises related to gilt market stress
reasoning: Bronte owns a UK-listed share in a company whose pension fund is large relative to current profitability, trading at approximately 8x trailing earnings. quote: We own a few British shares, but only one of them (which we will not name) has a pension fund that is large relative to current profitability. We do not know whether the pension funds involved have oversized long dated gilt exposure, but have been trying to find out. We are not keen to sell the stock, as it is not hugely liquid and is trading at eight times trailing earnings. It is a tiny position (well under one percent of the fund). But negative surprises are of course possible.

headline: Bronte Capital highlights UK pension fund LDI strategies as a systemic risk exposed by the sharp rise in long-duration bond yields in 2022
reasoning: UK pension funds adopted liability-driven investment strategies over decades of falling interest rates, buying long-duration swaps to hedge their growing accounting liabilities. These swaps were designed to protect against further rate declines but created enormous margin call exposure when rates rose sharply. Bronte Capital frames this as another example of risk transformation rather than true hedging, with the pension system now facing a liquidity crisis analogous to the AUD currency hedge disasters seen in 2008-2009.
quote: Pension funds have very long obligations. People will be collecting pensions in thirty years. Every time interest rates fell, especially long bond interest rates, the accounting value of those obligations increased, and the UK pension fund became just a little bit more underfunded. And for the last 40 years or so interest rates have fallen and fallen some more. Eventually many pension funds, mostly in the UK but also some we know in America, decided to 'hedge' further declines in the long interest rate. They bought swaps, swapping the duration of their portfolio to the longest bonds they could find. After all they were carrying a balance sheet risk that long interest rates would decline further (and that long bonds would appreciate further). The problem with the hedge was...

headline: Bronte Capital finds numerous assets with multi-billion dollar market caps that have no realistic prospect of returning their valuation to shareholders by 2060, consistent with Grantham's superbubble thesis
reasoning: Consistent with their secular bear market view and endorsement of Jeremy Grantham's superbubble thesis, Bronte Capital highlights that they can identify many assets with market caps of many billions that have no real prospect of returning value to shareholders over a nearly 40-year horizon. They also note that during the bull market, assets that seemed ludicrously expensive often doubled further, driven partly by the bubble itself elevating demand for capital equipment and margins. They contrast this with how bear markets ultimately resolve such mispricings.
quote: We find plenty of assets with market caps of many billions that have no real hope of returning their valuation to shareholders between now and 2060. Also, the behaviors we witness are just more extreme versions of that described in the many books on our shelves about late market cycle behavior. During the bull market, we saw assets that basic logic indicated were ludicrously expensive. And then their prices doubled. Earnings did often grow faster than one would reasonably think. The bubble itself for instance pushed up the demand for capital equipment and the margins from selling it.

headline: Warns of systemic liquidity risk from UK pension fund LDI strategies amid rising rates and forced gilt selling
reasoning: UK pension funds adopted liability-driven investment (LDI) strategies by using interest rate swaps to hedge against falling long-term rates, effectively creating leveraged long positions in very long-dated bonds. When inflation caused a sudden sharp rise in rates, these funds faced massive margin calls on their hedges, forcing distressed selling of UK gilts at prices as low as 25 pence on the pound. The Bank of England intervened with gilt purchases — itself an ironic use of quantitative easing, a policy many argue contributed to the inflation that caused the crisis in the first place. Bronte views this as an example of how modern finance transforms ostensibly safe, long-term pools of capital into leveraged vehicles vulnerable to bank-run-like dynamics through the use of derivatives. The firm expects more such 'surprises' in a bear market, with the market likely to trade at lower multiples of lower earnings.
quote: A 75 percent loss on recently issued UK Government bonds was not on our bingo card for 2022. The Bank of England intervened by buying long dated UK government bonds (gilts). Note the beauty of this too. There is a reasonable argument that quantitative easing is a cause of recent inflation. That inflation caused interest rates to rise – and the solution is to do more quantitative easing. There is a reasonable argument that the Bank of England is putting out the fire with gasoline. We mention all this only because weird stuff happens in markets on the way down.

headline: Bronte Capital notes that shorting hype (new-age technology stocks pitched by honest but misguided funds) has been a very profitable trade
reasoning: Bronte Capital observes that well-known, honestly run funds pitching new-age technology stocks to retail investors have underperformed even an index of stocks Bronte believes are run by dishonest management. Shorting speculative hype stocks has been a very profitable trade for the fund this quarter. By contrast, shorting stocks they consider outright dishonest or fraudulent has been a less rewarding trade, as those stocks have not yet re-rated as badly as expected. The firm remains confident that shorting dishonesty will outperform over time.
quote: Disappointingly though, there are famous and honest funds pitching new-age technology stocks to retail. These funds are honestly run – but – believe it or not – these funds have underperformed an index of stocks we think are run by crooks. Shorting hype (something we do a little bit of) has been a very good trade. Shorting dishonesty (something we do a lot of) has been a less good trade. Generally, though we think we will continue outperform by shorting dishonesty, this quarter that outperformance was less than we would like.

headline: Bronte Capital expects low-quality stocks to fall 90% from current levels while quality indices decline only modestly, favouring a long-quality short-dross approach
reasoning: Bronte believes the current environment rewards a long-quality, short-dross portfolio construction, expecting that dross — the lowest quality stocks — could fall 90 percent or more from current levels. Meanwhile, the broader indices may decline modestly. The firm acknowledges the primary risk to this strategy is a period when low-quality outperforms high-quality, as happened during the retail gambling mania, but believes that phase of the cycle is now behind us. The positioning in large consensus longs like Google and over 500 shorts supports this view.
quote: We think there is a reasonable chance the indices behave relatively well (down, but modestly [we are still bearish]) while the dross in the market behaves truly badly, with 90 percent drops from here a common outcome. We know we are talking our book here. We are long quality and short dross. But we think the portfolio may do just fine – even in a continued bad market. And we are net long (just) so we should be okay (although underperforming) if the market rises.

headline: Bronte Capital views current market as early-to-middle stage of a multi-year secular bear market, recommending caution over heroism
reasoning: Bronte Capital believes markets peaked in early January and have been declining, with September weakness producing new lows in many markets. They characterise the current environment as the early to middle stage of a multi-year secular bear market and expect powerful bear market rallies but a general downward direction for some time. They reference Jeremy Grantham's 'Entering the Superbubble's Final Act' as supporting their thesis. They note that despite this view, they position the portfolio to generate adequate returns even if they are wrong on broad market direction.
quote: Intellectually however, we are in the camp that what we are seeing is the early to middle stage of a multi-year secular bear market. It is not time to be an investment hero. Like all bear markets we expect some powerful "bear market rallies" but we think the general direction for some time will be down. There are people with the same opinion, some who lay the case out more eloquently than we have. We recommend you read Jeremy Grantham's "Entering the Superbubble's Final Act," which lays out the case based on a normal market cycle theory. Everything Grantham says about the Superbubble rings true to us.

headline: Bronte Capital observes quality stocks have outperformed very low-quality stocks in the quarter but not to the degree typically expected in a secular bear market
reasoning: The fund's strategy is premised on quality outperforming junk in a secular bear market environment, which has historically been the case. While there was some quality outperformance in the quarter, it was much less pronounced than the firm would expect at this stage of a weak market. Prior to COVID the long book was markedly better than the index, but since the pandemic onset there has been little evidence of value-add from stock selection on the long side. The short book, by contrast, has performed well, falling further and faster than comparable indices.
quote: Our returns for the quarter were better than many alternative investments but were lower than what we hoped and expected. The problem is that whilst quality has outperformed very low-quality stocks over the quarter it was nowhere near what we would expect at this stage for a secularly weak market. ... Quality outperforms junk by a lot in most secular bear markets – but it has not happened thus far to the extent we would have expected.

headline: Bronte Capital holds Regeneron as a major long position, with the stock being one of the best performers in the S&P 500 year-to-date
reasoning: Regeneron was written up in Bronte Capital's June 2021 letter and has remained a major position in the fund. The stock has been one of the best performers in the S&P 500 for the year. quote: There have been some bright spots in our long book. Regeneron, a major position and a stock we wrote up in our June 2021 letter, has been one of the best performing stocks in the S&P 500 this year. Alas it has not been enough to offset some of our weaker stocks, let alone our overweight exposure to the UK (and Europe) which have suffered from both stock and currency weakness.

headline: Amalthea Fund underperforms in August as retail-driven short squeeze hurt short book before Fed Chair Powell's hawkish remarks weighed on longs
reasoning: In the first half of August, the fund's short portfolio suffered as retail enthusiasm and professional short covering levitated 'story stock' favourites. quote: In the first half of the month our short portfolio suffered as story stock favorites were levitated by retail enthusiasm and short covering from professional investors. Fed Chair Powell's dark and foreboding words then sobered up the market, and hurt our longs. Whilst our shorts then proved helpful the earlier damage could not be undone, and the net result was disappointing for a month where we would typically outperform.

headline: Bronte Amalthea Fund underperforms in July 2022 as retail meme-style stocks rally sharply against the fund's short book
reasoning: The fund lost 0.73% in July 2022 versus a +5.97% gain for the MSCI ACWI Index in AUD terms. The underperformance versus their internal model was estimated at approximately 3%. There were no single large culprits, but rather a variety of small negative contributors. quote: The fund lost 0.73% vs. a boisterous +5.97% for the globally diverse ACWI Index (in $A) - with the market actively hostile to our strategy. Nonsense retail stocks performed exceptionally well and we are short those. That said, we run a fairly balanced book and would expect to underperform - but not by quite this much. We think we performed about 3% worse than "model" (or what we would have expected given market moves). There were no real culprits. Just a variety of little nicks. More seriously our leverage has increased and so we are marginally reducing the size of our portfolio to offset this.

headline: Maintains short positions in speculative retail stocks that surged strongly in July 2022
reasoning: The letter explicitly identifies 'nonsense retail stocks' as the primary source of pain in July, as these stocks rallied sharply while Bronte Capital held short positions in them. quote: Nonsense retail stocks performed exceptionally well and we are short those.

headline: Bronte Capital bearish on Australian dollar due to structural interest rate differentials versus US
reasoning: Bronte argues that Australia's prevalence of variable-rate mortgages means RBA rate hikes flow through directly to household budgets and consumer spending, requiring fewer rate rises to control inflation compared to the US. This structural difference means Australia will end up with lower interest rates than the US in the current tightening cycle, which should weigh on the AUD. Despite commodity prices being supportive of the AUD (the consensus long trade), Bronte takes a contrary bearish position on the currency.
quote: Central banks have – for the first time in nearly 40 years – become concerned with inflation. They will raise interest rates until they control inflation. We have no idea whether that means 2 percent rises or 6 percent rises. But we do have one strong view. Australia is a land of variable rate mortgages. Central bank interest rates flow directly through to mortgages and household budgets. That makes consumer spending very sensitive to interest rates in Australia. By contrast the US is largely a land of fixed rate mortgages. Central bank interest changes flow through to mortgages only with a new mortgage and affect consumer spending only on the margin. This means that the Reserve Bank of Australia needs to raise interest rates far less than the Federal Reserve to control spending and hence inflation. In an environment where central banks are raising rates to control inflation, Australia will wind up with structurally lower interest rates than the US. This seems to indicate that the Australian dollar will be weak.

headline: Bronte highlighted Target at 12x PE as attractively valued in 2011 alongside Walmart

headline: Bronte bullish on US mega-cap equities as generationally cheap relative to cash, bonds and other assets (2011 letter)

Cash yields almost minus 3 percent after inflation and less post tax. Bonds are scary as hell and yield minus 1% after tax and inflation. Big though difficult-to-run companies are at low teens multiples. Great franchises are at mid-teens multiples... Mega-cap equities are generationally cheap compared to other assets - and certainly compared to the cash/bond/levered asset complex.

headline: Bronte Capital has no exposure to energy stocks despite the sector being one of the few areas of market strength in Q2 2022

headline: Bronte viewed Tesco as a truly great franchise at an attractive 14x PE in 2011 with a historically cheap pound as additional tailwind

headline: Bronte short several frauds targeting European ESG investors, with shorts confirmed by visits to Total and Air Liquide

headline: Bronte Capital concludes the broad equity market is not yet cheap, with only a handful of genuinely attractive long opportunities
reasoning: The fund applies a valuation framework asking what must go right (or wrong) to generate an adequate return. In a cheap market, many things must go wrong for losses to occur; in an expensive market, many things must go right. The current market does not resemble the cheap conditions of 2011. Only about 10% of the portfolio is in stocks where it is hard to find reasons not to own them. The fund laments the scarcity of truly cheap quality businesses.
quote: Alas the market today is not priced like that. To justify owning a large slab of the market, a lot of things must go right for a long time in a lot of businesses. Things are not cheap yet. ... So how many ultra-cheap stocks do we own? Very few stocks in total and only about ten percent of the portfolio is so cheap we have to look hard to find reasons not to own it. Most of what we own is just not that screamingly attractive. And it is a pity.

headline: Bronte owned Google in 2011 as attractively valued at high-teens PE ex-cash (2011 letter)
reasoning: Hempton highlighted Google as one of the 'less difficult' parts of Silicon Valley trading at a high-teens PE ratio once excess cash was stripped out, contrasting it favourably with HP which was cheap but too hard to run. Google represented one of Bronte's preferred mega-cap positions at the time.
quote: The less difficult parts of Silicon Valley (Google for instance) are at a high teens PE ratio once you take out the excess cash. We own that.

headline: Bronte noted HP was cheap at under 10x PE in 2011 but chose not to own it due to operational complexity
reasoning: Hempton acknowledged HP was cheap at well under 10x PE but explicitly said Bronte felt no need to own it, characterising it as one of the 'difficult parts of Silicon Valley'. This reflects a quality filter: cheapness alone was insufficient without confidence in the business's operability.
quote: The difficult parts of Silicon Valley (e.g. HP) are well under 10 times PE ratios (and we feel no need to own that one).

headline: Bronte Capital long several unspecified stocks with fast-growing earnings that market wrongly attributes entirely to Covid tailwinds
reasoning: The fund holds a small number of other 'super-cheap' stocks where earnings grew rapidly and the market assumes these gains will fully reverse as Covid tailwinds dissipate. Bronte's view is that the earnings are partly correlated to rather than driven by Covid and will not decline as sharply as the market anticipates. The fund cannot be certain of this but views the valuation as sufficiently depressed to justify ownership.
quote: Our other super-cheap stocks have had very fast-growing earnings which people perceive as having been driven by Covid-19 and we perceive as partly correlated to rather than driven by Covid. Our view is that earnings will not decline anything like as fast or far as the market is anticipating. Only time will tell. We are sure that if we had 25 stocks that looked this cheap in 15 diverse sectors and in five different jurisdictions, overall, the portfolio would work out extremely well.

headline: Bronte Capital's short book benefited enormously from the collapse of SPACs and hyper-promoted speculative stocks, many down 80%+
reasoning: The fund ran a large diversified short book concentrated in what it calls 'absolute-nonsense hyper-promoted scams' and recent market promotions including SPACs. These positions delivered astonishing outperformance on the short side, with many positions down 80% or more. The fund added to these shorts on the way down, confident the underlying businesses were approximately worthless.
quote: Midnight struck and a surprising number of shorts have turned into rotting pumpkins, down 80 plus percent. Moreover, often we added to the shorts on the way down, confident in the knowledge that the stocks in question were approximately worthless... The absolute-nonsense hyper-promoted scams and the recent stock market promotions (such as SPACS) have cratered.

headline: Bronte Capital remains long high-ROE 'bond proxy' compounders but acknowledges they are still not cheap after 30-45% falls
reasoning: The fund has owned high-ROE, defensible, consistent-growth 'compounder' stocks for many years and almost never sells them. These stocks fell 30-45% as discount rates rose but remain above historical average valuations. The fund acknowledges these stocks are still not cheap in absolute terms, even if they remain cheap relative to bonds — a relative argument that did not prevent further losses as bond yields rose.
quote: We are long a few bond proxy stocks. We aspire to own stocks with defensible positions which will be bigger and better in five, ten or twenty years. We have owned many for many years and we almost never sell them. That said many of these stocks got very expensive and have since dropped 30-45 percent. They are still not cheap (It was these stocks that helped us roughly match the market in the period until 2020 even though we carried a substantial short book). We would love to say – after 30-45 percent falls – that these stocks are cheap. But it is not true, they are still way above their average historic valuations and above valuations that we think are highly likely to generate good returns.

headline: Bronte Capital never got comfortable owning no-earnings SaaS hyper-growth stocks trading at 60x revenue despite acknowledging long-term potential
reasoning: The fund avoided high-growth SaaS companies growing 50% per annum at 60x revenue multiples, even though many will mature into important businesses. The valuation requirement — revenue needing to grow 15x or more with fat margins and limited competition — is possible (Google being a reference point) but unlikely to materialise across dozens of similarly-priced companies. This category has been among the worst performers in the current downturn.
quote: We do not have much exposure to the hyper-growth stocks. We never got comfortable owning no-earnings SAAS companies growing 50 percent per annum that traded at 60 times revenue, even though we are sure many of these businesses will mature into big and important institutions. ... To believe you will get a good return buying that stock and holding it forever, you needed to assume that revenue will increase 15 or more times and at that point the company will have a strong position with fat margins and a lack of competition. It is possible of course. Google's revenue is up 12-fold since 2009, its margins remain enviable, and competing with them is still quite difficult. But it is not likely to happen to each of the dozens and dozens of companies that were priced this way.

headline: Bronte Capital reflects on missed opportunity in March 2009 when equities were generationally cheap in absolute terms
reasoning: The speaker references the March 2009 market bottom as a generational absolute cheapness in equities, noting they were buying at the time but not aggressively enough, and even carried losing short positions through the second half of 2009. This serves as a cautionary lesson underpinning the current call to become incrementally longer, implying the speaker does not want to repeat the mistake of being too cautious when pessimism is widespread.
quote: Equities were generationally cheap in absolute terms in March 2009. I was buying but nowhere near enough - and indeed we carried some losing shorts through the second six months of 2009.

headline: Bronte Capital maintains significant short book driven by historically high fraud levels, expects to remain net short until fraud opportunities diminish
reasoning: The speaker observes that the underlying level of fraud is as high as they have ever seen it, which by itself justifies maintaining a large short book. The portfolio is described as 'plenty short' and likely to remain so until frauds are no longer easily found. This suggests a disciplined, fraud-focused short strategy rather than macro-driven shorting. Despite the bullish stance on long equities, fraud opportunities keep the overall portfolio from becoming overly net long.
quote: The underlying fraud level is as high as I have ever seen it. We can see plenty of reasons to be bearish - but just the frauds make our portfolio short enough. Indeed, we are plenty short and likely to remain so until I can't find frauds with ease. Beyond that, there is a lot of pessimism around. It has got to be time to be bullish. We certainly do not desire being 125 percent net long or hyper-aggressive like that - but we will take steps to become incrementally longer. We are if anything too short.

headline: Bronte Capital warns that even after sharp declines, equities broadly remain expensive by historical standards
reasoning: Despite significant market drawdowns in 2022, Bronte Capital is cautious about calling the market cheap. The team states that stocks are down a long way but are still expensive by historic standards, and is skeptical of fund managers who have fallen 40% or more and are now claiming their portfolios are bargains. The fund has deployed profits from its short book but finds few salivatingly attractive opportunities on the long side.
quote: Moreover with a few exceptions we discuss below, we do not believe our long book is especially cheap. Stocks are down a long way, but they are still expensive by historic standards. We would love to say that we have deployed our (considerable) profits from shorts well, but in truth with a few exceptions, what we have been buying is not salivatingly attractive. We are deeply skeptical of fund managers who, being down 40 percent or more, are now telling you that their stocks are bargains.

headline: Bronte warns of elevated stock fraud levels particularly in Asia, small caps and smaller resource companies
reasoning: Hempton cautioned that 25 years of deregulation combined with high innovation had produced historically high levels of stock fraud, concentrated in Asia, small caps and smaller resource companies. He contrasted this with mega-caps, which he considered to have much lower fraud risk. This shaped Bronte's quality filter toward larger, better-known businesses.
quote: The places that there have been high returns (Asia, small caps, smaller resource companies) are riddled with fraud. Twenty-five years of deregulation and the high levels of innovation mean we have high and rising levels of stock fraud. Fortunately, there is much less fraud risk in mega-caps.

headline: Bronte bullish on France and Germany in 2011, citing deep manufacturing and productive capacity
reasoning: Hempton expressed a positive view on 'Old Europe', specifically France and Germany, based on their substantial manufacturing and productive capacity. He argued this productive power was underappreciated and made the region an attractive investment destination alongside US mega-caps.
quote: Oh, and we are also bullish on France and Germany. Old Europe has manufacturing and production power of enormous levels. (Remember what they produced to fight wars? Their productive capacity is very [large].)

headline: Bronte Capital remains heavily short hyper-promoted growth and SPAC stocks despite significant collapse in valuations
reasoning: The fund has maintained large short positions in highly promoted, no-earnings SaaS companies and SPACs, which have cratered. As these stocks collapsed the short book has become smaller and migrated to slightly less egregious names. The 'fish-in-the-barrel' phase of shorting is over but shorts remain attractive. The fund believes medium-term returns will still be tilted toward shorts, with longs only incrementally better from current levels.
quote: We have been and remain heavily short the highly promoted nonsense. Alas as these stocks have collapsed our short book has become smaller and has begun to migrate to slightly less scummy stocks. It is not problematic to find shorts – but it is certainly less easy than it was six months ago. The demise of SPACs was good for investors but heralded the end of the fish-in-the-barrel phase of our short book. We used to think all prospective returns were in our short book and that our long book was not especially attractive. Recently, it turned out that way. We also think that the medium-term future will be similar: great returns from shorts, difficulty with longs, though we think from this market level our longs will be incrementally better and shorts incrementally worse.

headline: Bronte Capital identifies Meta Platforms as the most notable cheap stock at 3.5x revenue, 12x earnings and under 8x EBITDA
reasoning: Meta trades at a significant discount to its historical valuation and to the broader market, priced at 3.5x run-rate revenue, 12x earnings and under 8x EBITDA. Earnings are suppressed by metaverse investment spending, which the fund is sceptical about but views as optionally valuable. The core advertising business has delivered over a decade of 20%-plus revenue growth, though growth will now slow. Key risks include TikTok competition, EU privacy regulation hostile to Facebook's business model, declining appeal of the Facebook platform among young people, and the Cambridge Analytica-style ethical controversies. The company bought back over $50bn of stock in the year to March 2022, mostly from operating cash flow.
quote: The most notable cheap stock is Meta Platforms (née Facebook). Meta is priced at 3.5 times run-rate revenue, 12 times earnings and under 8 times EBITDA. The earnings are suppressed by large expenditures on a future 3-D world (the 'metaverse') which presumably has lots of revenue opportunities (but which strains our sense of credulity). Whatever – the traditional business has had revenue growth for over a decade and the revenue growth has never gone under 20 percent. Realistically it will now though. headline: Bronte Capital's Hempton outlines framework for when to average down positions and the dangers of doing so in leveraged or obsolescence-prone businesses
reasoning: Hempton argues that averaging down is one of the most dangerous traps for value investors, citing leverage and technical obsolescence as the two primary scenarios where averaging down is categorically prohibited. At Bronte, each stock has a hard maximum exposure limit (typically 3–9% depending on assessed risk), and the fund manager cannot exceed that limit regardless of price action. A modification allows adding one additional percentage point every six to nine months at the risk manager's discretion, on the theory that waiting reveals whether the original thesis was wrong. Hempton advocates for ex-ante written descriptions of the circumstances under which a position may be averaged down, to prevent the psychological trap of always wanting to add to losing positions.
quote: We have a default at Bronte - and the default at Bronte is that we have a maximum percentage for a stock (typically say 9 percent but often as low as 3 percent depending on how we assess the risk of the stock) and as the fund manager I am allowed to spend that whenever I want but I am not allowed to overspend it. If we have a 6 percent position with a 9 percent loss limit and it halves, I am allowed to add three percentage points more to the exposure. But that is it. Simon, being the risk manager, isn't particularly fussed if add the extra when the stock is down 30 percent of 50 percent, but I can't add it twice. If it is a position on which we agree we are allowed to risk 9 percent then I am allowed to risk 9 percent.

headline: Bronte outlines framework for when to average down: avoid leveraged and obsolescence-prone business models
reasoning: Bronte argues that averaging down is only appropriate when the circumstances under which you are wrong are identifiable and the business model is not highly leveraged or operationally vulnerable. Heavily levered business models (e.g. banks, financials) can go to near-zero and should not be averaged down. Operationally levered models such as commodity miners without debt can still lose 95% of value. Stocks susceptible to technical obsolescence (e.g. Kodak) are also value traps. By contrast, businesses like Coca-Cola with durable economics and no path to bankruptcy are safer to average down.
quote: At a very big picture: averaging down when you are right is very sweet, averaging down when you are wrong is a disaster. At the first pick the question then is 'when are you wrong?', but this is a silly question. If you knew you were wrong you would never have bought the position in the first place. So the question becomes is not 'are you wrong'. That is not going to add anything analytically. Instead the question is 'under what circumstances are you wrong' and 'how would you tell'? When you put it that way it becomes obvious that you must not average down (much) on highly levered business models.

headline: Bronte Capital warns retail-driven market mania is forcing short-sellers to cover across sectors, but sees the environment as ultimately unsustainable

This means that collectively we have spent over USD100 million buying back stock we think is worthless. We are appalled. But it is also the right thing to do. The market is irrational, but we need to remember the aphorism often attributed to Keynes: 'the market can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent'. After all, someone must mop up all of that speculative demand and teach new investors and the deluded a lesson.

It also had an explosion of cases, but the virus is now going roughly sideways at levels much higher than Sweden. headline: Bronte Capital's behavioral epidemiology model suggests COVID-19 R0 tends to one globally, rendering ideological lockdown debates largely moot from an investment perspective
reasoning: Bronte Capital argues that individual risk-benefit calculations naturally equilibrate viral spread so that R0 tends to one regardless of lockdown policy or virus severity. This model superseded their earlier science-based approach, which made them more bearish than warranted. They contend that neither libertarian anti-lockdown nor pro-lockdown narratives correctly explain observed infection curves — both are simply observing the behavioral equilibrium. The virus will remain at this equilibrium until interrupted by herd immunity, a vaccine, or enforced lockdown. This framework has significant implications for how long economic disruption persists and for cross-country investment comparisons.
quote: We argue that the new curves do not indicate anything much about the virus. They are just what you would expect to happen (although to be fair we did not expect it at the time). The idea is simple. For any individual there is a risk to social activity. Getting on a bus entails risk. Singing in a choir much more risk. Working from home and minimizing exposure entails very little risk. And there is a benefit from taking risk. You might be able (or need to) go out to work to earn a living and feed your family. You might have a good time at a party (or choir practice). Any individual will make a decision (partly in knowledge, partly in ignorance) that equilibrates the perceived risk of doing something with the perceived benefit of doing something. This is true across society. As the virus becomes more common the real and perceived risk of going out becomes higher. People will choose to stay at home or take less risk. As the virus becomes less common the risk of going out and doing things is lower so risk taking will increase. The end result is a rough equilibrium where the virus goes sideways. To use the jargon, R 0 tends to one. This seems to happen everywhere.

headline: Bronte Capital concludes enforced lockdown works to control COVID but notes policy appropriateness depends on virus mortality, with authoritarianism benefiting autocratic regimes
reasoning: The behavioral model implies that the only ways to interrupt the R0-tends-to-one equilibrium are herd immunity, a vaccine, or enforced lockdown. That is how China controlled the virus and is how Melbourne, Australia is currently controlling the virus. In other words enforced lockdown works. That doesn't mean that enforced lockdown is the right policy. It would be with Ebola (huge mortality). It almost certainly was the right policy with SARS (it worked, and mortality was high). But it is not the right policy with say a seasonal influenza. We will leave open where this virus sits (although we have our personal views). You can however control this virus if you are prepared to trample civil liberties enough. China did. Suffice to note authoritarianism is good for the virus and the virus is good for authoritarians. The virus has cemented Xi's power in China for instance.

headline: Bronte Capital remains deeply bearish on US equities, viewing the market as historically expensive with aggregate earnings capacity at risk
reasoning: Bronte Capital maintains a bearish portfolio positioning informed by their view that US markets are historically expensive. They see structural risks to aggregate US earnings from historically high income inequality and historically low corporate tax rates, which they believe are both politically and economically unsustainable. quote: Our bearish positioning is informed by our view that markets, particularly the US market, are historically expensive. We could be wrong in this view, so let's explore it. Bulls will point out that the price-to-earnings (PE) ratio of the US market is well within historic norms. Sure, they say, we have an above-average PE ratio—but it was much higher in (say) the tech bubble and at other market tops. Moreover, the market is supported by historically low interest rates and easy monetary policy. Interest rates are indeed low. If you believe that interest rates stay at zero forever then stocks whose earnings are unlikely to decline much (such as say The Coca Cola Company) should be valued at very high PE ratios. But there's the rub: businesses whose earnings are not going to decline much deserve such a valuation. Looking from the top down reveals the risk. We think – instinctively – that the aggregate earnings capacity of US business is at risk.

headline: Bronte Capital discusses the bull case that COVID-19 will permanently increase income inequality and therefore corporate profit share, supporting higher equity valuations

headline: Bronte Capital warns that a broad simultaneous rally in speculative stocks across all sectors is their biggest portfolio risk, as it would undermine the diversification of their short book.

headline: Bronte Capital warns that the simultaneous rise in every category of low-quality stocks on US exchanges is the most extreme 'crap flies' market in their professional career, signalling an irrational market rather than a fundamentally driven rally
reasoning: Bronte Capital observes that every category of low-quality stocks is rising simultaneously on US exchanges, which they describe as historically unprecedented in their experience. But when there is a crazy-strong market for genuinely drossy stocks we conclude the market is just high. This appears to be the most extreme 'crap flies' market we have seen in our professional career.

headline: Bronte Capital maintains large diversified short book in small-cap biotech stocks, flagging COVID-19 announcement hype as a significant risk to short-sellers

It makes Perth-based small cap gold mining stocks promoted at Gold Coast investment conferences (to pick an Australian example) look entirely righteous and honest. We short biotech stocks based not on the science predominantly, but on the people. There are people in the industry with a twenty-year history of hyping stocks for money. When they hype stocks again we short the company. We are short literally dozens of biotechnology stocks all the time, and on average it works, but regularly enough one comes up with a big announcement... headline: Bronte Capital flags historically high income inequality and historically low corporate tax rates in the US as structural risks to aggregate earnings

headline: Bronte Capital confirms decade-long short in Wirecard, ultimately profitable but net a loser due to forced covers during price spike to 191 EUR

The CEO (Markus Braun) has been arrested. The Chief Operating Officer (Jan Marsalek) has disappeared... Eventually we made a bit on the short. But we will never recover our prior losses. Over the past decade Wirecard declined from 8 Euro per share to complete disgrace via 191 Euro. We talk in meetings with clients about frauds on which we are right going from 10 to zero via 100, and unfortunately this discussion is not theoretical. In such cases we are forced to cover to manage our risk, and we will lose money even if we are right. You can't see the Wirecard losses in the past decade's results – but we assure you that they are there. Wirecard is our bête-noir stock, our biggest loser. A loser on which we were eventually right.

headline: Bronte Capital does not view the US equity market as cheap at S&P ~2500 despite a 20-30% decline from highs

And in those times we did not have the sword of COVID-19 threatening to wreak havoc over the economy.

As the currency almost immediately appreciated to 60c we took the hedge off again. The net effect was an extra half of a percent or so in performance for the Australian clients. Should the Australian dollar weaken, you can expect the Australian fund to start currency hedging.

headline: Bronte Capital Amalthea Fund at lowest net investment level ever, holding large cash reserves amid elevated macro uncertainty

headline: Bronte Capital purchased cheap put options on global markets as COVID-19 academic data appeared alarming, providing meaningful downside protection in February

quote: Also, volatility was very low in the market – especially in Europe – and in the face of what we thought was alarming academic information about the new disease we bought a handful of what seemed at the time (and certainly in retrospect) very cheap puts. We do not expect to make money in a market meltdown, we just expect to lose less than most fund managers. We do expect to make money on our shorts and to use that to buy longs at lower prices.

headline: Bronte Capital maintains a structural short book in biotech, sizing positions at 10-20bps due to binary risk of fraudulent promotions
reasoning: Biotech is described as a honeypot for scammers due to ease of promotion and near-total lack of prosecution. Bronte actively shorts biotech stocks they believe are fraudulent, but sizes positions very small (10-20bps) because even a high-conviction short can go up 5-10x on a bullish press release before eventually going to zero. The firm has experienced at least one false-positive (up over 500%) and several correct calls that went up 500% before eventually collapsing. System improvements are being pursued to allow more positions at smaller starting sizes (10bps) for better trading flexibility, particularly around secondary raises which improve borrow availability.
quote: Ease of promotion and the almost total lack of prosecution for frauds makes biotech a honeypot for scammers. We know multiple people who have cashed hundreds of millions personally promoting biotech scams. Thus biotech schemes proliferate, particularly when investors are in a mood to speculate... Thus we tend to size our positions at or below one-fifth of one percent of the portfolio (20 basis points or bps in the jargon). An unlikely, but nonetheless possible, 10x jump in the stock gives us a bad day in the portfolio but does not permanently impair us... With improving systems, we hope to have more biotech shorts – and the starting size will be 10bps rather than 20 bps. We expect to have more trading flexibility.

headline: Bronte Capital warns that widespread adoption of Huawei telecoms equipment is an underappreciated bankruptcy risk for large European carriers, singling out Orange.
reasoning: Many telecommunications companies globally are installing Huawei equipment because it is cheaper, but Bronte believes that if it is proven beyond doubt that the equipment leaks data to China, those companies may be forced to replace the equipment at their own cost. This could be a bankruptcy risk for some very large companies. Bronte is particularly critical of European companies' cavalier attitude to this risk, and specifically names Orange — a very large company — as potentially facing bankruptcy as a result. The firm describes its level of alarm as shocking.
quote: Another one, more realistic, is that many telecommunications companies are installing a large amount of Huawei equipment primarily because it is cheaper. One day it may be shown beyond any doubt that this equipment leaks data back to China. Those companies may have to replace a large amount of equipment on their own dime. Huawei is a bankruptcy risk for some very large companies. We are shocked at the cavalier attitude to this risk shown by some European companies in particular. Orange – which is a huge company - might go bankrupt because of this.

headline: Bronte Capital sees regulatory risk for nicotine pouches as similar to vaping but believes pouches are less likely to drive new teen addiction.
reasoning: Bronte draws a distinction between vaping products (e.g. JUUL) and nicotine pouches such as Zyn. Vaping products came in teen-friendly flavours and were promoted in ways that appeared to target young users, expanding nicotine addiction among youth in the US. Pouches are seen as less likely to attract new users, as the customer base skews toward existing smokers rather than new initiates. While regulatory risk remains a concern for the pouch category, the firm views it as more manageable than for vaping. The cigar business within Swedish Match is specifically flagged as a more direct regulatory target.
quote: The regulatory concerns involving this business are similar to the regulatory concerns over vaping. Vaping products such as JUUL are probably more addictive than cigarettes but much less likely to kill you than cigarettes. If the only customers of vaping products were former cigarette smokers, then concerns about vaping would be lessened. They would, overall, save lives. But vaping products came in teenager-friendly flavours and with promotion that looks like it was targeted at teens. Vapes can and did increase nicotine addiction amongst the young, especially in the USA. For a variety of reasons, we think the pouch business is less likely to attract new users than current smokers. Alas Swedish Match also owns a (much smaller) business selling cheap cigars. That business is a regulatory target, and bad regulatory news is possible.

headline: Bronte Capital views global equity markets as expensive but sees no near-term catalyst for a downturn, with central bank accommodation supporting prices.
reasoning: At year-end 2019, Bronte acknowledges it was privately bearish entering 2019 and was proven wrong by strong returns. Now the firm believes markets are 'often frighteningly expensive' but cannot identify what would knock them down. Central banks are accommodative globally and there are structural factors — including productivity improvements — that could support further gains. The firm admits it is as likely to be wrong again as it was at the end of 2018.
quote: At the end of last year we were privately convinced we were already in a bear market. Returns this year proved us wrong. Now we think markets are expensive – often frighteningly expensive – but we can't see what knocks this market down. Central banks are accommodative everywhere in the world and there are lots of things that should improve global productivity a lot. Markets look like they are going to continue to go up. We are just as likely to be wrong at the end of this year as the end of last year.

headline: Bronte Capital concedes its December 2018 bear market call was wrong, but reaffirms core long/short strategy is unchanged
reasoning: The fund explicitly acknowledges it incorrectly believed a bear market had begun in December 2018. Despite this macro misjudgement, the team did not significantly alter their portfolio construction or process. They are iteratively improving systems and plan to scale up the number of short positions over time, but the fundamental approach remains constant.
quote: We thought in December 2018 that we had entered a bear market. And we were wrong... We didn't change what we did (much) and the outcome didn't change (much). However the external circumstances changed a lot... We won't be changing what we do (much) next year. We will of course be iteratively improving our process. We make mistakes, we make corrections, but the basic portfolio long a relatively small number of high-quality companies and short a highly diverse pile of frauds, fads and failures isn't going to change.

headline: Bronte Capital reflects on 2019 underperformance vs global markets, maintaining long/short strategy through cycle
reasoning: The fund scored high single-digit returns in 2019 while the ACWI was up mid-twenties and S&P500 up low thirties. The team had incorrectly anticipated a bear market entering 2019 following 2018's sharp falls. They consider relative returns important but only over a full market cycle, not in the short term. The core strategy — long high-quality companies, short a diverse mix of frauds, fads, and failures — is not changing, though systems improvements are underway.
quote: In 2019 we scored high single-digit returns. If you had offered us those returns at the beginning of January we would have taken them gladly. We thought in December 2018 that we had entered a bear market. And we were wrong. The All Countries World Index (ACWI) was up in the mid-twenties and the (American) S&P500 up in the low 30s during 2019. In 2018 we had superior returns and they felt much better as global markets fell fairly sharply. We didn't change what we did (much) and the outcome didn't change (much). However the external circumstances changed a lot. We do consider relative returns important, but we believe they should be measured over a cycle.

headline: Bronte Capital has followed Desmarais family-controlled Power Corporation of Canada into a circa 2% position after 15 years of coverage
reasoning: Power Corporation of Canada is described as a financial conglomerate run by sensible people with a mix of good and average businesses. Even its biggest problem, Putnam Investments, is characterised as a fixable management failure rather than a structural one — surprising given it is a multi-hundred-billion dollar asset manager generating only weak profits. Recent corporate restructuring steps have seen the controlling Desmarais family increase their economic interest, which Bronte views as a positive signal and has followed with a circa 2% portfolio allocation.
quote: Power Corporation of Canada is a financial conglomerate run by sensible people with some good businesses and some average businesses in it. Even the biggest problem business in it (Putnam Investments) isn't that bad. It is a miracle of management failure (which they will fix) that allows a multi-hundred-billion-dollar asset manager to be only weakly profitable. There have been several changes in corporate structure which amount to the controlling Desmarais family buying more stock or increasing their economic interest in the underlying assets. We have followed them for a couple of percent of your funds. John followed this business for over fifteen years before we ever purchased any of the stock.

headline: Bronte Capital fully exited Rolls Royce on engine cost overruns, pension headwinds, and management concerns
reasoning: Rolls Royce was sold entirely due to continuous overruns in fixing Dreamliner engines and increased pension costs. Although the stock appeared cheap on valuation, the range of operational problems and management's inability to demonstrate control over them was concerning. quote: We sold out of our Rolls Royce position in its entirety. The continuous overruns in the cost of fixing the engines for Boeing Dreamliners, along with increased pension costs, had us concerned. The stock looks cheap – but there is plenty that can go wrong – and the management has not demonstrated control over their wide range of problems. After we sold, ValueAct (an investor we much admire) exited the board. Presumably they will be selling too and as they are insiders in every sense, we figure they must be worried too.

headline: Bronte Capital increases Swedish Match to its biggest position, driven by explosive US growth of Zyn nicotine pouches.
