Bronte sharply increased its position — now its largest — based on the success of Zyn nicotine pouches in the US, where the non-Scandinavian segment is growing over 100% per annum. The firm believes part of the growth is driven by consumers shifting from cigarettes to vaping products and then to pouches. Regulatory risk is acknowledged (similar to vaping concerns), but pouches are seen as less likely to attract new teen users compared to flavoured vapes. A smaller cigar business within Swedish Match is identified as a regulatory risk and potential source of bad news.
quote: Swedish Match is a long-term holding of Bronte. It is a seller of non-cigarette tobacco products, mostly Snus and nicotine pouches. Snus, and to an even greater extent, nicotine pouches, are very high dose nicotine products but with substantially lower cancer risks than cigarettes. Scandinavia has had a major shift from cigarettes to these products thereby increasing aggregate nicotine addiction but reducing deaths from tobacco illness. We increased our position in Swedish Match sharply (it is now our biggest position) based on the success of Zyn, a high-dose nicotine pouch business in the US. The growth rate of the non-Scandinavian Snus and nicotine pouches business is over 100 percent. We think in part this is driven by a shift from cigarettes to others' vaping products and then to pouches (especially Zyn).

headline: Bronte Capital identifies a serious global climate policy response as a tail risk that could strand carbon-intensive assets and associated debt.

Bronte sees this as a genuine long-term tail risk, though a realistic political analysis suggests it is not highly likely in the short term. quote: The World might get really serious about dealing with greenhouse gases. This will leave more than a few carbon-intensive assets stranded and the associated debt worthless or nearly worthless. A realistic political analysis does not suggest this is very likely in the short term.

headline: Bronte Capital flags the US corporate credit market, especially private equity-owned companies, as a potential systemic risk with comically poor credit metrics.
reasoning: Bronte observes many companies with sky-high equity valuations but single-B or worse credit ratings for which debt repayment appears unrealistic. The situation in corporate debt — particularly American corporate debt — is described as 'comical.' Credit metrics for private equity-owned companies are flagged as even worse than for public companies, with limited visibility. The firm warns of a potential nasty corporate credit cycle as a tail risk.
quote: We have seen many companies with sky-high equity valuations and single B credit ratings (or worse) for which we can't see any reasonable way they will pay back their debt. The situation in corporate debt, especially American corporate debt, is comical. Nobody cares about credit any more. Credit metrics for private-equity owned companies (which are sometimes invisible) are even worse than with public companies. There could be a nasty corporate credit cycle.

headline: Bronte Capital exited General Electric on 737 Max exposure and debt load concerns
reasoning: GE was held as a sum-of-the-parts play on its good businesses, particularly jet engines via CFM's sole-supplier relationship with the 737. The 737 Max crisis made Bronte deeply uncomfortable given GE's heavy debt load and difficult-to-estimate obligations in long-term care and power systems. Management of the bad businesses (power systems, long-term care) created enough uncertainty that the position was fully exited. The combination of debt, problematic subsidiaries, and the 737 Max overhang proved too much to hold.
quote: General Electric is a classic case of some good businesses (jet engines, some medical and a few other bits) being mixed with some problematic businesses (power systems) and loaded with difficult to estimate obligations (notably long-term care) and way too much debt. Some of the good bits (especially jet engines) were within our circle of competence. We bought it because we liked the good bits and we were comfortable enough with a sum-of-the-parts valuation. The problem is that the most valuable part of the jet-engine business is that CFM (the engine consortium with Safran) is the sole-supplier of engines to 737 planes. The 737 Max situation, given the debt load, made us deeply uncomfortable – to the extent that we simply exited the position.

headline: Bronte Capital identifies biotech as the most attractive short-selling sector due to pervasive fraud, speculative promotion, and near-zero regulatory enforcement
reasoning: Biotech is described as the most attractive sector for scammers because small biotech stocks are lottery tickets that almost always fail, even with honest management. Promoters exploit the complexity of the science and investors' inability to evaluate drug prospects, combined with the appealing narrative of curing diseases. Crucially, regulatory and legal recourse for defrauded investors is extremely limited, making fraud low-risk for promoters. The fund notes it knows multiple individuals who have personally cashed hundreds of millions promoting biotech scams. The firm is actively expanding its short book in this sector and sees the opportunity as particularly rich in the current speculative investor mood.
quote: Biotechnology is possibly the most attractive sector for scammers in the stock market and the most attractive sector for us as short sellers. A small biotechnology stock is a lottery ticket. Either the technology results in a therapeutic drug and (maybe) a lot of money or it doesn't. Usually it doesn't, even if the scientists and the management are entirely honest... Ease of promotion and the almost total lack of prosecution for frauds makes biotech a honeypot for scammers. We know multiple people who have cashed hundreds of millions personally promoting biotech scams. Thus biotech schemes proliferate, particularly when investors are in a mood to speculate.

headline: Bronte Capital heavily overweights Australian short positions, citing improving ASIC regulatory environment and structural conditions ripe for fraud.
reasoning: Bronte previously identified Australia as fertile ground for stock promoters, citing historically weak regulation, strong defamation laws, and index-driven equity markets. The firm notes an improvement: ASIC has become proactive for the first time in living memory, taking legal action and requesting new legislative powers. This combination of a fraud-friendly environment and a newly aggressive regulator is described as ideal for short-sellers. Bronte's biggest short positions are heavily weighted to Australia. The firm acknowledges the risk that regulators may disappoint and notes that shorts are driven by business concerns as well as regulatory ones. It declines to name specific targets due to Australian defamation laws.
quote: In our last letter, we noted that Australia—a land without a substantial downturn since the early 1990s—is nirvana for stock promoters. We identified several reasons, including an historically weak regulatory environment, strong defamation laws, and an index-driven equity market. Our view has improved, slightly. For the first time in living memory we are seeing the Australian securities regulator (ASIC) becoming proactive. They are observing problems, they are taking some legal action, and where they do not have legislative powers they are asking the government to act. For a short-seller, an environment ripe for fraud but with a newly-aggressive regulator is a great combination. Our biggest short positions are thus heavily weighted to Australia.

headline: Bronte Capital warns that growth of passive investing creates both a threat and opportunity for short-sellers as index inclusion increasingly transfers wealth from passive investors to stock promoters
reasoning: As passive investing grows as a percentage of all money managed, index inclusions generate forced buying that can cause massive price spikes in promoted or fraudulent stocks, enabling insiders and related parties to sell into a captive buyer base. Bronte cites a historical example of a stock under SEC fraud inquiry that spiked dramatically upon Russell 3000 inclusion in 2009, directly transferring wealth from passive investors — including retirement funds — to people they regard with deep scepticism. The firm believes this dynamic will become more frequent and more severe as passive investing continues to grow, both creating risks (forced short-covering around inclusion events) and opportunities (index funds normally lend out their securities, facilitating short-selling).
quote: Getting put in an index is the best thing that can happen to a stock promote. You get lots of forced buyers. Indexing is growing rapidly as a percent of all money managed. Things in financial markets that are sensible when only three percent of money does it (like indexing) are often stupid when two thirds of money does it. But the opportunity is real too. Index funds normally lend

headline: Bronte Capital warns rapid growth of passive investing will create both threats and opportunities for short sellers as stock promotes gain forced index buyers
reasoning: Bronte argues that indexing, which was sensible when only a small fraction of money used it, becomes problematic at scale. As passive money grows, stock promoters can engineer inclusion in broad indices like the Russell or S&P500 to attract forced buying. Index funds typically lend their shares at low borrow rates ('General Collateral'), making large-scale promotes more vulnerable to short attack. Bronte sees this as both a threat (needing to avoid momentum spikes) and a major opportunity to find large, heavily promoted names with cheap borrow.
quote: Things in financial markets that are sensible when only three percent of money does it (like indexing) are often stupid when two thirds of money does it. In this case the rapid growth of passive (or nearly passive) money will result in the best opportunity stock promoters will ever have. From our perspective the growth of passive investing will cause opportunities and threats. Spikes like the one above when promotes go into the Russell (or worse into the S&P500 or the Dax or another major index) will become more common and we will need to duck them. But the opportunity is real too. Index funds normally lend their shares – so we may find large-scale promotes with rock bottom ("General Collateral") borrow rates and large market caps. That makes us salivate.

headline: Bronte Capital warns Australia's 200-stock index is disproportionately large relative to market size, making it susceptible to index-inclusion fraud relative to narrower global benchmarks
reasoning: Bronte notes that Australia's main index has 200 holdings in a much smaller economy compared to the US S&P500 which has 500 stocks but in an economy 13 times larger with far better-researched companies. The breadth of the Australian index relative to the depth of the market creates structural entry points for fraudulent or suspect companies. They note the ASX has partially acknowledged this by shrinking the All-Ordinaries from 300 to 200 stocks.
quote: A smaller market like Australia already has this problem to some extent because its main index has 200 holdings. Compare this with USA where the main index admittedly has 500 stocks but they are much bigger businesses in an economy 13 times larger and are much better researched. We think the sheer number of stocks in the Australian index will wind up being a problem for the Australian market. The ASX however is wising up to this threat. The all-ordinaries used to have 300 stocks. The main index now has only 200.

headline: Bronte Capital meaningfully reduces oil and gas short book as most fraudulent promotes have gone to zero or become too real to short
reasoning: Bronte Capital has significantly shrunk its oil and gas short positions after finding a large number of hype-driven companies and promoters with sketchy records, many of which have now gone to zero or become too small to pursue. Some promoters used their stock to raise capital, bought real assets and bootstrapped into legitimate businesses with real optionality — making them unsuitable shorts. A few residual shorts remain where debt levels suggest companies should still go to zero, but in aggregate the sector has become a small position and is no longer a focus of the firm.
quote: There has been one major change in our portfolio which is that we have meaningfully shrunk our oil and gas short positions. This might disappoint some readers. One mathematically inclined allocator put our portfolio through Novus (a portfolio assessment tool) and decided of all the sectors we invested in that we were best at oil and gas. They wondered what the trick was. Well there was no trick as such. We just found (a) a lot of hype in the industry and (b) a lot of people who have sketchy records associated with stocks with market caps above US $1 billion and financial plans promising a lot of cash in future years but with terrible current cash flows. We shorted them. Most of the frauds we were short have gone to zero (or at least to market caps so low that we are no longer interested in chasing them). But some of our sketchy people used their dodgy stock to raise money, bought real assets and boot-strapped themselves into businesses we regard as too real, and with too much optionality, to short. We think the juice has been squeezed from that lemon.

headline: Bronte Capital views US equity market as expensive and flags growing risk of over-reliance on its extended outperformance

The flip side of US outperformance driving away investors is a more attractive prospective return in markets that have lagged. Bronte implicitly positions this as a reason to avoid overweighting US equities.
quote: As the performance differential has grown so, to our way of thinking, has the risk of over reliance on the expensive USA market. The extended run of outperformance has driven away many capital allocators – and therein lies the prospect of reduced future downside risks and higher potential returns.

headline: Bronte Capital reconfirms belief that European equity valuations are much more sensible than North American valuations, with growing risk premium in the US
reasoning: Following a trip to Europe including England, Bronte reaffirmed its multi-year view that European equities are more attractively valued than US equities. While this view has not yet been rewarded, the growing performance differential has increased the risk of over-reliance on the expensive US market. Bronte notes the extended US outperformance has driven away many capital allocators, which they see as a potential source of reduced future downside and improved return prospects in Europe.
quote: Our trip to Europe (and, in particular, England) reconfirmed our belief that valuations are much more sensible in Europe than in North America. That is a belief we have held for a few years and it hasn't helped us yet. Nonetheless, as the performance differential has grown so, to our way of thinking, has the risk of over reliance on the expensive USA market. The extended run of outperformance has driven away many capital allocators – and therein lies the prospect of reduced future downside risks and higher potential returns.

headline: Bronte Capital notes US market at all-time highs while non-US markets remain weak, a positioning headwind that the fund has so far navigated successfully
reasoning: The American market is trading at all-time records while many non-American markets are weak. Bronte's general positioning — with most shorts in the US and longs scattered across the US, Europe, New Zealand and other markets — would typically be expected to be hostile to performance in such an environment. Despite this, results for the four months to October were described as acceptable for the September quarter and excellent in October.
quote: As we have said many times the bulk of our shorts are in the USA and our longs are scattered mostly between the USA and Europe with one large New Zealand position and some small positions in other markets (Indonesia, Canada, Japan). The American market is trading at all-time records but many non-American markets are weak. This market should be hostile to Bronte's general positioning – but despite this our results for the four months were pretty good.

headline: Bronte Capital expects to be overweight Australian short positions given proliferation of suspect companies with large market caps
reasoning: Bronte sees a rich field of 'spivvy people associated with companies with large market caps' in Australia, analogising the current environment to their earlier overweight in oil and gas shorts. They acknowledge regulatory reform is possible but unlikely to be comprehensive or timely, reinforcing the structural opportunity for short selling in Australian equities.
quote: Inevitably we are likely to wind up overweight in Australian shorts much for the same reason we were once overweight in oil and gas shorts. headline: Bronte Capital views Australia as uniquely fertile ground for stock fraud due to weak regulation, strong defamation laws, and heavy index/quasi-index ownership by large superannuation funds

Clear cases of fraud (like Astarra-Trio) have resulted only in industry-bans for most participants. And those that did go to prison got relatively short sentences. Frauds that are difficult to prosecute are mostly not prosecuted at all. Second, defamation laws in Australia are very strong. It is simply not open for an Australian to say what they think of many companies in the market unless they want to spend considerable amounts of time with lawyers. Thirdly, and most importantly – the market is very heavily index or quasi-index held. The large retirement funds (particularly some "industry funds") are amongst the largest shareholders of companies we regard as fraudulent (or at least highly suspect). The combination of these things means that a lot of money is going to be taken from retirement accounts with passive or quasi passive-management and given to stock promoters.

Competent multilingual executives who can take the best of Japan to the world are rare. That said, thirty years of deflation has produced some cheap and good companies. It is our job to find them.

headline: Bronte Capital uses market-cap-to-GDP as a key valuation signal to dynamically tilt portfolio net exposure, consistent with Warren Buffett's preferred market valuation metric.
reasoning: The firm notes that dynamic adjustment of the 60-40 equivalent portfolio requires a reliable measure of market expensiveness. quote: It would be better (but requires some judgement) to be slightly dynamic, having a 60-40 portfolio whenever the market is cheap, a 50-50 portfolio when it is middling and a 40-60 portfolio when it is expensive. You would need a measure of 'expensive' and the one we might choose would be market cap to GDP. This is also a measure that Warren Buffett cites. We have another measure, which achieves a similar result: if our system for finding shorts is identifying limited opportunities we get longer... If by contrast – we can find shorts at will – but finding rational longs is difficult we will run with that too. And our portfolio will look more like it does now – something like 110 long, 60 short.

headline: Bronte Capital outlines a dynamic long-short framework targeting ~0.5 net beta, replacing bond allocation with a short book to improve risk-adjusted returns over the 60-40 benchmark.
reasoning: Bronte Capital proposes replacing the bond leg of a 60-40 portfolio with a short book that generates genuine alpha rather than near-zero real yields. Targeting a net portfolio beta of 0.5, the stylised portfolio runs approximately 150% long and 50% short, with the short book estimated to carry a beta of around 2. The advantage of the short book is not primarily to profit in down markets but to enable a larger long exposure without proportionately increasing downside risk. The firm also dynamically adjusts gross exposure based on valuation signals (e.g. market cap to GDP) and the relative availability of short vs long ideas, ranging from 140L/40S when markets are cheap to 110L/60S when expensive.
quote: We (usually) do not own bonds though. We can obtain far more negative correlation to equities via our short book. Our default positioning is to reconstruct a 60-40 portfolio but throw out the (very low return) bonds and add in our (genuinely alpha generating) shorts... If we were to manage to a portfolio beta of 0.5 we could set our portfolio as 150 percent long and 50 percent short. The long book would be beta of one and the short book a beta of two. The net beta of the portfolio would 0.5... In this stylized portfolio the advantage of the short book is not that it makes you money when the market goes down. Rather it allows you to make more money when the market goes up without losing as much when the market goes down. You don't short to make money per-se, rather you short because it allows you to go more long.

The beta appears to go well over two in a falling market. We hope this is generally true – but to be honest we do not have enough data points. If it is true then the fund should be positive when the market eventually retreats – at least for the first part of the retreat. That said – we are as short as we have ever been – and even then, we think our effective beta is between 0.1 and 0.4.

quote: We bought a sizable position in Visa early this year. The logic was simple enough. Visa is a very high-quality business taking a very small amount (basis points) of every transaction on its network. Profits were rising for two reasons: a) The integration of Visa Europe, and b) The advent of smart-chips and other things that drive transaction volumes, especially small transactions. It is now common to buy your coffee merely with the tap of a card. The smart-chip integration happened earlier in Australia than in the rest of the world, so living here gave us a (slight) advantage in seeing how this has panned out. When we purchased Visa shares, the stock had a price/earnings ratio about 5 points higher than the market, though the company enjoyed obvious growth and some potentially excess capital that could be used to buy back stock. Even after the (then hypothetical) buy-­‐back, the PE ratio was about 25. We thought this an okay value, but we do not imagine Ben Graham (the godfather of value investing) would have cheered. Fortunately, the stock has continued to rise, such that today's PE ratio is closer to 40. We still think it is okay, but Ben Graham has gone from not cheering to jeering slightly from the sidelines. The position is for sale if we see a genuine threat materialize.

headline: Bronte Capital flags poor Australian mortgage underwriting standards as a structural risk, with brokers helping borrowers 'embellish' loan applications
reasoning: Approximately two years ago, Bronte Capital and Jonathan Tepper of Variant Perception conducted a field trip to mortgage brokers in Western Sydney to assess bank underwriting standards. They found standards to be unambiguously weak, with brokers openly able to help applicants embellish loan applications, and some lenders identified as easier to deceive than others. UBS survey data corroborated these findings, showing that a third of customers with interest-only loans were unaware they had such loans, with brokers competing by structuring lowest monthly payments and placing borrowers into homes they could not afford. The firm draws a parallel to pre-GFC US subprime mortgage behaviour.
quote: Almost two years ago Jonathan Tepper of Variant Perception and John Hempton went for a tour of mortgage brokers in Western Sydney. The goal was not to determine when or even if the Sydney housing market would cease its ceaseless rise. Rather, we simply aimed to determine whether bank underwriting standards were good or bad. In our view, they were unambiguously bad. The banks' diligence appeared to be weaker than widely believed. We had no trouble finding a broker who could help you 'embellish' your loan application. Some banks (and bankers) were less diligent than others, and the brokers could identify them for you. Such brokers preferred the lenders they considered to be easier to deceive. In this regard UBS has been surveying Australian mortgagees in recent years and the results are not encouraging. headline: Bronte Capital warns Australian mortgage underwriting standards are unambiguously bad, creating asymmetric downside risk in housing
reasoning: Bronte Capital conducted primary research into Australian bank underwriting standards and concluded they were unambiguously bad. Brokers were able to help borrowers 'embellish' loan applications, with certain banks identified by brokers as easier to deceive. UBS survey data corroborated this, finding a third of interest-only borrowers did not even know they had interest-only loans. The firm draws a parallel to pre-GFC US mortgage broker behaviour. While bad underwriting does not guarantee a housing price fall, the firm argues the asymmetry is against investors: in a downturn, losses will be larger than expected and assurances from banks and fund managers about their due diligence should be viewed with suspicion.
quote: we simply aimed to determine whether bank underwriting standards were good or bad. In our view, they were unambiguously bad. The banks' diligence appeared to be weaker than widely believed. We had no trouble finding a broker who could help you "embellish" your loan application. Some banks (and bankers) were less diligent than others, and the brokers could identify them for you. Such brokers preferred the lenders they considered to be easier to deceive. UBS has been surveying Australian mortgagees in recent years and the results are not encouraging. For example, they discovered that a third of customers with interest-only loans did not even know they had interest-only loans. How this happens is that brokers compete in part by structuring the lowest monthly payment, placing customers into homes they cannot actually afford. This is the same behavior that was seen from brokers prior to the mortgage crisis in the USA. But bad underwriting does not imply the housing market is going to fall, just as high equity prices do not imply that the stock market is going to fall. What it does indicate, in our view, is that the asymmetry is against you: in a retreat, the downside will be larger than expected.

headline: Bronte Capital warns US wireless carriers could become structurally short candidates if spectrum proves genuinely unlimited and price wars intensify.
reasoning: Bronte Capital's original thesis was predicated on low-frequency spectrum scarcity giving carriers pricing power. The fund draws an analogy to the airline industry: businesses with high fixed costs, low marginal costs, and intense competition are structurally dangerous because competition drives prices toward marginal cost, making fixed-cost recovery impossible and risking bankruptcy. Bronte has shifted its view from the carriers being exceptional longs to potentially good shorts, but wants to see actually falling wireless revenue before establishing short positions.
quote: We actually think it could get quite bad at the carriers. The world's worst business is one with high fixed costs, low marginal costs, and lots of competition. In that case the competitive forces will drive prices down to the low marginal costs – and it will be impossible to recover fixed costs. When the fixed costs are debt financed, bankruptcy often follows. That is precisely why the airlines have been bankrupt many times. The marginal cost of filling the otherwise empty seat is very low – and competition at times drives prices to those very low marginal costs. If wireless telephony capacity really is unlimited and the carriers insist on price wars then the future is bleak indeed. (For shareholders, if not for consumers.) We have gone from thinking the carriers were exceptionally good longs to believing they might be good shorts. We are not there yet: we would like to see falling wireless revenue first. But if spectrum isn't truly scarce this could get ugly.

headline: Bronte Capital's short of Valeant Pharmaceuticals was one of their most profitable short positions in years, driven by fraudulent revenue reporting and a fundamentally flawed acquisition-driven business model.
reasoning: Valeant built a business model of acquiring drug companies, raising prices, cutting R&D and non-revenue staff, and running drugs through its existing sales channels. Despite the stock doubling after Bronte initially went short, effective position sizing and risk management meant they still generated strong returns on the short. Bronte's core principle — 'there is rarely just one cockroach in the kitchen' — drove them to keep digging after spotting initial discrepancies.
quote: Valeant is a huge pharmaceutical company which peaked at a market capitalization of over $USD90 billion. This stock was held in size by numerous sophisticated hedge funds, and it is possible they lost more money on this stock than any in history. Valeant was a core Bronte short and the most profitable short we have done in a few years... Our favorite example was registering about 70 pharmacies in names borrowed from Stephen King novels so that, we suspect, insurance companies could be hoodwinked into paying for over-priced prescriptions... We make an assumption when shorting stocks that is often but not always correct: there is rarely just one cockroach in the kitchen. It has an often forgotten corollary: if you spot one cockroach as an investor—whether long or short—it behooves you to go looking for more. And in the Valeant case we did. Sadly, this alone is insufficient to make money as a short-seller. Valeant stock doubled after we initially spotted it. We made money because our position was small and our risk management approach effective.

quote: Our put options in Valeant (VRX), a much debated drug company, expired in January and whist they had long been marked to a significant profit it was nonetheless pleasing to close them out so successfully. On the way up Valeant was a volatile and difficult short and put options proved the lowest risk way to express our disquiet with its contentious business model.

headline: S&P 500 aggregate earnings likely to fall within 12 months as wage pressure rises and the dollar strengthens, reversing a 20-year golden age of corporate profit expansion
reasoning: Bronte argues that two structural tailwinds for US corporate earnings — globalisation (which allowed offshoring and margin expansion) and wage stagnation — are both weakening. A protectionist political turn threatens the internationalisation trend, while a stronger US dollar reduces the dollar value of foreign earnings on translation. Critically, US wage growth has now exceeded nominal GDP growth for the first time in a while, with Atlanta Fed data and sub-indices for job-switchers suggesting further acceleration. Higher wages are good for workers but compress S&P margins. The firm is 'fairly comfortable' that S&P aggregate earnings will be lower in 12 months, though they flag this is outside their usual bottoms-up bailiwick and internal debate continues. They also note non-GAAP adjustments make reported 'earnings' a malleable concept.
quote: We would argue that both of these trends— internationalization and wage stagnation— are weakening. A protectionist/anti-globalist streak has appeared in politics. Moreover the US dollar has strengthened considerably, and mere translation diminishes the US dollar value of foreign earnings. But more importantly US wage pressure is clearly upward. Anecdotal evidence abounds, such as Walmart voluntarily giving pay rises to their staff (because they had trouble holding on to them). For the first time in a while, nominal wage growth exceeds nominal GDP growth. The sub-indices in this series (such as wage growth for people who are shifting jobs) suggest accelerating growth in wages. This is, of course, great for workers. But it is not so good for S&P earnings. Bronte is fairly comfortable that S&P aggregate earnings will be down in twelve months.

headline: Buffett market-cap-to-GDP measure at all-time highs, though structurally higher ratio is partially justified by US global share gains and reduced competition for large-cap tech
reasoning: The Wilshire 5000 total market cap as a percentage of US GDP is at all-time highs, suggesting large potential falls. Bronte notes this measure should trend up over time because US businesses are capturing a larger share of global business than in prior decades, and dominant companies like Google face less competition than the large-cap incumbents of 50 years ago (e.g. US Steel), justifying structurally higher earnings-to-GDP ratios. Even so, the measure supports the view that markets are more expensive than the simple P/E of 21 implies.
quote: It is however fair to say that this measure should trend up over time. US businesses are capturing a larger proportion of global business than, say, in 1970. Further, the big companies now (such as Google) are probably less subject to competition than big companies of 50 years ago (such as US Steel). Because they are less subject to competition, the earnings as a proportion of GDP should be higher now than 50 years ago. That said, this measure is supportive of the idea that markets are more expensive than the simple PE ratio of 21 would suggest.

headline: S&P 500 appears 10-20% overvalued on trailing PE of ~21x, implying muted future returns but not imminent catastrophic losses
reasoning: With the S&P 500 at 2,269 and a trailing 12-month PE of just under 21, Bronte views the index as elevated versus history but not at dot-com extremes (which peaked near 30). They note that lower interest rates justify higher PE ratios than historical averages. On their assessment the index is 10-20% too high, enough to temper future return expectations but not so extreme as to imply large permanent capital losses imminently. The median NYSE stock PE, compiled by Professor Ken French, is at an all-time high, suggesting stock-picking pickings are thinner than normal.
quote: On January 10, 2017 the S&P 500 stands at 2269, with a trailing 12-month price-to-earnings (PE) ratio of just under 21. This PE ratio is elevated versus history but not astoundingly high especially if compared to the peak of the dot-com bubble when it nearly touched 30. Moreover interest rates are much lower than they were then, so PE ratios should be higher now than at most times in history. Taking these numbers seriously means the S&P looks high but not astoundingly so. If anything, the index is 10-20 percent too high, which is high enough to make one cautious about future return expectations but not so high as to imply large and imminent permanent capital losses.

headline: Running net short the US on a beta-adjusted basis; US market expensive as good companies unavailable at attractive prices and iffy companies elevated
reasoning: Bronte's bottom-up lens reads the US market as expensive because good companies cannot be bought at attractive prices and there is a plenitude of weak companies trading at high prices (ideal short candidates). Notwithstanding counterarguments about S&P 500 P/E ratios not looking particularly high by historical standards, Bronte is running as close to neutral as prudent risk management allows, with a net short position in the US on a beta-adjusted basis.
quote: From our perch, we think markets are expensive, particularly in America. As a result we are running as close to neutral as prudent risk management allows. We are – on a beta-adjusted basis – net short in America and long in Europe. We believe markets are expensive when the good companies we find cannot be bought at prices we consider attractive and when we find a plenitude of iffy companies at high prices to short.

headline: Added at reasonable if not spectacular value as part of European allocation
reasoning: Bronte Capital added a decent sized position in Bayer over the past year. The position was described as being at reasonable if not spectacular value. The addition contributed to the fund being overweight Europe and overweight the Euro, which hurt returns due to a strong US dollar.
quote: We have added a few decent sized positions to the portfolio over the past year – notably Bayer (from Germany) and Elementis (which is listed in the UK but is really a US dollar company). Both of these were at reasonable if not spectacular values. This has left us a currency imbalance which we have fought for a while. We are overweight Europe and as we did not have much currency hedging we wound up being overweight the Euro.

headline: Monsanto acquisition at a much higher multiple than Bayer itself is a key risk; German governance structure prevents buybacks that would be the obvious alternative
reasoning: The big problem with the Bayer investment thesis is that Bayer is acquiring Monsanto at a much higher multiple than its own trading multiple. For an American CEO the obvious alternative would be buybacks, but German supervisory boards include union representatives and are focused on preserving the company's solvency and pension guarantees, making buybacks unlikely. The deal will lever up Bayer's currently under-utilised balance sheet significantly if it closes.
quote: The big problem is that Bayer is buying Monsanto at a much bigger multiple than itself. For the average American CEO the solution would be obvious: do not buy Monsanto, buy your own stock back. This is Germany and that is not going to happen. German supervisory boards have union representatives – and as the company's solvency guarantees pensions the boards are opposed to buy-backs. So the company is doing a highly priced and unpopular acquisition.

headline: Bullish on a heads-I-win-tails-I-win structure: if Monsanto deal closes, PE compresses to 10-12x and stock rises; if deal is blocked politically, stock also rises
reasoning: Bronte sees Bayer as a near-no-lose position. If the Monsanto acquisition closes, Bayer's under-utilised balance sheet gets levered up and the price-earnings ratio falls to well under 12, possibly as low as 10, which should push the stock higher. Conversely, if the deal is blocked on economic nationalism grounds (US journalists put the probability at 50-50), the stock should also re-rate upward as the overhang is removed. The firm acknowledges Bayer is not their highest-quality holding but says quality is still well above average and they are not paying a full price. They frame the German CEO's appetite for global domination via acquisitions as a macro-style observation about strategic intent.
quote: We think this is one where it is very hard to lose. If the Monsanto deal closes the under-utilised balance sheet of Bayer will be levered up fairly hard. The price-earnings ratio of the stock comes down – probably to well under 12 and maybe as low as 10. The stock will go up if this happens. However economic nationalism has raised its head. There is a real possibility, which American journalists put at 50-50, that the Monsanto deal will be politically blocked. The stock will also go up if this happens. This is not the highest quality company in our portfolio – but we have not had to move the quality standards very much. It is certainly a way higher quality business than average. And we are not paying a lot for it.

headline: Lucentis priced at ~$24,000/year for Wet AMD; Genentech avoids double-blind Avastin trial to protect revenue, raising sustainability questions in Europe
reasoning: Genentech (Roche subsidiary) developed Lucentis as a treatment for Wet AMD, priced at around $24,000 per year ($2,000 per injection). The drug works on the same mechanism as the much cheaper Avastin (~$50/dose), which Genentech markets for cancer. Genentech has not subjected Avastin to a proper double-blind study for AMD, allowing Lucentis to remain the prescribed option in most markets. Some European governments are beginning to mandate Avastin use, creating pricing pressure.
quote: So Genentech came up with a very similar drug (Lucentis) which works the same way as Avastin and which they tested as a treatment for Wet AMD. It works. They charge a large amount for it (about $24,000 a year or $2,000 an injection). They never subjected Avastin to a proper double-blind study. As Avastin is not 'proved' to be effective it is not prescribed – and so Genentech gets lots of extra money from selling Lucentis instead.

headline: Eylea co-developed with Bayer generates significant revenues priced around $24,000 per year for Wet AMD; sustainability of pricing open to debate
reasoning: Regeneron developed Eylea together with Bayer as an alternative to Lucentis and Avastin for treating Wet AMD. It is priced similarly to Lucentis at approximately $24,000 per year. European governments are beginning to mandate the cheaper Avastin in some cases, creating pricing sustainability risk. Australian government currently reimburses only Lucentis and Eylea, not Avastin, suggesting some durability but with ongoing debate.
quote: Eylea is yet another version of the drug developed by Regeneron (listed in the US) and Bayer. It also gets a lot of money and is priced about the same as Lucentis. Whether these prices are sustainable is open for debate. Concerningly however, some European governments dictate Avastin.

headline: Bayer's acquisition viewed as financially questionable — paying over 4x revenue for a company that sells GMO seeds and sues farmers, making the combined entity unattractive to pharma-focused investors
reasoning: The Monsanto acquisition is the primary market concern overhanging Bayer. Bronte notes Bayer is paying well over 4 times revenue for Monsanto, and it is far from obvious financially why they should do this deal. Monsanto's products — genetically modified seeds, pesticides, and seed royalty litigation — are deeply unpopular, especially in Europe. The deal makes Bayer's seed technology business too large to attract its natural pharmaceutical investor base, creating a valuation discount. The market is described as hating this deal.
quote: The main knock on the stock is that they are buying Monsanto to create by far the biggest seed technology business in the world. They are paying well over 4 times revenue for Monsanto. It is far from obvious financially why they should do this acquisition. Moreover, it is pretty clear that the market hates this deal. This is now too big a seed technology business to attract pharmaceutical focused investors. Monsanto is a company that sells genetically modified seeds (unpopular in Europe) and pesticides (also unpopular) and sues farmers for not paying seed royalties (unpopular everywhere). As far as the market is concerned this is a big bad deal.

headline: Long Europe on a beta-adjusted basis as bottom-up research finds more attractive valuations than the US
reasoning: In contrast to the US, Bronte's bottom-up research is finding more attractive long opportunities in Europe, as exemplified by Bayer. The fund is beta-adjusted net long Europe versus net short America, reflecting a relative value view driven by bottom-up stock-finding rather than explicit macro forecasting.
quote: We are – on a beta-adjusted basis – net short in America and long in Europe. As experts on individual trees, it behooves us to occasionally have a look at the forest in which they're growing. That is, to understand the macro environment in which we're operating, even if we do not attempt to specifically forecast it ourselves.

headline: Expensive markets force value managers to lower quality standards, a trap the team explicitly refuses to fall into
reasoning: In a rising market, genuinely cheap quality companies become scarce, and the only stocks that screen cheaply tend to be cheap for a reason. Bronte Capital warns that many fund managers come undone by purchasing progressively lower quality stocks as markets become more expensive. The team commits to maintaining quality standards rather than chasing apparent value in an expensive market.
quote: There are two iconic ways value managers get themselves into trouble. The first John blogged about recently: by 'averaging down'—buying more as the stock drops— when they are wrong. The second is by purchasing lower and lower quality stocks as the market price increases. When stocks are cheap, good quality companies with great prospects will sell at prices less than ten times their normalized earnings. But when markets unerringly rise, the only stocks that look so cheap (and which attract value investors because they screen well) are cheap for a reason. Many a fund manager has come undone by lowering standards in a bull market. We will not do this.

headline: Pharma division deserves little or no discount to major peers; Eylea and Lucentis franchise generates large revenues despite Avastin pricing controversy
reasoning: Bayer's pharma business includes Eylea (co-developed with Regeneron) and Lucentis, both priced around $24,000 per year for Wet AMD treatment. Wet AMD is a leading cause of blindness in the elderly and drugs that prevent blindness command very high prices from medical systems globally. Key patents have many years left to run, and the pipeline is decent. Despite the ethical complexity around Genentech not conducting double-blind trials on cheaper Avastin, the franchise is durable and well-reimbursed even by cost-conscious governments like Australia.
quote: We think that Bayer's pharma business is not worth much of a discount (if any) to some of the majors despite these problems.

headline: Low unemployment historically predicts negative subsequent five-year S&P returns; current 4.7% rate fits that pattern
reasoning: Using 60 years of data, periods when US unemployment was below 5% have been followed by mostly negative and always low five-year S&P 500 returns. When unemployment is very low, wages grow faster than GDP and profit shares shrink, putting pressure on corporate earnings. Valuations are also typically stretched at such moments, compounding the downside risk. The current unemployment rate of 4.7% squarely places the market in this historically unfavourable zone.
quote: This, for many, may be a deeply counter-intuitive result. When the economy is performing well, the subsequent five-year returns of the S&P 500 are mostly negative, and low always. There are good reasons for this. Firstly, when unemployment is below five percent (currently 4.7 percent) the economy has done well and valuations are high.

headline: S&P aggregate earnings likely down in twelve months, with a 20-40% price decline possible as record-high median P/E meets falling earnings
reasoning: Bronte argues that S&P aggregate earnings will fall within twelve months due to two compounding factors: rising nominal wage growth exceeding GDP growth (which compresses corporate profit share via leverage on margins), and the strengthening US dollar hurting international earnings. The S&P median P/E is at record highs just as earnings are poised to fall. Either factor alone could cause a 10-20% decline in prices, but combined they imply a risk of a 20-40% decline. The Buffett measure (Wilshire 5000 market cap as a percentage of US GDP) is also at all-time highs, reinforcing the view that markets are more expensive than the headline P/E of 21 suggests. Non-GAAP earnings manipulation adds further uncertainty to the quality of reported profits.
quote: So in aggregate the S&P median price earnings ratio is at record highs just as S&P earnings look like they are going to fall. While either one of these factors might cause a 10-20 percent decline in prices, combined they could imply the risk of a decline closer to 20-40 percent.

headline: Hurt by being underweight the very strong US dollar; not claiming macro expertise and will not swing for fences on currency
reasoning: The fund's currency positioning was a significant drag on returns over the past twelve months, as being overweight the Euro and underweight a very strong US dollar hurt performance. Bronte Capital acknowledges they are not macro-economists and do not claim expertise in currency forecasting. They commit to not making large directional currency bets, accepting that currency outcomes will sometimes be right and sometimes wrong.
quote: If you look at our returns over the past twelve months we have been way better than average stock pickers (okay on the longs, okay on the shorts but without spectacular wins). But we have mucked up currency badly (being underweight the very strong US dollar). As we are not macro-economists we don't pretend to expertise on currency. Sometimes we will get it right, sometimes wrong, but we will not swing for the fences on it ever.

headline: Not adding to North American net exposure; prefer European markets relative to US given valuation and earnings outlook
reasoning: Given the expensive valuations in the US and the expected earnings weakness, Bronte is not adding significantly to its North American net exposure. The fund is positioned such that if the US market falls relative to European markets, it could do very well. Bronte frames this as a discipline issue — expensive markets should not lead managers to lower their quality standards when searching for investments.
quote: If the US markets goes down especially relative to European markets we could do very well indeed. Rest assured that we have not given up the hunt for value in North America. While bargains are hide to find, it does not absolve us from trying. And we do. But if we don't add very much to the North American net exposure, it is because we do not believe one should lower one's standards for quality (much) when markets become expensive.

headline: Used as valuation benchmark at 4.2x sales to highlight Bayer's cheap multiple; no direct view expressed
reasoning: Pfizer is cited purely as a valuation comparable — it trades at 4.2 times sales, illustrating how cheap Bayer is at 2–2.5 times sales. No direct investment view is expressed on Pfizer itself.
quote: Bayer is a genuinely large pharmaceutical company. The right valuation comparison is the mega-giants. Pfizer trades at 4.2 times sales. Novartis trades at 4.1 times sales. We could go on. Most pharmaceutical companies trade above 4 times sales.

headline: Initiated 5% position; trades at 2–2.5x revenue vs pharma peers above 4x sales, with key patents still running and visible drug revenue growth despite Monsanto acquisition overhang
reasoning: Bronte Capital has built a 5% position in Bayer, describing it as genuinely cheap at 2–2.5 times revenue compared to mega-cap pharma peers like Pfizer (4.2x) and Novartis (4.1x). Bayer's four-and-a-half businesses — pharma, OTC, seed technology, animal health, and a majority stake in Covestro — are collectively described as pretty good businesses that should earn high margins and trade at larger multiples. The key drag on the stock is the controversial Monsanto acquisition, which the market hates because it makes Bayer too large a seed-tech company to attract pharmaceutical-focused investors and is priced at over 4x Monsanto's revenue. Despite this, Bayer's key patents have many years left to run, the pipeline is described as decent, and its two flagship drugs — Xarelto (blood thinner) and Eylea (wet AMD treatment) — have obvious revenue growth characteristics. The main drug risks are litigation exposure for Xarelto (no antidote unlike Warfarin) and potential low-cost competition for Eylea.
quote: We have added one new big position to the portfolio in the last quarter. We now hold a 5 percent position in Bayer – the largest company in the German index. Bayer has four and half businesses which they collectively call "life sciences" but in fact fit into no specialist portfolio. The whole contraption trades for between 2 and 2.5 times revenue depending on how you net out Covestra. This is really cheap for this type of businesses. Ultimately most of these are pretty good businesses that earn high margins, should earn even higher margins and normally trade at bigger multiples.

headline: Seed technology division a wonderful recurring consumable business worth well over 2.5x sales; neonicotinoids the one regulatory risk
reasoning: Seed technology is an inherently attractive business: a small input (seed coating) materially improves a large output (annual farm yield), creating strong farmer loyalty and annual repeat purchases. Bronte has interests in other seed companies and considers this squarely in their wheelhouse. The neonicotinoids insecticide business within Bayer, however, is under regulatory pressure due to alleged harm to bee populations, similar to issues at Monsanto, and is valued at less than 2x sales.
quote: Seed technology is inherently a wonderful business. It is a very small thing (say a seed coating) that makes a big thing (the year's output for the farm) better. If it is demonstrated to work once the farmer is reluctant to experiment and try other things (it really matters to them). And it is a consumable – the farmer is back every year. This is right-up Bronte's alley and we have interests in other seed companies as well. And the good bits are clearly worth well over 2.5 times sales. There are bad bits in this. Bayer has a neonicotinoids business. These are insecticides and they are very controversial – the allegation being that they are the underlying cause of global problems in bee hives.

headline: Used as valuation benchmark at 4.1x sales to highlight Bayer's cheap multiple; no direct view expressed
reasoning: Novartis is cited as a valuation comparable trading at 4.1 times sales, reinforcing that most pharmaceutical companies trade above 4 times sales and that Bayer at 2–2.5 times is unusually cheap for its peer group.

headline: OTC medicines division, including Aspirin and Elevit, comparable to Reckitt Benckiser at 5x sales; margins should expand from here
reasoning: Bayer has what is probably the world's largest OTC medicines business, with inherently fat margins. Products like Aspirin (which Bayer developed and still owns the brand name for) and Elevit pregnancy vitamins command premium pricing. The right comparable is Reckitt Benckiser, which trades at over 5x sales with fatter EBITDA margins. Bayer's OTC margin should increase meaningfully, making this segment clearly worth well over 2.5x sales.
quote: The right comparable for this business is Reckitt Benkeiser who market consumer products and OTC medicines. RB trades at over five times sales. It has a slightly fatter EBITDA margin but quite a lot fatter EBIT margin. We think (with good reason) the margin of Bayer's business should increase a fair bit from here. This part of Bayer is clearly worth well over 2.5 times sales.

headline: Trump tax cuts could boost post-tax EPS but are a one-off, partly offset by higher rates from looser fiscal policy — one last reason to celebrate, not a structural bull case
reasoning: Bronte acknowledges that Trump's tax cuts are within the president's power to deliver and could increase post-tax earnings per share for S&P companies. However, this is characterised as a one-off uplift that will be partially offset for valuation purposes by higher interest rates induced by looser fiscal policy. Pre-tax earnings are still expected to fall regardless of Trump policy. The net effect is described as 'one last reason to celebrate' rather than a durable re-rating catalyst.
quote: But post-tax earnings are within President Trump's power to change. Large tax cuts could increase post-tax earnings per share. This is a one-off increase and will to some extent be offset for valuation purposes by higher interest rates (induced by looser fiscal policy). Tax cuts give the market one last reason to celebrate.

headline: Animal health division of similar quality to Zoetis (6x sales); hope Bayer sells it to Zoetis at a good price but future uncertain
reasoning: Bayer's animal health business is quite good overall, with particularly profitable pet pharmaceuticals, though livestock pharmacy is more competitive. Zoetis, the most important comparable, trades at 6x sales and is of similar quality. Bronte hopes Bayer sells this division to Zoetis to realise good value, but acknowledges uncertainty about the future of this segment.
quote: Again this is a really profitable business – we are not entirely sure how sustainable. But the Australian government is far more rational about drug pricing than most – and it is not doing the cheap thing here. The most important competitor (Zoetis) trades at six times sales – and this business is of similar quality. We hope however they sell to Zoetis because they will get a good price. We are unsure of the future here.

headline: Tighter credit regime post-Trump likely to hurt non-financial corporate earnings and reduce lender accommodation to semi-distressed companies
reasoning: Bronte notes that credit markets reacted very differently to Trump's victory compared to equity markets. A tighter credit regime is expected to hurt non-financial companies' earnings and may reduce lenders' willingness to be as accommodating to semi-distressed companies as they have been recently. This is presented as a further headwind to S&P earnings that is independent of the wage/dollar argument.
quote: Note that the credit markets had quite the opposite reaction to Trump's victory as the equity markets. A tighter credit regime will hurt non-financial companies' earnings and perhaps diminish lenders' willingness to be as accommodating to semi-distressed companies as they have recently.

headline: Undervalued sum-of-parts: most divisions worth 3-4x sales but whole trades at a discount; very few ways to lose
reasoning: Bayer's key pharma patents still have many years to run with obvious revenue growth drivers. Its OTC medicines business, seed technology business, and animal health division each merit 3-4x or more in sales multiples given fat margins and competitive positioning. The neonicotinoids business is the one drag, likely facing regulatory pressure and worth less than 2x sales. Despite the Monsanto acquisition concern, the overall package is trading well below what individual parts would command, making it very hard to lose on a sum-of-parts basis.
quote: The observation here is that apart from smaller things like the neonicotinoids business there is very little here that you would not pay 3x sales for (especially in this market) and there are several things you would pay 4x or more times sales. The whole thing is much cheaper than that and we think there are very few ways to lose here.

headline: Dot-com era PE was illusory: excluding bubble stocks with no earnings, the median NYSE stock PE is now at an all-time high, making value harder to find
reasoning: Bronte notes that the headline S&P PE in the dot-com period was inflated by a handful of companies (e.g. i2 Technologies at over $200bn market cap with negligible earnings) that distorted the index-level ratio. Using Professor Ken French's median NYSE stock PE series strips out this distortion and shows the current median PE is at an all-time high. Because Bronte invests in the best stocks rather than average ones, a high median valuation signals that attractive opportunities are thinner on the ground than usual — but this does not mean they cannot find anything.
quote: In the dot-com era there were a very few stocks (some of which you have likely never heard and many of which are consigned to the dustbin of history) that had enormous market caps and little or no earnings. For instance, i2 Technologies at one point had a market value over $200 billion. If one excludes from the overall PE ratio the most absurd bubble stocks, the PE ratio in (say) the year 2000 was far more modest. Professor Ken French (of Dartmouth) compiles a lot of data which we find useful. One table works out the price earnings ratio of the median stock on the New York Stock Exchange. The current PE ratio of the median stock is an all-time high. We do not invest in 'average stocks'. We invest in the best stocks we can find (which we hope of course to be way better than average stocks). When the median stock is at an all-time high in price earnings ratio our pickings are likely to be thinner than average.

headline: Bronte Amalthea Fund running net short in the USA ahead of Trump election, which hurt performance as US market and USD rallied sharply.
reasoning: The fund had been positioned net short in the USA and long in Europe for an extended period, as communicated in prior letters. The Trump election outcome triggered a sharp rally in both the US equity market and the US dollar, which was unfavourable for this positioning. This macro stance was a key driver of the fund's monthly loss in November 2016.
quote: We have – as stated in many letters – been running net short in the USA and long in Europe. The market reaction to the Trump election was not good for the portfolio – with both the US market and US currency rallying sharply.

headline: Bronte Amalthea Fund long European industrials, which contributed gains in November 2016.

Gains were concentrated in these European industrial longs during November 2016, partially offsetting losses from US tech and biotech short positions being squeezed by the post-Trump rally.

headline: Bronte Amalthea Fund held short positions in US tech and biotech, which generated losses as these sectors rallied post-Trump election.

Management noted that the gyrations in futures and equity markets caused by exit polls, early polls and election results whipsawed many active traders. The team's preferred approach was to allow the dust to settle while adding to their target list of global longs and shorts positioned to benefit from the changed political landscape.

headline: Bronte Capital's European industrial long positions were the key source of gains in October 2016

headline: Bronte Capital flags Wendy's CCC+ bonds as emblematic of poor risk/return in credit markets, citing highly leveraged balance sheet from buybacks

headline: Bronte Capital maintains long despite Herbalife's shocking post-period correction to Active New Member metric, concluding the error was honest and does not affect financials
reasoning: After month end, Herbalife disclosed a material database scripting error that caused the Active New Member metric to be grossly overstated; global active new members excluding China dropped from reported 16.7% growth to 3.0%. Critically, reported earnings numbers and cash balances were unaffected, which is the key test for fraud — faking earnings requires faking two sets of numbers simultaneously. The firm views the sloppiness as painful but not as evidence of deliberate fraud.
quote: After month end Herbalife put out a truly shocking correction to their results where they indicated the number of new active distributors was grossly overstated. They claimed this was due to a coding error in their (mostly laudable) Oracle database system... Some of the changes were ugly. For instance global active new members excluding China went from 16.7 percent to 3.0 percent growth. We have agonised about this error. Nobody likes mistakes, but they are twice as painful for companies operating under exacting public scrutiny. It was sloppy but we have – on balance – decided we believe the honest-error explanation. And it did not affect reported earnings numbers or cash balances... Incorrect earnings do not generally happen by accident because double-entry accounting is self-correcting. It is unlikely you will accidentally have two offsetting incorrect numbers. If there had been an adjustment to earnings and cash balances we would not be so sanguine.

This is a stable growing business... volume points (a good measure of sales volume) in Europe rose 15 percent. This was the best for any region other than China. The business methods in Europe are being transitioned over the globe... We expected growth in volume points in the transitioned countries to be higher. Unless this growth comes our eventual target for the stock lowers to about $80 (it trades at about $55 currently). headline: Bronte Capital characterises current environment as a bear market and will not substantially lengthen equity exposure until US market cap-to-GDP falls to ~80%

quote: Warren Buffett wrote two articles in Fortune about the valuation of the entire US stock market. They have had a large influence on Bronte. In it he outlined his favorite measure of stock market pricing -­‐ the ratio of the market cap of the S&P500 to GDP. This is our favorite measure too. And so far in this bear market that ratio has not fallen below 100%. By historic standards the market is still expensive. We are not going to substantially lengthen our exposure until we think the market is more reasonably priced. We have two measures of when we will do that: (a) the market cap to GDP gets to an historically buyable ratio (about 80 percent); and/or (b) we can't find dozens or even hundreds of dubious stocks promoted for the purpose of separating 'investors' (meaning speculators) from their money.

headline: Bronte Capital identifies global bear market conditions with violent rallies driven by trend-following investors, choosing discipline over dynamic trading

The typical bear-­‐market spike-­‐rally is 8-12 percent with bigger moves in the lower-­‐quality stocks. Trading those violent reversals requires ice water running through your veins which is unlikely for most of us, and looking at the truly lousy performance of some trend-­‐following investors we doubt they have it either.
