headline: Progressively selling a long-held position into strength; valuation analysis implies combined Google and Facebook market cap prices in near-perfection, leaving little margin of safety
reasoning: Bronte has held Google since 2011 and has been progressively selling it on the way up. They are not proud to own it despite its performance. Their analysis of global advertising spend implies that even in an enormously generous scenario — where Facebook and Google capture 30% of 1% of global GDP in advertising, achieve 40% pre-tax margins, and pay 30% tax, valued at 15x terminal earnings — the combined valuation ceiling is approximately $970 billion, only marginally above the then-current combined market cap of ~$780 billion. They describe the most expensive momentum stocks as priced not for perfection but for a rosy scenario, and they feel no compulsion to sell entirely only because alternatives are similarly expensive or more challenged.
quote: Whilst we have been trimming our Google position as it rose, we don't feel compelled to sell it entirely, as alternatives are similarly expensive or more challenged. The other thing that worked in 2015 was European stocks IF you hedged the Euro exposure back to USD.

headline: No position; valuation analysis shows stock priced for a rosy scenario with minimal upside even if everything goes right for global advertising dominance
reasoning: Bronte's valuation framework shows that even under enormously generous assumptions — Facebook and Google together capturing 30% of global advertising (over three times current revenue at the time), 40% pre-tax margins, 30% tax, and a 15x terminal multiple — the combined valuation ceiling is around $970 billion versus a then-current combined market cap of ~$780 billion. This implies minimal upside if everything goes right, and significant downside risk if anything goes wrong. The fund held no position in Facebook.
quote: Here is a rough-sort-of-calculation on Facebook and Google which shows how richly valued they are... Now suppose that you want to put that on 15 times absolutely terminal earnings assuming everything goes right. The valuation should be $970 billion dollars. Well the combined market cap of Google and Facebook is about $780 billion. If everything goes right for them then you should get - from here - a reasonable return. But the world is complicated and plenty of things can go wrong. The most expensive momentum stocks in the world are priced - if not for perfection - but for a rosy scenario.

headline: Euro-hedged European equity ETF (HEDJ) flagged as unusually consensus and risky in prior letter; 2016 expected to be more problematic after strong 2015 returns
reasoning: Bronte Capital had previously warned that HEDJ — an ETF providing European equity exposure with Euro hedged back to USD — represented an unusually consensus and risky trade. That call proved correct as the trade turned problematic in early 2016. Despite strong 2015 returns from this strategy, they expect 2016 to be more difficult for this trade.
quote: We observed in our last letter that HEDJ - an ETF that did precisely that - was an unusually consensus and risky investment. And so it has turned out to be in the New Year. We have seen plenty of great returns this year based on this trade. We think 2016 will be more problematic.

headline: Trimming as price rose but not selling entirely; alternatives equally expensive or more challenged; priced for rosy scenario rather than perfection
reasoning: Bronte Capital has been trimming their Google position as the price rose, but does not feel compelled to exit entirely. They frame Google and Facebook combined at ~$780bn market cap, versus a terminal valuation of ~$970bn if everything goes right, implying limited upside from current levels. The most expensive momentum stocks are priced for a rosy scenario, and alternatives are similarly expensive or more challenged, making a full exit unattractive.
quote: Whilst we have been trimming our Google position as it rose, we don't feel compelled to sell it entirely, as alternatives are similarly expensive or more challenged.

headline: Europe offers more reasonably priced equity longs than the US, but currency gains have been surrendered; cautious on the consensus Euro-short/equity-long HEDJ trade despite Draghi's explicit easing commitment
reasoning: The fund has found more investible opportunities in Europe than the US, describing European stocks as 'reasonably priced' rather than exciting. However, currency moves have given back equity gains. They are wary of the consensus trade of long European equities hedged to USD (embodied in the HEDJ ETF) because the Euro already looks cheap in purchasing power terms and Europe has disproportionately benefited from falling energy/commodity prices, which typically supports currency appreciation rather than depreciation.
quote: In Europe there is more hope. We keep finding things to invest in that are 'reasonably priced' as opposed to salivatingly good. And we have done fairly well on the stocks - but have given up those gains in currency. Most people we have said this to just suggest hedging the currency - but we are scared of that trade too even though it is the consensus trade. Our reason for being unsure the Euro is going down however is that (a) it feels pretty cheap in many of the European countries already and (b) Europe has disproportionately benefited by the fall in energy and commodity prices. Europe has had an improvement in their terms of trade, and terms of trade improvements are usually correlated with currency appreciation.

headline: Visited ASML's Eindhoven factory for advanced lithography equipment; in-depth technical due diligence conducted via analyst with plasma physics PhD — investment thesis not yet disclosed
reasoning: The fund visited ASML's Eindhoven factory as part of a European research trip. ASML makes advanced lithography equipment for the semiconductor industry and the factory was of sufficient sensitivity that cameras were not permitted. The fund's new analyst Luke, who holds a PhD in plasma physics, was able to ask and receive precise technical answers. No explicit investment stance is stated beyond the fact that the visit was part of the long-book research process.
quote: This was Luke (on left) and John visiting the ASML factory in Einhoven Holland. ASML makes advanced lithography equipment for the semiconductor industry. We wish we could show you the factory - but we can't. They would not let us have a camera. However Luke (with his PhD in plasma physics) could ask precise questions about the technology and we received some precise answers.

conviction: core holding — described as biggest long-book disaster
headline: Biggest long-book position and biggest disaster; duopoly in wide-body jet engines provides privileged structural position but stock has severely underperformed
reasoning: Rolls Royce is described as the fund's biggest long-book disaster despite holding a privileged structural position as one of only two manufacturers of wide-body jet engines globally. This duopoly is seen as durable for at least a decade given the implausibility of new entrants. The fund remains invested, suggesting continued conviction in the thesis, but acknowledges significant losses on the position to date.
quote: Every long book has a disaster somewhere, sometime. Our biggest is Rolls Royce. Rolls has a privileged position: it is one of only two makers of engines for wide-bodied jets in the world. Moreover, this privileged position should last a long time. It is inconceivable than there will be a meaningful new entrant to the industry in the next decade.

headline: Holding despite cash risk: privileged duopoly in wide-body jet engines but A350 ramp-up financing uncertain and dilution risk looms if cash doesn't stretch to 2018
reasoning: Rolls Royce holds a near-irreplaceable duopoly position as one of only two makers of engines for wide-bodied jets, and supplies the engine for the A350, the most fuel-efficient plane in the world. However, as of the visit only 11 A350s were flying, with meaningful production scale not expected until around 2018 at 15 per month. Several headwinds compound the problem: airlines are delaying wide-body orders given low fuel prices (undermining the new planes' fuel-efficiency value proposition), and Rolls's large diesel engine business is suffering from the distressed oil industry. There are also hints of mismanagement and potential capex requirements for the A350 ramp-up. The key risk is whether the company has sufficient cash to survive the lean period before the A350 annuity maintenance stream becomes large enough to sustain it; if not, it will raise equity and dilute shareholders. On-the-ground visits and conversations with mid-level staff gave some comfort that management is controlling costs toward that objective, though the cost-cutting had not reached investor relations (they received a notably generous lunch). The fund concludes they probably get through but there remains too much uncertainty for comfort.
quote: Rolls has a privileged position: it is one of only two makers of engines for wide-bodied jets in the world. Moreover, this privileged position should last a long time. It is inconceivable than there will be a meaningful new entrant to the industry in the next decade. Further Rolls currently supplies the jet to the most fuel-efficient plane in the world - the A350. Alas (as of the time of visit) only 11 of these planes are flying and the production levels don't ramp up for some time. By 2018 they should be producing 15 or so of these planes per month. Rolls has a lot of businesses that are in some trouble at the moment. Airlines are delaying orders for new wide-bodied planes because the fuel price is low. Also Rolls makes very large diesel engines that are disproportionately used in the now deeply distressed oil industry. On top of this there is a hint of mismanagement and the company may have capex requirements for the A350 ramp-up. It's not obvious that they have enough cash to make it through to when there are enough A350s flying around to give them truly large annuity maintenance streams. And if they can't make it that far they will dilute us (meaning you) raising equity to protect their credit rating. We think they are - but there is still too much uncertainty to make this a comfortable position.

headline: Modest exception to universal capital overbuilding — fuel-efficient long-haul aircraft not oversupplied — but low oil price diminishes the investment relevance
reasoning: The fund sees fuel-efficient long-haul aircraft as one of the few sectors not suffering from overcapacity. However, this is described as a modest exception that matters little in practice because the low oil price reduces the economic premium of fuel efficiency, undermining the investment case for aircraft manufacturers and related suppliers.
quote: We don't think the market is over-supplied in fuel-efficient long-haul aircraft - but that is a modest exception which matters little because the oil price is low.

headline: Previously shorted on questionable accounts; JAB Holding bid a 78% premium, forcing intellectual concession that acquirer with inside information disagrees — position was fortunately not held on takeover day
reasoning: Bronte had periodically shorted Green Mountain Coffee Roasters on the basis of questionable accounts, but was not short on the day JAB Holding Company launched a 78% premium takeover bid. JAB performed full due diligence and had access to non-public information, which forces the concession that they may be right. The fund takes intellectual satisfaction in reserving the right to be vindicated if JAB destroys capital, but acknowledges the acquirer has superior information.
quote: We were (fortunately) not short Green Mountain Coffee Roasters when a JAB Holding Company investor group bid a 78% premium in a takeover. But we have been short GMCR periodically - we just were not on the fateful day. We have questioned Green Mountain's accounts but JAB did due diligence and presumably have inside information - and they disagree with us. We will get some intellectual satisfaction if JAB blows up a lot of capital - but so far we have to allow that they have (a) more and better information than us and (b) disagree with us.

headline: Bearish overall: debt markets skittish, capital equipment oversupplied, cyclical recovery unlikely in medium term, market full of questionable accounts and collapsing business models
reasoning: Bronte Capital sees a broadly uninvestible market at current prices. Debt markets are getting skittish, capital equipment appears oversupplied across almost every sector, and cyclicals show no sign of near-term recovery. Consumer goods and healthcare companies have pushed margins to unprecedented levels that competition will mean-revert. The firm expects negative earnings surprises to be commonplace for the next few years and sees the market as 'a trap' unlike the good-value opportunity they saw in 2011.
quote: We don't like this market. The debt market is getting skittish, capital equipment looks oversupplied in almost every market and cyclical businesses do not look like they will recover in the medium term. Consumer good companies and health care companies have also pushed margins to hitherto unheard of levels. Competition causes margins to mean-revert. We think there could be some problems there too. We think negative earnings surprises will be commonplace for the next few years. Moreover the market is laced with companies whose valuation does not reflect either (a) questionable accounts or (b) questionable to collapsing business models. It seems to us to be full of stocks which are uninvestible - at least at this price.

headline: Associate pitched as short on structural decline — losing down-market to discounters, up-market to Whole Foods — Cerberus disagreed with 78%-premium bid but subsequently failed to re-IPO
reasoning: An associate had argued Safeway was a structural short due to competitive pressure from discounters at the low end and Whole Foods at the high end. Cerberus, a large private equity firm, acquired Safeway, implying disagreement with the short thesis. The fund did not short Safeway and attributes this to luck rather than skill. The subsequent failure of Cerberus to re-IPO Safeway provides some intellectual vindication of the original short thesis.
quote: Last year's 'what-are-they-thinking' takeover was the bid by Cerberus [a large reputable private equity firm] for Safeway (a US grocery store). An associate of ours had been pitching Safeway as a short based on the inevitable demise of their business from losing the down-market sector to discounters and the up-market sector to Whole Foods. Fortunately, we did not act on that advice either though we agreed with it. Cerberus disagreed. That we did not lose money there is best put down to luck. We take some intellectual satisfaction that Cerberus failed in their attempt to re-IPO Safeway.

headline: Small long initiated after on-the-ground factory visit confirmed steam-trap supply — shop-floor validation of product adoption
reasoning: During a site visit to a chemical plant in Northern England, the team observed steam-traps in the boiler system and confirmed with the engineer that Spirax-Sarco was the supplier. This type of shop-floor validation reduces the firm's error rate and gave them confidence to initiate a small long position. The investment was driven by real-world evidence of product usage rather than financial analysis alone.
quote: We were walking through a chemical plant when Luke pointed out steam-traps in the boiler system. We got the engineer to tell us who the supplier was and what the supplier did and we got the answer we expected. We have a small long in the supplier (Spirax-Sarco). This sort of shop-floor confirmation is invaluable. It reduces our error rate.

headline: Wary of the consensus HEDJ (long European equities, short Euro) trade despite Draghi's explicit easing pledge; terms-of-trade improvement argues for Euro appreciation not depreciation
reasoning: HEDJ — the USD-hedged European equity ETF — has attracted among the largest inflows of any US ETF, making it a crowded consensus trade. While the logic of following Draghi's explicit commitment to print Euros is straightforward, Bronte sees countervailing forces: the Euro already looks cheap and Europe's terms of trade have improved materially from lower energy prices, historically a currency-positive development. The fund is scared of being short the Euro even if they believe the consensus logic.
quote: HEDJ is an exchange traded fund marketed in the US. Its positioning is simple, long European equities hedged back to the US dollar. This has had amongst the biggest inflows of all US ETFs. [The trade really is the consensus and it has been a great trade.] Our reason for being unsure the Euro is going down however is that (a) it feels pretty cheap in many of the European countries already and (b) Europe has disproportionately benefited by the fall in energy and commodity prices. Europe has had an improvement in their terms of trade, and terms of trade improvements are usually correlated with currency appreciation.

headline: Even cash is not safe: can't rule out inflationary end to quantitative easing era, so no risk-free asset class exists
reasoning: The fund argues there is no asset class free from risk in the current environment. While they do not expect an inflationary resolution to the quantitative easing era, they cannot discount it entirely. This means even holding cash carries risk, and the common belief that professional processes can remove risk from investing is characterised as misleading.
quote: There is no asset class we can see that is free from risk. Pretending the risk is not there is a good way of losing a lot of money. Even cash is not a safe way to preserve wealth. Whilst we don't think there will be an inflationary end to the quantitative easing era it's a possibility we can't discount. Even cash is risky.

headline: Consumer goods and healthcare margins at unprecedented highs are vulnerable to mean-reversion via competition — expect earnings disappointments
reasoning: Consumer goods and healthcare companies have achieved historically unprecedented margin levels. The fund's view is that competition will force margins to revert toward the mean, which will produce negative earnings surprises. This is part of a broader bearish thesis on the market and a reason to be cautious about holding such stocks at current valuations.
quote: Consumer good companies and health care companies have also pushed margins to hitherto unheard of levels. Competition causes margins to mean-revert. We think there could be some problems there too. We think negative earnings surprises will be commonplace for the next few years.

headline: Broadly cautious on market; nonsense stocks are everywhere and many admired fund managers hold portfolios of dangerous stocks, maintaining as many shorts as can prudently be held
reasoning: Bronte expresses significant caution about the overall market environment, noting that 'nonsense stocks are everywhere.' They observe that some fund managers with impressive five-year records hold portfolios they believe are dangerous, and they want to take the other side of those positions. Despite this bearish aggregate positioning, October 2015 proved that markets can violently rip higher — the S&P 500 rose 8.4% in the month, its best performance in over four years — making a heavily short book deeply uncomfortable even if ultimately profitable for Bronte. The firm acknowledges the tension between their market scepticism and the risk of being short in a momentum-driven rally.
quote: As noted in prior letters, we are wary of this market. Nonsense stocks are everywhere. We also see fund managers with fantastic five year records where we think almost every stock in their portfolio is dangerous. We want to take the other side. And yet – as October proved – the market is perfectly willing to rip up. October was the best month for the S&P in over four years (+8.4%), and broad based global indices also rose by over 6% when adjusted into Australian dollars. Being heavily short in that sort of market can be deeply uncomfortable, even injurious to your wealth.

headline: Short position maintained; faces existential threats including bankruptcy risk, with bonds trading around 85 cents in the dollar after Philidor pharmacy fraud exposure
reasoning: Bronte has held a short position in Valeant Pharmaceuticals since at least February 2015, when they first became aware of Philidor, a specialty pharmacy Valeant consolidated but never admitted owning. Philidor was exposed as a mechanism to deceive insurance companies into covering prescriptions they would not otherwise cover, and to prevent generic substitution at huge cost to insurers. The political pressure on Valeant's price-rise strategy compounded the damage from Philidor's exposure. Bronte believes Valeant's 'cash EPS' metric is essentially 'earnings before the bad stuff,' with management having discretion over what is included or excluded. The bond market is pricing in meaningful bankruptcy risk, with debt trading around 85 cents on the dollar. Valeant remains one of Bronte's biggest shorts, though not the largest, and is viewed as facing existential threats.
quote: We have made very good money on this trade – but nowhere near as much as we should have. Valeant remains one of our biggest shorts, but it is no longer our largest short. For many reasons, we think the company faces existential threats. The bond market believes bankruptcy is a possibility, with debt trading around 85 cents in the dollar.

headline: Cited as the highest-quality metallurgy-based business and its Berkshire Hathaway acquisition validates the investment case for the broader sector
reasoning: Precision Castparts is highlighted as the premier example of a high-quality metallurgy and advanced manufacturing business, validating the thesis that materials science companies can be surprisingly good investments. Its acquisition by Berkshire Hathaway is used as evidence that such businesses trade at relatively attractive prices and attract sophisticated long-term capital. The mention is used to support the broader sector opportunity in beaten-down materials science companies.
quote: The highest quality metallurgy based company we know (Precision Cast Parts) just got purchased by Berkshire Hathaway. These companies can be surprisingly good businesses – and their relatively low prices at the moment are attractive.

headline: PE ratio is a poor predictor of future equity returns; earnings variability is the key driver, not multiple levels
reasoning: Historical S&P 500 data since 1960 shows that market peaks typically had PE ratios around 18x (excluding dot-com), which is not substantially different from PE ratios at good buying opportunities. The early 1980s offered excellent returns from very low PE ratios (~10x), while the financial crisis bottom also proved a great buying opportunity despite a PE of ~18x. The fundamental insight is that business profitability is far more variable than market PE ratios, making earnings the key swing factor rather than multiples.
quote: The PE ratio is, it seems, not a very good indicator of future returns. The basic problem is that the earnings number is highly variable. The profitability of business is far more variable than the market PE ratio. Profitability is abnormally high at the moment. Demand has been good. Financing costs low. Wage pressure (particularly at the bottom end) has been abnormally low. Profits have thus been strong.

headline: S&P earnings growth stalling for first time since the financial crisis; quality stocks de-rating promptly while 'hope stocks' stay elevated on loose monetary policy
reasoning: Goldman Sachs sharply downgraded S&P 500 earnings estimates for 2015 to 114, barely above 2014 levels, suggesting this could be the first year since the crisis that S&P earnings are flat or decline. Profitability has been abnormally high due to strong demand, low financing costs and suppressed wage growth, but is now clearly slowing. In the current environment, stocks hold up until they disappoint, at which point they de-rate sharply; quality stocks with stable earnings tend to disappoint and de-rate quickly, while 'hope stocks' sustain their valuations longer. Loose monetary policy keeps investors buying growth hopes even as aggregate earnings growth is absent. The fund is positioned long quality and short hope, which is a headwind in the near term but expected to outperform when the trend reverses.
quote: S&P profitability however is clearly slowing. Goldman Sachs has sharply downgraded their estimate for S&P earnings in 2015 to 114 (only a small rise on 2014). It is possible earnings estimates are still too high. This may be the first year since the crisis that S&P earnings are flat or might decline somewhat. What is happening in the market is stocks stay high until they 'disappoint'. When they disappoint (and many stocks will) they de-rate sharply. Alas quality stocks (mostly those with fairly stable earnings) tend to fess up fairly promptly and de-rate quickly. The 'hope stocks' maintain hope for a long time. Monetary policy is still loose – so people want to buy – and they can't buy earnings growth (because it is not there in aggregate) so they buy hope. As we are long quality and short hope the present trend is not good for us; but these days will end and we will outperform.

headline: Beaten-down materials science and advanced metallurgy companies attractive; Chinese government cyber-espionage targets suggest strategic value, and oil industry exposure has created a buying opportunity
reasoning: The fund is actively looking at beaten-down material science companies, including those that sell into the oil industry (e.g. deepwater oil pipeline technology), where missed earnings have depressed share prices. The fact that Chinese government actors have tried to hack these companies is cited as evidence of their strategic and technological value. The acquisition of Precision Castparts by Berkshire Hathaway is held up as proof that high-quality metallurgy-based businesses can be surprisingly good. A newly hired PhD physicist with hands-on experience in high-tech solar and medical device companies is being deployed to evaluate these opportunities.
quote: We are looking at some beaten down material science based companies. Think the sort of thing that the Chinese Government spies have tried to hack. Many of these companies sell some kit to the oil industry (e.g. deepwater oil pipeline technology) and they have missed earnings and the stocks are 'beaten up'. We think this is an opportunity. The highest quality metallurgy based company we know (Precision Cast Parts) just got purchased by Berkshire Hathaway. These companies can be surprisingly good businesses – and their relatively low prices at the moment are attractive. There is a lot of good science and engineering in these businesses – and Luke is just the guy to understand it.

headline: No true bargains in energy space until major bankruptcies arrive; many companies still regarded as frauds and promotes
reasoning: In the oil and energy space, despite large price falls, the fund believes there are still many companies they regard as frauds and promotes that have not yet failed. They do not expect genuine bargains to emerge before the big bankruptcies begin. This caution extends broadly to the energy sector.
quote: In the oil space (where the falls have been large) plenty of companies we regard as frauds and promotes have not yet failed. It is unlikely there will be true bargains (particularly in the energy space) before the big bankruptcies begin.

headline: Swapped Terraform Power position for higher-risk parent; cheap but complicated accounts and high leverage cap position size
reasoning: Bronte Capital swapped their relatively low-risk Terraform Power (yieldco) position for a higher-risk position in the parent Sun Edison. They view Sun Edison as cheap and believe the reasons it is cheap are manageable, including the Vivint MLM regulatory risk and leverage concerns. However, the complexity of Sun Edison's accounts and the very high leverage mean they are unlikely ever to get comfortable enough for a large position. They also already carry significant MLM risk via their large Herbalife position, which further limits how much Sun Edison they want to own. The fund notes the Vivint acquisition was 'stupid' but expects some solution will be found — either the deal doesn't close, Vivint is spun out, or Sun Edison is structured to be 'Vivint remote'.
quote: This month we swapped the relatively low risk position in Terraform Power (the yield co) for a higher risk position in the parent (Sun Edison). Sun Edison is cheap and the reasons it is cheap are manageable. However we now have a position to rival Herbalife and Senomyx for day-to-day volatility. On many days a small position is either our biggest winner or biggest loser. If we did not have the large Herbalife position (and hence plenty of MLM risk) we would be buying more. But there is a limit to how many times we can accept that risk. And because we have done more work (and hence have more conviction) we prefer taking our MLM risk at Herbalife. Moreover Herbalife has simple accounts and the cash generation is obvious. Sun Edison accounts are really complicated and leverage is really high. It is unlikely we could ever get comfortable enough with Sun Edison for a large position.

headline: Rooftop solar structurally less attractive than utility-scale solar; grid-cost underpricing is reversing, with PG&E proposing explicit charges for solar households
reasoning: Bronte Capital notes that rooftop solar benefits from underpriced use of the electricity grid, which is beginning to be addressed by regulators. Pacific Gas and Electric is proposing changes that would explicitly charge solar-panel households more for grid access. The fund believes the direction of travel is correct and will become a trend, making rooftop solar less attractive over time. This structural headwind is distinguished from the specific Sun Edison stock collapse, which is driven by the Vivint MLM regulatory risk.
quote: That said, there are good reasons why roof top solar is less attractive than utility scale solar farms. The main one is that rooftop solar gets under-priced use of the grid. The grid is essential here – unwanted solar is sold to the grid and the grid provides electricity when the sun doesn't shine... Pacific Gas and Electric is proposing changes which explicitly charge households with solar panels more to access the grid. Whilst we have no view on the size of the charge the direction is probably right. This will become a trend and make roof top solar less attractive in the future.

headline: Yield co assessed as a non-bank financial; credit risk, duration mismatch and funding stability are the key analytical lenses
reasoning: TerraForm Power is Sun Edison's yield co and has also been smashed in the sell-off. The fund, drawing on Nemo Incognito's framework, argues it must be evaluated as a financial company rather than a semiconductor/manufacturing business. The critical questions are whether counterparty credit risk on projects is acceptable, how contract and funding structures (floating vs fixed) work, and whether short-term project development funding can roll into long-dated project finance. The fund found that funding cannot be called and a Northern Rock-style run is unlikely.
quote: If you want to assess TerraForm Power (Sun Edison's yield co) you need to assess whether the credit risk on the projects (the counter-party) is okay, how the contract and funding is (eg floating/fixed etc) and all the ways in which project development funding is able to roll into long-dated funding.

headline: Preferred MLM risk vehicle over Sun Edison — simple accounts, obvious cash generation, high conviction large position
reasoning: Bronte Capital explicitly describes Herbalife as their preferred vehicle for taking MLM regulatory risk, citing simpler accounts and more obvious cash generation compared to Sun Edison. The position is described as large, and the fund notes it already provides substantial day-to-day volatility, which limits their appetite to add further MLM-exposed names. The fund has done more work on Herbalife and therefore has greater conviction there.
quote: And because we have done more work (and hence have more conviction) we prefer taking our MLM risk at Herbalife. Moreover Herbalife has simple accounts and the cash generation is obvious. Sun Edison accounts are really complicated and leverage is really high. It is unlikely we could ever get comfortable enough with Sun Edison for a large position.

headline: Acquisition was foolhardy — MLM regulatory risk combined with high leverage is toxic for a finance company
reasoning: Bronte Capital describes the Vivint acquisition by Sun Edison as 'stupid' and 'foolhardy'. Vivint is characterised as a multi-level marketing scheme that sells solar panels door to door, which inherently invites regulatory scrutiny — the kind of scrutiny that is poison for a highly leveraged finance company. The fund believes Sun Edison management, who came from a semiconductor background, failed to adapt their decision-making to the reality of running a financial institution. The fund suspects a solution will be found — either the deal breaks (at a meaningful fee), Vivint is stripped and spun out, or Sun Edison is structured to be 'Vivint remote'.
quote: The issue is that Vivint is an MLM. MLMs – even honest MLMs – invite regulatory scrutiny. We have been living that scrutiny with Herbalife. MLMs regularly trade at a discount because there are regulatory risks associated with them. Moreover any MLM must rigorously guard against fraud... Alas this sort of scrutiny is poison for a highly levered finance company. The last thing a finance company needs is regulatory entanglement. This doesn't speak well for the management of Sun Edison. They were originally semi-conductor guys. They wound up running a financial institution and they did not change the decision making to meet the new reality.

headline: Market has not fallen far enough to create genuine bargains; expecting further declines
reasoning: The fund does not believe the August 2015 sell-off has been large enough to make stocks cheap. They characterise the sell-off as not historically unusual—these kinds of market funks happen every few years on average. There is no substantial change to portfolio positioning and they expect worse to come, though the timing is uncertain.
quote: We do not think the sell off has been large enough to make stocks cheap and there is no substantial change to our positioning. We expect worse. We just don't know when.

headline: Exited the relatively low-risk yieldco position in favour of the higher-risk parent
reasoning: Bronte Capital sold their Terraform Power (the yieldco) position and rotated into Sun Edison (the parent). The yieldco was characterised as relatively low risk compared to the parent, and the swap was made to access higher potential upside in the parent at a time when Sun Edison was trading cheaply.
quote: This month we swapped the relatively low risk position in Terraform Power (the yield co) for a higher risk position in the parent (Sun Edison).

headline: Acquisition of door-to-door solar MLM by Sun Edison characterised as foolhardy and a key driver of market panic
reasoning: The fund characterises the Vivint acquisition as 'brave (that is foolhardy)' and directly blames Sun Edison management for contributing to the current panic. Vivint is a multi-level marketing scheme that sells solar panels door to door, similar to Avon or Herbalife. The economic reality of Vivint's customer deals is that households effectively take a loan repaid by sharing utility bill savings, which is not inherently a bad deal for customers, but the acquisition invited scrutiny and compounded concerns about Sun Edison's complexity.
quote: Sun Edison management are not blameless in this panic. They did something wrong. That something was the brave (that is foolhardy) acquisition of Vivint. Vivint is a multi-level marketing scheme (an MLM) like Avon or Herbalife that sells solar panels door to door.

headline: Purchased a tiny stake after it was 'similarly smashed' alongside Sun Edison despite being a separate yield-co with distinct fundamentals
reasoning: TerraForm Power is the yield-co associated with Sun Edison, structured to hold completed solar projects and distribute income to investors. When Sun Edison's stock was hammered by momentum-driven selling on minor conference call comments, TerraForm Power was similarly sold off despite having a different risk profile as a yield vehicle. Bronte viewed this contagion selloff as an opportunity and purchased a tiny stake.
quote: The associated yield company (TerraForm Power) was similarly smashed and we purchased a tiny stake.

headline: Steep AUD decline contributed substantially to the fund's large July monthly gain when measured in Australian Dollars
reasoning: The fund's 6.12% net gain in July — its largest individual monthly gain to date — was substantially aided by the steep decline in the Australian Dollar. The fund runs global money from Australia, meaning AUD depreciation mechanically boosts returns when converted back to Australian Dollars. This currency dynamic is flagged as a meaningful contributor rather than pure alpha.
quote: Of course the steep decline in the Australian Dollar contributed substantially to the large monthly gain.

headline: Advantage of being outside mainstream sell-side flow: less prone to momentum stocks, which proved beneficial in recent months of market volatility

headline: Not held; stock collapsed on minor conference call comments after momentum unwind — stock chart and fundamentals do not align; acquisition of Vivint Solar (a door-to-door MLM) added investor skittishness
reasoning: Sun Edison was a high-quality solar project developer benefiting from falling panel costs, cheaper debt, and the ability to drop projects into yield-cos sold to yield-hungry investors. The stock rose dramatically on momentum. SunEdison then announced acquisition of Vivint Solar, a door-to-door multi-level marketing solar sales company, which made investors skittish even though it did not immediately drive the stock down. Very minor negative comments on a subsequent conference call triggered a sharp selloff as momentum followers rushed for the exit. Bronte highlights this as a case where famous hedge fund managers owned the stock and momentum followers piled in — when momentum broke they all sold simultaneously, divorcing the stock from its fundamentals.
quote: Our particular favourite chart at the moment is Sun Edison – a high quality solar project company. This has been a great business. The cost of panels (the main input cost) has gone down (and then down further). Debt has become cheaper (which matters in 25 year debt-financed projects) and it has been possible to drop finished projects into yield-companies sold on relatively low yields to yield-hungry investors. So the stock went up-and-up. Recently Sun Edison announced that they were buying Vivint Solar. Vivint has many small rooftop projects – worthwhile projects. And a solar developer needs a huge pipeline of projects - the acquisition has a purpose. Vivint however is a multi-level marketing company like Avon, Mary Kay cosmetics or Herbalife... Even this did not drive the stock down even though multi-level marketing schemes are controversial on Wall Street. But it did make investors skittish. What drove the stock down are some (very) minor comments in a conference call... Famous hedge fund managers own this stock. That – plus momentum – gave momentum followers plenty of excuse to own the stock – and they did so in increasing quantity. Then when the momentum looked broken they rushed for the exit. The stock chart and the fundamentals do not align.

headline: Momentum strategies have outperformed, attracting capital and crowding into few 'unbroken' stories — when any story cracks, violent exits create large price moves disconnected from fundamentals; market becoming increasingly narrow and skittish
reasoning: Momentum has been a winning strategy and momentum managers have attracted new capital, feeding a cycle of further concentration into a narrowing set of 'unbroken' stories. When any one of those stories shows even a minor crack, momentum holders become skittish and crowd into remaining unbroken stories, making the market even narrower. The large idiosyncratic stock moves on relatively small underlying changes — visible in both Google's rocketing up and Sun Edison's rocketing down — are symptoms of this dynamic and are not visible in broad aggregate index levels.

headline: Long; stock rocketed after results showed underlying revenue still growing and optional costs stabilising, though fundamental change less dramatic than the price move
reasoning: Google's revenue has grown to exceed US broadcast television revenue, which is significant given all the costs broadcast TV supports. For about 18 months Wall Street was focusing on optional costs like self-driving car development rather than the growing underlying business. Results showing revenue still growing and optional costs stabilising triggered a sharp re-rating. Bronte owned the stock and it was a big performer for the month, though the change in fundamentals over the past two months is less dramatic than the stock move — indicative of momentum-driven crowding dynamics.
quote: Google is – as almost everyone with a computer or an Android phone knows – a very powerful business. Revenue is large and grows fairly nicely albeit at a slower rate. Revenue is now larger than US broadcast television. This is significant when you consider all the costs that broadcast TV supports (all that production, all those stars and their expensive lifestyles). Google also supports a lot of costs – e.g. development of self-driving cars and a huge number of other research projects – and for about 18 months it seemed like Wall Street was focusing a lot on these (optional) costs and less on the growing underlying business. Then there were results which showed the revenue still growing for the underlying business and the optional costs stabilizing – and lo – the stock took off. We owned the stock and it has been a big performer – but the change in fundamentals over the past two months is less dramatic than the stock move.

quote: Apple (which we do not own) is the ultimate hidey-hole for a lot of managers. The business (and the stock) has been fantastic but the new product this year (a watch) has underwhelmed (at least by Apple's standards). Apple has started moving as much as 5 percent in a day without news. These are $30 billion market cap swings on nothing. That is a skittishness in the market you can't see in the underlying aggregates.

headline: Interested in an unnamed UK industrial with privileged niche businesses but deterred by an oversized legacy pension plan creating financial-stability risk
reasoning: The company is a former large British Empire conglomerate that slimmed down via asset sales in the 1990s, leaving behind high-quality, privileged niche businesses the managers would want to own for decades. However it also retained a pension plan sized for the much larger pre-restructuring entity, currently in drawdown phase, which will drag for roughly 20 more years. The pension effectively makes the company a leveraged bet on financial-market stability, and given global imbalances in China and Europe, the managers see too many ways they could get hurt. The fund has not taken a position.
quote: At the moment John is becoming obsessed by an English listed industrial company with extremely fine businesses weighed down by an oversized pension plan. Forgive us for not naming the stock – but it was a large British Empire conglomerate that slimmed down through asset sales and capital returns in the 1990s. After the restructure the company was left with much smaller but much nicer businesses – ones that have truly privileged positions which you may wish to own for decades. The sort of stuff that makes us excited. However the company is also left with a pension plan based on the much larger pre-restructuring company... In a real sense the company is a bet on the stability of financial markets. It is a real business attached to a big pile of supposedly matched assets and liabilities. In a stable financial world it should wind up okay. We would like to own it except we can see ways we get very hurt indeed.

headline: Greek can-kick will recur every six months; real risk is contagion to Italian and Spanish banks which are too-big-to-bail, with losses that would dwarf Lehman Brothers
reasoning: The fund argues Greece's structural problem — accelerating emigration and capital flight shrinking the economy and increasing debt relative to capacity to pay — has not been addressed by the latest deal. The crisis will therefore recur periodically. On its own Greece is trivial, but contagion to Italian and Spanish banks is the true systemic risk; those are too large to bail and losses would exceed Lehman Brothers. The fund sees German intransigence as the main obstacle to an optimal solution and believes the German electorate is not being levelled with about what a sufficient bailout would require. A generous enough but carefully structured bailout — one that punishes the Greek establishment without destroying the Greek people, and is designed so Italy and Spain do not want the same deal — is the right answer but politically very hard to deliver.
quote: Greece is tiny relative to Europe let alone the global economy. On its own it does not matter. What matters is contagion. If the Euro is not forever a run on Italian and Spanish banks is possible. These are too-big-to-bail. The losses would dwarf Lehman Brothers. And at the moment intransigence rather than a realistic assessment is the order of the day... Still without a sustainable solution to the Greek debt issues truly spectacularly bad outcomes are possible.

headline: Not adding risk: prices are high, imbalances pervasive, difficult to find cheap-enough stocks or make safe returns on shorts
reasoning: The fund sees no safe way to generate superior returns in current market conditions. Prices are high and imbalances are widespread globally. quote: We just don't see how to get them safely in this market – and we do not think that this is a time to add risk. Prices are high and imbalances are pervasive. Lots of things can go wrong in capital markets. We have a few ideas in the portfolio that we think will work out better-than-okay over five years – but it is not easy to find cheap-enough stocks – and it is doubly difficult to make money on shorts without too much risk.

We were wary of being short given the active role being played by the Chinese authorities in supporting their market. headline: Has not yet faced serious discounter damage but does not own property, leaving safety cushion very thin if Aldi-Lidl-style disruption accelerates
reasoning: The team highlighted Woolworths in Australia as a retailer that has not yet seen serious damage from discount grocers. quote: And the safety cushion for something like Woolworths in Australia -­‐ which by-­‐and-­‐large does not own its property -­‐ is very thin indeed.

headline: Short thesis confirmed via channel checks with industry competitor: dodgy origins as stock promoter pick, product claims not credible to operating mine operator
reasoning: The team had identified a junior mining company listed on the TSXV/OTCBB through short research, having seen it promoted by a stock promoter they track. When meeting an operating mine company in London that competed with the junior miner, the operating company could not understand the product claims being made. The two parties exchanged intelligence and confirmed each other's negative assessments, validating the short thesis ahead of formal market confirmation.
quote: One company we met in London had observed a 'hypothetical competitor': a junior mining company listed on the TSXV/OTCBB. We'd run into the junior miner in our short research. It had appeared on the website of a stock promoter we track. The company we met -­‐ which operates a very successful mine for a highly specialized mineral they use as an input and couldn't understand the claims the Canadian company was making for their products. We shared what we knew of its dodgy origins and matched what their more thorough and different checks told them. We prefer confirmation in the market -­‐ but this was pleasing nonetheless.

headline: Aldi-Lidl discount format commands 45% German grocery share with 1% margins becoming the new normal — safety cushion for European grocery retailers is much thinner than desired
reasoning: In Germany, Aldi-Lidl formats have captured 45% of the grocery market, with even affluent consumers buying discount groceries. One percent margins appear to be the new normal in German grocery retail. The team is trying to assess how far discounters can roll out into other markets and what the downside is for incumbents, concluding that the safety cushion for European grocery retailers is much thinner than they would like, particularly given billions of euros in property holdings.
quote: We were trying to work out how far could the discounters roll out in other countries and hence what the downside was for discounter-­‐challenged retailers in the UK (e.g. Tesco) or for ones that have not seen discounters do serious damage yet (such as Woolworths in Australia). Trust us -­‐ the extreme German case is not pretty. One percent margins seem to be the new-­‐normal. We are not sure it will get that bad in the rest of the world. Germany, relative to income, is probably the world's worst consumer market. But the safety cushion in our European retailers is much thinner than we would like.

headline: Former private equity-owned companies are better run post-relist than expected, though PE extracted high prices on IPO leaving limited upside for public investors
reasoning: The team had previously held a negative 'strip-it-and-sell-it' view of private equity operations, but was surprised to find companies that had passed through PE hands were well-run and substantially better institutions than when they entered. Performance since relisting was not brilliant, but this was attributed to PE pricing the IPO at high valuations rather than poor underlying business quality.
quote: One surprise was the companies we visited previously owned by private equity. They were really well run – and we believe they had come out of private equity as substantially better institutions than they went in. This is contrary to much of our pre-­‐existing 'strip-­‐it-­‐and-­‐sell-­‐it' negative impression of private equity operations. Perhaps these were the successes – the ones that could be resold to the market at substantial profits. But, regardless – the impression was good. These previously private equity owned stocks have not performed brilliantly since they were relisted – but that was generally not because the business was poor. Rather it was simply that the PE guys extracted good (i.e. high) prices on relisting.

headline: European equities cheaper than US peers, margins rising on weak Euro, QE just beginning — adequate but unexciting returns expected; prefer stocks with downside protection

However, the team wanted to select better stocks with downside protection to mitigate risk if the situation turns ugly.
quote: The equities were not cheap – but they were not nose-­‐bleed expensive either. They are clearly cheaper than their USA peers. Margins the companies were earning were higher than normal – but if anything the margins were going up (with the weak Euro) rather than down. All in all we thought most prospects would provide adequate returns but they were relatively unexciting. Quantitative easing is just beginning in Europe whereas it is ending in America. Profits are going up and there is so much liquidity that people will chase stocks. We would however like to pick the better stocks in those countries with downside protection at least to mitigate the risk that the situation turns really ugly.

headline: Short book is the most obvious opportunity given significant bond and currency volatility; long bull market means betting only on equity appreciation is brave
reasoning: Recent bond and currency market volatility has raised the risk that naive index investing — relying on Wall Street to price everything correctly — will be challenged. In this scenario the most obvious opportunity lies in our short book. There are valuations on many stocks which have benefitted from years of excess liquidity and a lack of investor understanding about their true characteristics. Our investors can benefit from a fall back to earth of these stocks. In summary, this has been a long bull market and it is a brave person now who is betting only on equity market appreciation.

headline: Short with only marginal profit so far; Einhorn's bear case at Sohn mostly understated — massive Wolfcamp resource claims contradicted by insider selling and well decline rates
reasoning: The fund has been short Pioneer Natural Resources and many other shale oil companies for some time, generating only marginal levels of profit. quote: We have been short many shale oil companies including Pioneer for some time with only marginal levels of profit. If anything on Pioneer we think that Mr. Einhorn (mostly) understated the case. Our observation was of a large disconnect between what Pioneer says – and what they do. Pioneer have been more than willing to tell you about the jaw-dropping size of their oil play in the Wolfcamp Texas... Despite this enormous discovery they have merrily sold stock (in the billions) thereby diluting this enormous asset. Insider selling has also been phenomenal. Diluting your ownership is not what you do when you have a resource like that. We did a check of the oil industry blogs (mostly places engineers like to talk about technical issues). There is some evidence that wells Pioneer has described as enormous have very rapid declines.

headline: Forced to cut short biotech exposure despite being guaranteed to fail eventually — timing unpredictable, promoters are recycled Chinese reverse-merger fraudsters

headline: Chinese third-tier city property development is delusional — vacant ghost cities with no transport, no occupants, no secondary market sales, financed by banks taking on extreme risk

headline: Evergrande's third-tier city developments are delusional — no car parks, no transport, construction stalled, and geopolitical overtones in site maps showing sea borders reaching to the Philippines

quote: After this we went to visit a development from Evergrande. Evergrande is listed in Hong Kong and will be known to our Australian clients because the Chairman (Xu Jiayin) was forced by Joe Hockey (the Australian Treasurer) to sell his $39 million house because he lacked proper foreign investment approval. headline: Short-book risk from hidden promoter correlations in January; cluster of small shorts sharing a common underlying promoter caused recurring early-January losses
reasoning: The fund identified a recurring pattern of losses in the first two weeks of January over several years, which was ultimately traced to a cluster of short positions that appeared independent but shared a common underlying promoter who habitually pumped stocks at the start of each year. The core short strategy is to follow bad actors in capital markets and short small quantities of what they are promoting, keeping position sizes at around 0.3% to limit loss on any single name. The key risk highlighted is hidden correlation among shorts — positions that appear uncorrelated but share an underlying driver — which had cumulatively cost the fund a meaningful amount of money before the pattern was identified.
quote: It was in our shorts where there were a cluster of shorts we thought were independent but there was a common underlying promoter. Moreover that promoter – through long-standing marketing habits – did much pumping at the beginning of each year. This is actually an artefact of our shorting strategy. Our core strategy on the short side is to follow bad actors in capital markets. And we find what they are promoting and short very small quantities of it. If the stocks go up we do more work and cover if need be, and if the stocks go down we take our profits. The reason the positions are so small is that any position can go up very substantially against us. But this is merely annoying if your starting position is only 0.3 percent of the fund.

At $60 oil bankruptcy is simply a matter of time. We did not predict $60 oil – but we have made money off it.

headline: Was a profitable long despite being priced for near-certain bankruptcy; debt yielding 15% at purchase, spectrum assets were the core value driver

Clearwire and Sprint were priced for bankruptcy. Clearwire's debt yielded 15 percent - a rate that implied that the debt market considered bankruptcy nearly certain. headline: LTE efficiency gains are largely played out; further spectral efficiency improvements possible via MIMO and beam-forming but sceptical of more radical claims such as Steve Perlman's wireless technology
reasoning: The fund explains in detail the physics of wireless spectrum, noting that digital upgrades from 2G through to LTE have delivered large efficiency gains but that this progression is largely exhausted — the 'purple light is flashing nearly as fast and efficiently as it can now.' quote: By the time we get to LTE for everything (including voice) this will largely have played itself out. The purple light is flashing nearly as fast and efficiently as it can now... However you can reasonably get another half order of magnitude of wireless efficiency via this method. It is also the basis of Steve Perlman's wireless technology. We are sceptical of Steve Perlman's project - but there are people out there more knowledgeable than us [and we would be very grateful for any reader who could put us in contact].

headline: Broken-thesis rule debated but Verizon retained: would repurchase on new thesis centred on spectrum-driven cost advantage lasting a decade or more
reasoning: The firm explicitly debated whether to apply its broken-thesis rule to Verizon, which would have required selling the position. Two explicit tests are set to monitor the thesis going forward. Risks include new wireless technologies such as Steve Perlman's project and outcomes from the 2015 auction.
quote: We have debated that rule with respect to the Verizon position. However if we threw it out we would buy it all back on the basis that its spectrum position gives it superior economics that will last a decade or more. We have two tests of whether this thesis is broken. The tests are a. Does Verizon wireless economics improve 3-5 percent or more per annum for a very long time? (which is what we think will happen) and b. Does the price of usable spectrum in negotiated transactions continue to rise over the world?

headline: Wireless spectrum is a fundamentally limited and increasingly scarce resource, driving long-term pricing power for carriers despite a nascent price war
reasoning: The thesis rests on the idea that wireless traffic is growing at a vast and accelerating rate, driven by app and content makers, while spectrum is a fundamentally limited resource. Spectrum prices in negotiated transactions have risen continuously since the first smartphone in 2007, now exceeding levels seen at the dot-com bubble peak, and this trend was not interrupted by the financial crisis. Despite a modest price war emerging in US telecom, the key proof point — rising spectrum prices globally — remains intact. The team has become more nuanced about what constitutes usable spectrum and more selective about which carriers to own as a result.
quote: The simple version of the thesis was that (a) wireless traffic was growing at a vast rate and that - due to the endless inventiveness of app and content makers not likely to slow and (b) spectrum was a fundamentally limited resource... The price of usable spectrum has risen pretty well everywhere globally and continues to rise. We have - as our technical understanding improved - become very much more nuanced about what constitutes usable spectrum. As we have become more nuanced we have become more selective about what phone companies to own.

headline: High conviction long: superior spectrum position gives cost advantages that should compound for a decade or more, with starting yield in the 4s and PE in the low teens
reasoning: Verizon's spectrum holdings allow it to avoid the capital expenditure of building additional towers, giving it structurally lower costs than competitors. As data demand continues to grow, Verizon's superior spectrum position translates into better economics relative to peers. The thesis is that wireless economics improve 3–5% or more per annum for a very long time, and that the price of usable spectrum in negotiated transactions continues to rise globally. Starting yield in the 4s and a PE in the low teens is considered cheap for a growth stock with durable superior economics. The firm maintains the position even after revisiting the thesis under their broken-thesis rule, as they would repurchase it at current prices anyway.
quote: Superior economics for a decade or more makes for a very attractive business. Hence the focus on Verizon. The starting yield is in the 4s and the PE is in the low teens. That is cheap for a growth stock with superior economics.

headline: Sceptical despite strong share price appreciation; spectrum disadvantage makes long-term economics unattractive
reasoning: T-Mobile's stock has appreciated sharply and holders appear comfortable, but the firm believes this is likely wrong given the structural disadvantage of T-Mobile's spectrum position relative to Verizon. The stock price performance may be driven by sentiment rather than durable underlying economics. The same poor cost structure logic that applies to Sprint is seen as applying to T-Mobile.
quote: There are plenty of people who are very happy with T-Mobile stock (which has appreciated fairly sharply). They are probably wrong too but the stock price has done the analysis - and they are uniformly fairly comfortable with their position.

headline: Spectrum scarcity thesis remains intact globally — usable spectrum prices rising everywhere — but thesis is more nuanced than originally held; capital can solve congestion but not cost-efficiently
reasoning: The fund's original thesis that spectrum scarcity would give phone companies enormous pricing power remains directionally intact, with usable spectrum prices rising globally. However, the Superbowl experience — where Verizon successfully handled the world's highest density data event using 1,100 towers and 18 months of preparation — showed that capital expenditure can technically solve congestion. The thesis has been updated: it is not that spectrum shortage is an overwhelming constraint, but rather that solving the problem cost-efficiently at scale is very hard, preserving pricing power but making the thesis less extreme. Additionally, the fund has become much more nuanced about what constitutes 'usable' spectrum as technical understanding has improved.
quote: The price of usable spectrum has risen pretty well everywhere globally and continues to rise. We have - as our technical understanding improved - become very much more nuanced about what constitutes usable spectrum... The thesis change was that we once believed Randall Stevenson when he said (as at that Milken conference) that it was going to be impossible to roll out enough towers to meet demand and that spectrum shortage was overwhelming. It was now just not possible to use capital effectively to solve the problem. It was still a good thesis - just not as good for Verizon as an overwhelming constraint.

headline: Exited position; broken-thesis rule triggered after original investment rationale no longer held
reasoning: AT&T was exited alongside Sprint under the firm's broken-thesis rule, which mandates selling when the original reason for purchasing is no longer valid. The broken-thesis rule dictates that if we bought something because of (a) and (a) turns out not be true we should throw it. If we want to buy it again we should do so on a new stated thesis. As described above we have exited AT&T and Sprint and our Clearwire position was a forced, but attractive, exit as well.

headline: One of three longs that did brilliantly in 2013, no updated stance provided this letter
reasoning: Herbalife is cited as one of the three long positions that drove strong performance in 2013, alongside Senomyx and Softbank. headline: Exited entirely; would be short versus Verizon on weaker relative spectrum positioning
reasoning: AT&T was previously the largest holding in the portfolio but was sold entirely after the spectrum analysis revealed it held significantly less spectrum than Verizon at comparable valuations. The fund views AT&T as the inferior relative value play in US telecom. AT&T's decision to ignore Globalstar's spectrum also raised questions about what insiders knew about spectrum quality. quote: If we were pairs traders (we are not) we would be short AT&T against Verizon mainly on relative spectrum positioning. Please understand how big a change in thinking this was. At one stage AT&T was the biggest stock in the portfolio. It has been entirely removed in favour of something we think is better.

headline: US spectrum is in its last low-frequency auction cycle in our lifetime; 30 MHz reserved for non-AT&T/Verizon carriers could reshape competitive dynamics if Sprint wins
reasoning: The upcoming 2015 US spectrum auction is described as likely the last of its kind for low-frequency spectrum in the speakers' lifetimes. Thirty MHz has been reserved specifically for carriers other than AT&T and Verizon, creating a potential inflection point for Sprint's competitive position. If Sprint acquires this spectrum, it would gain the high-value low-frequency component needed to make its large holdings of low-value high-frequency spectrum (from Clearwire) commercially viable in urban infill. This would make Sprint a valid and potentially serious competitor to Verizon, representing a key risk to the Verizon thesis.
quote: There is one last auction in the US of low-frequency spectrum. As the blog post makes clear it is probably the last such auction in our lifetime - and 30 MHZ is reserved for carriers who are not AT&T or Verizon. If Sprint buys that spectrum it will become a valid (and potentially nasty) competitor.

headline: Originally favoured over Verizon but since de-emphasised following detailed spectrum analysis; Randall Stephenson's aggressive spectrum acquisition strategy was the original thesis anchor
reasoning: AT&T was originally the preferred carrier holding, influenced by CEO Randall Stephenson's presentation at the Milken Institute about network congestion and the impossibility of meeting future demand without additional spectrum. AT&T's $100 billion in capex over five years and acquisitions like Leap Wireless (characterised as a pure spectrum deal) at above-historic prices underpinned the thesis. However, after a detailed comparison of spectrum holdings across carriers, the team shifted preference to Verizon. AT&T's proactive price increases were initially seen as a positive but the stock was ultimately de-emphasised.
quote: The first big change in our stock choice was that we originally favoured AT&T (AT&T were more directly raising prices and we thought that Randall Stephenson was a pretty good guy). However this changed after we compiled a large spreadsheet with the spectrum holdings of various phone companies... Randall Stephenson went on to say that with the amount of demand that they see coming they thought that there was no conceivable and capital efficient way that they could build for that demand and that there was no technical solution on the horizon.

headline: Core long position, now the most favoured carrier in the portfolio after detailed spectrum analysis, though conviction has moderated on the price war
reasoning: Verizon was until recently the single largest position in the portfolio and remains the preferred carrier holding. The team shifted focus toward Verizon from AT&T after compiling a detailed spreadsheet of spectrum holdings by company and region, finding Verizon's spectrum position superior. While Verizon has been forced to compete more aggressively on price in the past month (offering more data on family plans), management's capital discipline and spectrum holdings support the thesis. The broader wireless thesis — that carriers with strong spectrum would gain pricing power — remains intact for Verizon despite the price war.
quote: Verizon was until recently the biggest single position in the portfolio (a status it lost only because another position has outperformed it)... However on the key proof of thesis there has been nothing that has indicated we are long-term wrong. The price of usable spectrum has risen pretty well everywhere globally and continues to rise. We have - as our technical understanding improved - become very much more nuanced about what constitutes usable spectrum. As we have become more nuanced we have become more selective about what phone companies to own - and to a surprising extent we have focussed on Verizon as the right stock to own.

headline: Sceptical of promotional spectrum claims; AT&T's decision to ignore its spectrum is a red flag
reasoning: Globalstar is cited as an example of promotional stocks that claim to hold valuable spectrum and therefore warrant large valuations. The fund notes that AT&T, which has never been shy of paying up for spectrum, chose to ignore Globalstar's claimed spectrum assets entirely — suggesting that knowledgeable industry participants did not view the spectrum as genuinely usable or valuable. This raised a flag that something was amiss with such claims.
quote: Moreover very promotional stocks (the example of this month is Globalstar) claimed to have spectrum and be worth huge valuations. And AT&T who never seemed to be shy of paying up for spectrum ignored them. Something was amiss. This required a really deep think about spectrum, how it works and why it is valuable.

headline: Was a profitable long despite being wrong on the fundamentals; economics have barely improved and cash generation guidance has repeatedly failed to materialise, costing the CEO his job
reasoning: Sprint was originally purchased as a spectrum-rich but nearly bankrupt company, with its debt yielding 15%, implying near-certain bankruptcy in the debt markets. The stock was a winner despite the fundamentals not improving as expected. Sprint remains cash consumptive after what appears to be compulsory capital spending, and despite guidance for cash generation, this has never materialised — a failure that cost the CEO his job. The team acknowledges being wrong on Sprint's fundamental economics even while making money on the position.
quote: Both Sprint and T-Mobile are cash consumptive after what looks to be compulsory capital spending and whilst T-Mobile is guiding for cash generation we will believe it when we see it. Sprint were guiding for cash generation too - it just never happened and it cost the CEO his job.

headline: Exited after concluding the business economics are structurally impaired by a poor spectrum position, despite previously making good money on the trade
reasoning: Sprint's spectrum position is characterised as low-value, which saddles it with a cost structure that is uncompetitive relative to Verizon. The firm acknowledges making good money owning Sprint and Clearwire but concedes they were likely wrong about the underlying business quality. The broken-thesis rule triggered the exit: the original thesis no longer held. Sprint does hold a large amount of low-value spectrum from Clearwire that may eventually provide urban infill value, but only if combined with high-value low-frequency spectrum from a future auction.
quote: By contrast with Verizon, a company with a bad spectrum position will have a cost structure that - well frankly - sucks. It will be competed away. That is why the economics of Sprint (or for that matter T-Mobile) simply sucks. They are not getting any better and they probably don't get any better. We made a very good money owning Sprint and Clearwire - but we were probably actually wrong about the business.

headline: Was a giant winner driven in part by Alibaba, which was originally valued at $20–30 billion; originally bought as a spectrum-rich wireless carrier
reasoning: Softbank was originally purchased as part of the wireless carrier thesis as a spectrum-rich Japanese carrier. It turned out to be a giant winner, driven substantially by its Alibaba stake — a source of upside the team acknowledges was partly luck, as their original Alibaba valuation was only $20–30 billion. quote: This was why we originally invested in Softbank - and our original valuation of Alibaba was $20-$30 billion... All of these stocks were winners - and Softbank was a giant winner in part driven by Alibaba (for which we were somewhat lucky).

headline: Concession that the price war in US telecom went further than expected and that marginal carrier economics have barely improved despite making money on the longs
reasoning: The team acknowledges being wrong on the fundamental economics of Sprint, Clearwire and T-Mobile even while making money on these positions. A price war in US telecom was not anticipated; Verizon was not expected to need to compete as aggressively as it has. Despite these missteps, the team characterises the price war as mostly cosmetic thus far and points to continued global spectrum price appreciation as confirmation the long-term thesis remains intact. quote: However, and strangely we think, we were wrong on all these companies on which we made good money. The economics of marginal phone companies have barely improved. Both Sprint and T-Mobile are cash consumptive after what looks to be compulsory capital spending... We also did not expect a price war in US telecom. There is one. It is very minor (there are more cosmetic price cuts than real ones) but still Verizon reacted by offering substantially more data on their family plan... This part of the thesis is looking pretty frayed. However on the key proof of thesis there has been nothing that has indicated we are long-term wrong.

conviction: not short due to borrow cost (36% annually)

headline: Believe we are in the blow-off phase of a bull market — quality-minus-junk underperforming as junk melts up, consistent with late-stage dot-com-era dynamics
reasoning: Bronte draws on AQR's Asness quality-minus-junk research showing long-term outperformance in all 24 surveyed countries, but noting the strategy underperforms most sharply during the melt-up phase of a bull market. The underperformance in the blow-off period was damaging if you were not focused on risk control. Not everyone has focussed on risk control though - and we are watching our competitors in (particularly short-sellers) exit the business with alarming frequency. When this is over competition should be low and we might make a lot of money.

headline: Reduced net exposure because good shorts (junk promotions) are abundant but quality longs are scarce — year-to-date low net has not been profitable despite being the rational stance

headline: Actively shorting the most aggressive fads and promotions available, long high-quality large-cap names — quality-minus-junk strategy underperforming in current blow-off but expected to recover sharply

headline: Significant long exposure to German consumer and industrial businesses hurt by the Ukraine conflict and weaker economic data, with German markets down ~20% from highs

headline: Long/short portfolio with net ~80% exposure and sub-0.5 beta; longs are deep-value at 1.38x book and 13x PE while shorts are high-multiple momentum/fraud names at 2.67x book and 23x PE, accepting an imperfect hedge in exchange for alpha from both legs

headline: Large long position at a very low PE, contributing to the portfolio's depressed overall earnings multiple

headline: Rare high-dividend-paying growth stock in an expensive market with more pricing power than consensus assumes; low price-to-book and modest PE despite being viewed as a utility
reasoning: The managers view Verizon as a mispriced growth stock rather than a utility or defensive 'grandma stock'. It sits in the long portfolio at a time when that book trades at only 1.38x price-to-book and 13x trailing PE, though the overall portfolio metrics are also dragged by other low-PE positions. Some might view it as a utility or grandma stock but we see it as a rare high dividend paying growth stock in an expensive market and we think, with good reasons, that it has much more pricing power than the market gives it credit for.

headline: Shorts focused on frauds, fads and promotions — particularly opaque high-PE businesses in biotech, remote geographies, or legally tenuous foreign jurisdictions such as China reverse-merger companies
reasoning: The short book is deliberately constructed to target companies operating in fields where opacity makes analysis difficult: biotech, remote locations, and legally or politically tenuous foreign jurisdictions. China reverse-merger companies that listed on US markets are cited as a typical example. The primary goal is to generate alpha from the short book in its own right, with the hedge benefit treated as a secondary gain.
