Hope and dreams keep these stocks alive and often times they are exceedingly (and purposely) difficult to analyse because they operate in opaque fields of new technology (e.g, biotech), or in remote locations, or in legally and politically tenuous foreign jurisdictions (the China reverse merger company's that blossomed on US stock markets are typical). Price to book at 2.67x and price to earnings of 23x on our short portfolio are both roughly twice that of the longs.

headline: Short iron ore mining names on financing concerns; Ebola outbreak in West Africa provided unexpected near-term gains but was not the original thesis
reasoning: The fund holds a small short position in the iron ore mining industry. The original investment thesis was based on financing vulnerabilities within these businesses, not any geopolitical or disease-related catalyst. The Ebola outbreak on the West Coast of Africa caused localised economic disruption that delivered modest gains on the short ahead of schedule. The managers note this was fortuitous rather than by design and state they take no pride in profiting from a virulent disease. The short book had been painful for 18 months prior, making any gain notable.
quote: We have a small short exposure here to the iron ore mining industry. This short was never based on such a 'black swan' occurrence. Our analysis suggests the circumstances of the businesses would have given rise to financing problems – but a virulent disease provided some modest immediate gains. We take no pride in that. Still - after a torrid 18 months in which shorts have provided nothing but pain - we were pleased to get one right even if it was for the wrong reasons.

headline: Index-like long-only equity portfolios unlikely to generate great long-term returns from current starting valuations — most European longs appear ~30% expensive
reasoning: After visiting numerous European companies, the fund found almost everything on the long side appearing roughly 30% expensive. While not disastrous for a decade-long investment, it is hardly encouraging. They conclude that portfolios built purely with index-like long stock positions — which describes most investors' portfolios — are unlikely to provide great long-term returns from current levels.
quote: Almost everything we saw (on the long side) seemed 30 percent expensive – not diabolical for a decade long investment – but hardly encouraging... We think that portfolios that are built purely with index like long stock positions – that is most peoples' portfolios – are unlikely to provide great long term returns from where we sit today.

headline: Sector faces falling sales or margin compression as modern trade retailers gain pricing power over large FMCG suppliers — bullish era for Reckitt Benckiser and P&G may be ending
reasoning: The fund's conversations with Casino (a giant French retail and property chain) revealed that retailer pricing power over fat-margin FMCG suppliers has increased markedly over the past three to four years, reversing what had been supplier dominance. If this trend continues, almost all giant consumer goods companies face either falling sales, falling margins, or both. The fund views this as a structural risk to the long-running outperformance of names like Reckitt Benckiser and P&G. This risk applies broadly across the sector and reinforces their cautious stance on European consumer staples longs.
quote: Casino – a giant French retail and property chain – told us about their new-found ability to pressure their fatter-margin suppliers. They thought that three or four years ago the power lay with the P&Gs of this world – but less so now. If that is true then almost all of the giant consumer good companies will suffer either falling sales, falling margins or both – and the great march upward of Reckitt Benckiser and P&G stock will end.

headline: Short exposure maintained despite widespread pain; fraudulent/low-quality stocks feel toppy but have kept rallying — remaining short while consensus cuts exposure
reasoning: The fund notes that hedge fund short exposure has shrunk to its lowest level since the financial crisis, and they understand why: being short in this market produces significant pain. Despite this, they are maintaining short exposure while others cut. Stocks they regard as fraudulent are reaching market caps in the half-billion to multi-billion dollar range. They acknowledge it has felt toppy for a while yet some of these names have added 50% regardless. Their conviction comes from the view that eventually shorts will pay off through exposure of frauds, similar to Gowex.
quote: This is a market where stock-frauds no more robust than the average penny-stock mailer wind up with market caps in the half-billion dollar range. Some wind up with multi-billion dollar market caps. The exposure of Gowex (a Spanish WiFi provider) by Gotham Research demonstrates that some stock market stars are grotesque frauds. The dross feels very toppy. Contra: it has felt toppy for a while – and then added fifty percent. Despite this, we have maintained our short exposure as everyone else is cutting theirs.

headline: Long book no longer inspiring as market has risen; short book pregnant with profit but hedge fund retreat from shorting means losses drag while waiting for the turn
reasoning: The fund's long book is described as looking okay but no longer filling the managers with joy at current market levels. There are select longs like Rolls Royce with significant upside potential but meaningful risk attached, and very few situations where good returns appear locked in. The short book is described as 'pregnant with profit' and made more attractive by the retreat of other hedge funds from short-selling, but shorting has been a painful strategy for long enough that it is causing losses in the interim. The fund expects modest fluctuations while waiting for the market to turn in their favour, and expresses confidence in ultimately making money but uncertainty about timing.
quote: Our long book looks okay but, as the market has risen, it no longer fills us with joy. There are some things like Rolls Royce on which we could make a lot of money – but they have some risk. There are very few things where we think good returns are a lock. Our short book is pregnant with profit – a situation made more delicious by the retreat of hedge funds from shorting. But shorting has been a bad game for long enough now that it is hurting. We think we will make you money shorting – lots of money. But we need good long exposure to offset the losses whilst we wait – and they are difficult to find.

headline: Higher margins than Unilever at 19.6% but priced at 2.9x sales; faces same structural risk from retailer pricing power shift
reasoning: Procter & Gamble was discussed as a comparator to Unilever, with superior margins of 19.6% versus Unilever's sub-15%, but priced at a premium of 2.9x sales. They thought that three or four years ago the power lay with the P&Gs of this world – but less so now. If that is true then almost all of the giant consumer good companies will suffer either falling sales, falling margins or both – and the great march upward of Reckitt Benckiser and P&G stock will end.

headline: Surprisingly interesting at 1.1x sales on 7% EBIT margin — half-million employees with integrated logistics creating durable competitive advantage earning double typical outsourcing margins
reasoning: Compass Group was an unplanned meeting that turned out to be one of the two most interesting companies seen on the European trip. With over half a million employees and deep integration with quality logistics companies in every market, it earns roughly double the low single-digit margins typical of large simple-service outsourcing businesses. Priced at 1.1x sales with a 7% EBIT margin, the fund found the business model more defensible and interesting than expected. The valuation looks more reasonable than most European long candidates reviewed on the trip.
quote: They were: (a) Compass Group PLC – a global provider of food service at universities, hospitals, airport lounges, businesses, oil platforms and the like... Compass Group is vast. It has over half a million employees and has integrated itself with quality logistics companies in every market. Most vast-employee number companies doing simple things (e.g. laundry service outsourcing for hospitals and hotels) have low single digit margins and are ruthlessly competitive. Compass earns roughly double them.

headline: General Electric dominates the best wide-body franchise (Boeing 777) while Rolls has failed to attach to a truly great jet for a long time
reasoning: The Boeing 777 is described by a long-haul pilot contact as the best aircraft in the sky — roughly 60 tonnes less fuel burned across the Pacific than an A380. General Electric, whose engine business is described as very profitable, is the main provider to the 777. This gives GE the dominant position in the highest-utilisation, most fuel-efficient wide-body route, while Rolls Royce has been left attached to fuel-inefficient or commercially unsuccessful platforms (A340, A380). The read-through is that GE's engine division is structurally advantaged relative to Rolls in the current wide-body environment.
quote: Our pilot is pretty sure that the 777 will remain the best 'bird in the sky' for a long time. General Electric (whose engine business is very profitable) is the main provider to the 777. And therein lies the problem with Rolls - it has not attached its engines to a truly great jet in a very long time.

headline: Roughly 30% expensive at 20x unlevered earnings on 14.5% pre-tax margins; margin expansion optionality exists but risks from modern trade shift and retailer pricing power limit appeal
reasoning: Unilever was used as a typical example of European longs that appear roughly 30% expensive. At 2.1x sales with a sub-15% EBIT margin, the unlevered PE works out to just over 20x — which the fund considers 30% expensive for a long-term hold. Management is targeting margin improvement but progress has been slow. A key risk is the shift from 'traditional trade' (small street shops in emerging markets) to 'modern trade' (large chains with logistics scale and pricing power), which could compress margins across the whole FMCG sector. Additionally, Casino told the fund that retailer pricing power over fat-margin FMCG suppliers has increased significantly in recent years.
quote: $100 in sales represents $210 in market capitalization and $14.50 in pre-tax profits. At a 28 percent tax rate that $14.50 in pre-tax profits winds up as $10.44 in post-tax earnings. Against $210 in market capitalization that gives an unlevered PE ratio of just over 20 times. Twenty times earnings feels 30 percent expensive to us (at least versus a price where you stick the stock in the bottom drawer to hold forever). It certainly doesn't meet the Warren Buffett 'punch card' test.

headline: Exposed as a grotesque fraud by Gotham Research — cited as archetypal example of the fraudulent stocks reaching enormous market caps in this environment
reasoning: Gowex, a Spanish WiFi provider, was cited as a real-world example of market stars that turn out to be grotesque frauds. The exposure by Gotham Research illustrates the fund's thesis that many high-market-cap stocks in the current environment are fundamentally fraudulent. This validates their rationale for maintaining short positions in similar names.

conviction: small position, could become more substantial or could sell entire holding
headline: Bull case hinges entirely on A350 commercial delivery and fuel efficiency; sales and margins could double if validated, but the holding is conditional on proof
reasoning: Rolls Royce currently operates at an anemic ~8% EBIT margin and trades at 1.2x sales. The business has ceded the narrow-body regional jet market, which carries high take-off/landing cycles and fat maintenance revenue, retreating to wide-body planes with structurally lower margins. The legacy fleet is shifting toward lower-margin product as noted by Sanford Bernstein's bear case. The bull case rests entirely on the Airbus A350, for which Rolls is the sole engine provider with over 800 forward orders — if delivered and with adequately priced maintenance contracts, the slogan is 'sales double, margins double and a half.' However, all prior planes (A380, A340) looked great on paper too; real-world fuel efficiency and safety performance of the A350 is still unproven, and if it underperforms the order book could evaporate. The position will either be built up substantially or sold depending on thesis validation.
quote: Depending on validation of our thesis it could become a more substantial position or we could sell the entire holding... Our slogan: sales double, margins double and a half. This could be a very good stock indeed. But the bull case is on paper. The proof will be in safety (critical) and fuel consumption (also critical) of the A350. All planes are great planes on paper. The A380 was a great plane on paper. Even the infamous A340 was a great plane on paper.

headline: Priced fairly but not cheap; food's emotional pricing power drives superior margins vs other outsourced services, and the prison exit validates the thesis
reasoning: Compass Group operates at roughly 7% EBIT margin and trades at 1.1x sales, which appears similar to Rolls Royce on a price/sales basis but is actually a differentiated business. The key insight is that food service generates emotional pricing power that simple outsourced services like laundry or cleaning cannot command — clients such as Google and the University of Pennsylvania will not quibble over a 3-5% price increment if the food is good. Compass exited prison food service precisely because that emotional lever does not work in that environment, validating the thesis. Management believes margins can expand further, and Bronte does not disbelieve that, but the current valuation already prices in continuation of this advantage. The fund's conclusion is you could own it but it is not cheap, and the broader lesson is that genuine quality economics can be found in unexpected places.
quote: Compass say they can increase their margin even further. We don't disbelieve them (this trick looks awfully powerful) but the pricing of the stock requires a continuation. You could probably own this company but it is not cheap. For us, the lesson of Compass Group is that you can find genuine quality companies with superior economics in places you don't expect it.

headline: Best-in-class FMCG margins at 26% with a strong history of expansion from 16% a decade ago, but priced at 3.8x sales; structural retailer pricing power risk threatens further re-rating
reasoning: Reckitt Benckiser was highlighted as the best-margin FMCG player in the peer group at 26%, having expanded from 16% about twelve years ago, and is priced at the highest multiple of 3.8x sales. While this margin history is impressive, the fund flagged the same structural concern as for Unilever and P&G — that modern trade retailers are gaining pricing power over FMCG suppliers and the long march upward in Reckitt's stock may be ending.

headline: Long thesis on US mobile carrier revenue per user under review after Superbowl demonstrated 70,000-person dense-network coverage using ~1,000 hidden towers — if scalable cheaply, the capacity-scarcity pricing thesis fails

This thesis was challenged by the Superbowl, which demonstrated that roughly 1,000 transmitters hidden in an open arena could serve 70,000 high-usage people with decent coverage, suggesting the signal-noise scaling problem may be solvable. The team is actively investigating whether this dense-transmitter solution can be deployed cheaply and efficiently in urban streets.
quote: We have one largish potential shift in the long book. We are committed (intellectually and financially) to the view that average revenue per user for cell phones in the US and other high use markets (Seoul, Istanbul and other markets) will be considerably higher in five years. This thesis is dependent on the technical problems of scaling up data capacity indefinitely. We figure if the carriers cannot raise the capacity they will have to raise prices. Rising prices (or even mildly falling prices) will, given the massive increase in demand, be a very big win for the carriers. The thesis was challenged by of all things the Superbowl. In an Australian football stadium your cell phone simply does not work with 70 thousand people in the stadium. There is not enough network capacity. The Superbowl (sponsored by Verizon) demonstrated that 70 thousand high use people could be accommodated in an open arena and could still get decent coverage. There were roughly 1000 towers hidden in that arena and these were often not small transmitters. The signal-noise ratio issues seems to have been solved with enormous numbers of transmitters. If this solution can be taken cheaply and efficiently to the streets of Seoul and New York then our thesis is wrong.
